simpleEn: During the Korean War, the 40 Steps were where displaced refugees scraped together a living and waited to be reunited with family members they had lost track of. The railway-track and sea-route sculptures along the street recall the memory of Busan Station and the port, where people and relief goods once passed through. Stand at the top of the steps and look toward the harbor. The short staircase of today overlaps with the daily lives of people who kept going even in the middle of war.
detailEn:
Today the 40 Steps look like a short staircase with sculptures in a tourist street of the old downtown, but during the Korean War this was one of the places where refugee life was at its most intense. As huge numbers of refugees poured into Busan, relief supplies and everyday goods arrived in the Jungang-dong and Busan port area, and people bought and sold things here to get through each day. For those separated from family during the war, it was also a meeting point where they waited, hoping to see each other again. So the 40 Steps back then were not simply a passageway — they were a marketplace, a meeting place, and a center of life for people trying to start over.
Walking the street today, you'll see spaces and sculptures named things like "Railway Path," "Sea Path," and "Gate of Peace." These aren't just decorations meant to evoke an old-fashioned mood. The Railway Path recalls Busan Station and the railroad that once stood nearby, while the Sea Path evokes Busan Port, through which refugees and relief goods arrived. In particular, the lantern depicted at the Gate of Peace is a device linking the hope for life that never went out, even amid the hardships of war and displacement, to the image of peace. Once you know this meaning, the whole street begins to look like an open-air exhibition of everyday history.
How familiar the 40 Steps were to people at the time can also be confirmed through popular songs. The 40 Steps appear even in Park Jae-hong's "Gyeongsang-do Agassi," released in the 1950s, showing how deeply the place was woven into daily life in Busan, the wartime capital. Refugees living on the surrounding hillside roads climbed up and down the hill every day to work at the port and market, and the 40 Steps were part of that daily route. If you look from the top of the steps down toward Jungang-dong and Busan Port, you can imagine that although buildings stand there now, people and goods once poured in endlessly in that direction.
So rather than just counting the steps or looking at the sculptures, it's worth thinking about "who climbed these steps, and why." Once you know this, the 40 Steps stop looking like a retro street recreating old Busan, and instead appear as a site of everyday history in Busan's old downtown, layered with the days of people who had to search for family, do business, and simply survive in the middle of a war.
tipsEn:
Route: Look at the steps and sculptures around the 40 Steps Memorial Hall, then continue walking up into the alley above.
Photo spot: Frame the shot from below so the steps and sculptures appear together.
Caution: If using the stairs is difficult, check the alternate route around the area first.

simpleEn: Seongjigok Reservoir, at the heart of Busan Children's Park, was once an important city facility that supplied drinking water to Busan's citizens. Even the waterside, which looks like a natural lake, still bears traces of the dams and waterways once built and maintained here. Over time, this space for protecting water changed into a wooded trail and a family outing spot. Looking at the lake and the old forest together, you can encounter both Busan's growth and generations of picnic memories.
detailEn:
At the center of Busan Children's Park lies Seongjigok Reservoir. It is best known as a family outing spot, but this water was once essential infrastructure for the growth of Busan as a modern city. In the early 20th century, as Busan's population grew and the port city rapidly expanded, a stable supply of drinking water became necessary, and the reservoir was created by damming the Seongjigok valley. Knowing that the path you now walk through forest and past the lake was once "a facility that sent water to the city" changes the way the scenery looks.

Around the reservoir, it looks as smooth as a natural lake, but the shape of the dam and waterways still shows traces of people gathering and managing water. Back then, water from here was supplied to the city through pipes, and until newer water-supply facilities like Myeongjang Water Purification Plant were established, this served as an important water source for Busan. So Seongjigok Reservoir is less a simple mountain reservoir and more a piece of infrastructure heritage showing how a city once concentrated around the port grew inland.

What's interesting is that today's image of Children's Park is completely different from the character of the old reservoir. Once a managed space where water quality had to be protected, it later changed into an open resting space for citizens as forest trails, walking paths, and children's facilities were built. This place feels familiar to Busan residents not because of any single attraction, but because generations of memories — picnicking, exercising, spending time with family against the backdrop of Seongjigok's forest and water — have accumulated here.

As you walk, look at the waterside, the old forest, and the location of the dam together, rather than just following the children's facilities. It matters that such a large forest and reservoir remain so close to the heart of the city. Once you understand this shift — from a water facility that powered the industrial city of Busan to today's green space for citizens — Children's Park stops being just "a park to bring kids to" and starts to look like a place holding Busan's urban growth and the memory of everyday life.
tipsEn:
Route: From the main gate, walk the loop trail around the reservoir, then continue on to whichever children's facilities interest you.
Photo spot: The walking trail where the reservoir's waterway and forest appear together works well.
Caution: Check the operating hours and closed days of the children's facilities before your visit.

simpleEn: On the hill next to Bokcheon Museum lies the Bokcheon-dong Tumuli, the burial mounds of ancient Busan's people. The armor, helmets, and horse gear excavated here are traces of people who traded and built power through iron. After the exhibition, step out to the tumuli park. Reading the layout of the large mound on the hill and the smaller mounds around it reveals the power and daily life of that era, letting you encounter the ancient city hidden beneath today's Dongnae.
detailEn:
Bokcheon Museum is far more interesting if, before looking at the artifacts, you first ask "why is there a museum on this hill?" Right next to the museum, the Bokcheon-dong Tumuli is a cluster of tombs built between the 2nd and 7th centuries on a ridge extending from Maansan Mountain in Dongnae. Excavations conducted repeatedly since 1969 have uncovered over 190 tombs and more than 10,000 artifacts, including pottery and ironware, revealing an ancient Busan we knew little about. It showed that Busan was not simply a remote coastal area, but a place with a power that traded in and built strength through iron.

In the exhibition hall, pay special attention to the armor, helmets, iron weapons, and horse gear. The Bokcheon-dong Tumuli yielded a large quantity of artifacts showing Gaya's advanced iron culture. By following the period when tomb sizes and burial goods grew larger and more elaborate, you can trace how the power of the ruling class in this area grew. It's also fascinating that while both Silla and Geumgwan Gaya cultures appear together, the Dongnae area of Busan still shows its own distinct characteristics. As Silla's power later expanded, the gradual absorption of this region's culture into the Silla sphere can also be traced through changes in the artifacts.

After viewing the museum, step outside to the tumuli park and the story from the exhibition hall connects with the actual terrain. Notice how large tombs sit at the top of the ridge, while small and medium-sized tombs are located on the slopes and surrounding area. Placing large tombs in high places was not simply a burial custom — it was also the hierarchy of power at the time expressed on the land. The outdoor exhibition hall also lets you examine the shape of the tomb interiors as excavated, so the artifacts stop feeling like items in a display case.

So the core of Bokcheon Museum isn't that it's "a place to see a lot of Gaya artifacts." What matters is that it proves an ancient political power, trade network, and people with iron technology once lived beneath what is now downtown Busan. Looking down over the Dongnae city center while viewing both the tumuli and the present-day residential area together, the most striking realization is that the same hill has remained a central space for people for over 1,500 years.
tipsEn:
Route: View the permanent exhibition first, then move to the outdoor tumuli — the structure of the site is easier to understand that way.
Photo spot: From behind the museum, frame the tumuli together with the Dongnae city center.
Caution: Check on-site whether photography is allowed in the exhibition hall and the schedule for any special exhibitions.

simpleEn: The National Science Museum of Busan lets you directly experience the principles behind how cars move, ships float, and energy is generated. The exhibition themes connect to Busan and the southeastern region's development in automobiles, shipbuilding, and machinery. As you operate the exhibits, try changing the conditions little by little. Following the moment the results change brings the science that powers the harbor's massive ships and the city's traffic closer to everyday life.
detailEn:
The exhibits at the National Science Museum of Busan make more sense once you ask, "why was a science museum with this theme built in Busan?" Busan and the southeastern region are places where science and technology actually operate on industrial sites — automobiles, shipbuilding and marine engineering, machinery, and energy. So rather than simply presenting scientific formulas, this museum leans toward exhibits you can directly operate and experience — how cars move, how ships float, how energy is generated. Even the devices that look like children's exhibits are, in a sense, translations of regional industrial technology into everyday language.

When viewing the exhibits, rather than just pressing a button to check the result, try connecting "where in Busan is this principle actually used?" In the automobile exhibits, force, motion, and control technologies connect to parts and production processes; in the aerospace and shipbuilding sections, fluid flow and structural stability connect to the design of real vehicles and vessels. The energy exhibit shows how electricity is generated, transmitted, and made more efficient. Seen this way, the different exhibition halls aren't separate topics — they connect like a map of the scientific principles underpinning the southeastern region's industry.

Busan has long grown as a city built on ports and manufacturing, but the Busan tourists see is dominated far more by images of beaches and markets. The National Science Museum of Busan shows the "technological Busan" behind that image. The massive ships floating in the sea and the port's cranes are, in the end, the result of countless engineering principles gathered together, and the traffic and power that move the city are an extension of the same science. If you're visiting with children, it's better to ask "why does it move this way?" and actually operate the devices, rather than explaining the answer first.

Another thing worth noticing is that the museum is designed to encourage repeated experimentation and failure rather than handing over finished answers. Operating the same device under different conditions produces different results. A local guide would say that Busan's industry, too, wasn't built all at once, but grew as shipbuilding, automotive, and energy technologies accumulated over time. As you leave the museum and look at the new cityscape of eastern Busan, it's worth remembering that behind the play and exhibits lies another identity of Busan as an industrial city.
tipsEn:
Route: Focus on the permanent exhibition hall first, then choose to continue on to the Children's Science Museum or the planetarium.
Photo spot: Capture the large exhibits together with people in the middle of hands-on activities.
Caution: Some experience halls may require separate reservations or tickets.

simpleEn: Bosu-dong Book Street preserves the time of people who kept learning even during war. The everyday market where refugees and students once sought used textbooks and secondhand books has carried on into today's alley. The books stacked near the ceiling and the memories of the bookshop owners are this place's own shelving and search system. Open an old book and look inside — in someone's underlined passages and notes, you can find traces of how study and daily life continued in Busan.
detailEn:
The charm of Bosu-dong Book Street isn't fully captured by describing it simply as "a street that sells old books." This alley is closely tied to the market culture that began in the daily life of Busan as the wartime capital during the Korean War. For the refugees and students who poured into Busan because of the war, books were hard to buy new, so a trade naturally formed in used textbooks, reference books, magazines, and secondhand books. For children who had to resume their studies once schools reopened, this alley was less an ordinary shopping street and more a practical, everyday market for obtaining the books needed for learning.

Inside the alley, the bookshops aren't spacious like large bookstores — instead, you'll find books stacked nearly to the ceiling in narrow spaces. This very arrangement is Bosu-dong's history. For a long time, the practice was to store as many books as possible in a limited space, with the shop owner locating the exact shelf when a customer named a title. The bookshop owner's memory functioned as a kind of search system. The mix of old reference books next to literature, specialized texts, and out-of-print magazines is another reason these shops differ from ordinary bookstores.

Bosu-dong sits at the heart of the old downtown's daily routes, close to Gukje Market, Bupyeong Market, and Gwangbok-dong. As people shopped at the market, students sought books, and printing and publishing-related businesses gathered nearby, the character of the alley took shape. So looking at the signs, the stairs, and the bundles of books together reveals not just a "retro atmosphere," but the shape of a living economy in which postwar Busan residents bought and sold what they needed to rebuild the city.

These days, the number of used bookstores has declined because of online bookstores and e-books, but the experience of pulling out a single book in Bosu-dong is still special. Even the same title looks different depending on who read it — the notes, underlines, and worn cover carry a piece of someone's time. A local guide would tell you to look at the old book spines before taking a pretty photo. Those books are the smallest everyday artifacts showing how learning and culture carried on in the refugee city of Busan.
tipsEn:
Route: Walk slowly up from the entrance of the alley, viewing the bookshop displays and stepped alleys in turn.
Photo spot: Capture the shelves stacked layer upon layer with books together with the alley steps.
Caution: Ask the shop for permission before opening books or taking photographs.

simpleEn: The steps and retaining walls of Biseok Culture Village hold the desperate time when refugees built a foothold for life. On the hillside that once held a Japanese cemetery, people building homes used the stones from gravestones and burial markers in place of scarce building materials. Look closely at the lettering left on the stones in the alley and the layered rooftops. Still home to residents today, this is a site of Busan's modern history, where traces of colonization and war have turned into an everyday living space.
detailEn:
Biseok Culture Village (literally "Tombstone Village") has an unfamiliar name at first, but once you know its meaning, not even a single stone in the alley looks ordinary. During the Japanese colonial period, there was a Japanese cemetery in the Ami-dong area, and after liberation and through the Korean War, refugees pouring into Busan settled on this hillside to make a home. In an era of severe material shortages, tombstones and offering tables from the cemetery were reused as steps, retaining walls, and foundation and wall material for houses — traces of which still remain in some places today. So the name "Tombstone Village" isn't a nickname invented for tourism; it points to a history of repurposing space and materials given for survival.

When you spot a stone in the alley bearing traces of Chinese characters or lettering, consider that it may originally have been a gravestone marking someone's tomb. The fact that houses were built over a cemetery may feel uncomfortable, but that very discomfort is at the heart of this place's history. With almost no other options, refugees had to turn a steep hillside and even an existing cemetery into a place to live. The reason hillside villages formed along Busan's mountainside roads is connected to this same shortage of flat land in the city.

If you expect this village to be a flashy photo spot like Gamcheon Culture Village, you may miss what actually matters here. The old stairs, the retaining walls beneath the houses, the narrow alley widths, and the way roofs appear to overlap on the slope are themselves traces of life back then. Looking down from higher ground at the old downtown and the port, you can understand why refugees crowded onto hillsides close to the harbor. To find work and do business, they had to go down to the docks and markets, while housing was pushed up onto the hills, where land was cheap and space was available.

What makes Ami-dong's story special is that traces of Japanese colonization, liberation, wartime displacement, and the formation of hillside roads all overlap in one place. So a local guide would tell you to look here not for "a pretty village" but for "layered time." Keeping in mind that this is still a living space for residents today, when you look at the stones and steps of the alley, Biseok Culture Village shows that Busan's modern history remains not as abstract years, but as space actually reshaped by people who had to live.
tipsEn:
Route: Walk along the main road and key alleys of the Ami-dong hillside village, stopping along the way at stairways and viewpoints.

Photo spot: Capture the alley and old residential area together with the old downtown and harbor view of Busan beyond.

Caution: Since this is a village where residents live, avoid loud noise and do not photograph the inside of homes. Many alleys are steep, so comfortable shoes are recommended.

simpleEn: Haeundae Market is an alley where you meet the neighborhood's everyday life right behind the flashy beach. Between small shops selling fish cakes, side dishes, and seafood, tourists and local shoppers walk the same path. The low cooking counters and narrow display stands show the old market's way of life. Walk slowly from the entrance toward the back — within the Haeundae so familiar for its high-rise hotels and beach, you'll find the neighborhood's living face still intact.
detailEn:
Haeundae Market sits right behind the beach, so tourists tend to see it as a food alley, but the real charm lies in how "the front face of a tourist spot" and "the back face of a neighborhood" overlap within a single alley. On the beach side, hotels, cafes, and large commercial facilities change rapidly, but stepping into the market, you find fish cakes, tteokbokki, side dishes, and seafood — items Busan residents buy and eat every day. Haeundae had a resident shopping district before it became a nationally famous tourist destination, and even today, tourists and local residents share the same passageway, which sets it apart from other famous beach commercial areas.

Walking through the market and looking at the signs and display stands, the contrast with Haeundae's flashy skyline outside is stark. Cooking counters are set up right in front of narrow shopfronts, and customers eat standing up — a layout that shows the traditional market's way of using space. Foods like fish cakes and tteokbokki, in particular, carry the character of "quick, unpretentious food" tied to life in a port city. The many raw fish and seafood shops naturally reflect that this is a commercial area close to the sea.

What a local guide might tell you here is that Haeundae wasn't always a high-rise tourist destination like it is now. The sea, the railway, a small village, and a market came first, and only later did the beach become nationally famous and hotels and urban infrastructure multiply, dramatically changing the surrounding scenery. Even through that change, the market has kept its relatively low-key, everyday scenery. So walking just a few minutes in from the beach, you can feel the pace of the city suddenly shift.

Choosing what to eat at the market is enjoyable, but it's also worth watching the flow of people from the entrance to the back at least once. Residents shop for groceries next to tourist menu boards, and new shops open beside old storefronts, all at the same time. Once you notice this, Haeundae Market feels less like a place to consume famous food and more like a small observation window into how the old resident shopping district survives and blends within the massive tourist city of Haeundae.
tipsEn:
Route: Start at the market entrance browsing handheld snacks, then move inward toward the restaurant area.
Photo spot: Capture the signs and food stalls lined up under the arcade.
Caution: Watch out for hot cooking counters and narrow passageways, and inform vendors of any food allergies in advance.

simpleEn: The National Maritime Museum of Korea shows Busan's relationship with the sea through navigation, ships, maritime culture, and marine ecology. The compasses and ship models on display hold the history of the technology and exchange that once carried people and goods across the ocean. After viewing the exhibits, look out at the actual ships from the window or the nearby park. The stories inside the exhibition connect to today's Busan Port, letting you feel how the sea has long been the foundation of the city's jobs and daily life.
detailEn:
The National Maritime Museum of Korea is not simply a place to see ships and fish — it's closer to a single building that unpacks why the city of Busan grew through the sea. Busan Port has long been a gateway through which people, goods, technology, and culture passed, and this museum, which opened in 2012, shows the relationship between the sea and humanity by covering navigation, ships, maritime culture, and ecology together. Its location on the Yeongdo waterfront is itself meaningful — because actual shipping lanes and vessels are visible through the windows, the stories inside the exhibition hall connect directly to the reality of Busan Port outside.

Looking at old navigation instruments or ship models in the exhibition, it's worth considering how many combined fields of knowledge "crossing the sea" once required. Setting a course by stars and compass, reading wind and current, and developing the structure of ships is not simply a history of technology — it is also a history of trade, migration, war, and cultural exchange. Because Busan was a city where such movement repeatedly began and ended, a single maritime artifact connects directly to the city's history.

Another easy-to-miss point is that the museum treats marine ecology and industry within the same space. The sea is both a treasury of resources and an ecosystem that must be protected; ships and ports drive the economy but also affect the marine environment. Viewing the aquarium or biological exhibits and then moving on to the ship and navigation exhibits naturally contrasts "humans using the sea" with "the life of the sea itself." This connection is one of the National Maritime Museum's important messages.

Stepping outside, you'll see Amir Park, the waters of Busan Port, and distant moving ships. A scene that looked like simply a big ship before the exhibition begins to look, after viewing it, like a whole system of routes, logistics, sailors, and technology in motion. A local guide would say here that Busan's sea is not just a backdrop for tourist photos. The reason this museum feels so distinctly Busan is that this very sea has built the jobs, industry, food, migration, and open character of Busan's people.
tipsEn:
Route: Follow the permanent exhibition upstairs, then look around the aquarium and ocean-view spaces.
Photo spot: Capture the curved building together with the sea and the large exhibits.
Caution: Check in advance whether special exhibitions and experience spaces require separate reservations.

simpleEn: The specimens at the Busan Marine Natural History Museum are long-preserved records of marine creatures' forms and structures. Comparing organisms side by side reveals how, even within the same sea, different species adapted to different conditions. Rather than focusing on size or color, take a close look at the shapes of fins and shells. Thinking about why a creature came to look this way makes even the familiar animals you've seen at the beach or the market feel new, as the result of a long ecological history.
detailEn:
It's easy to think of the Busan Marine Natural History Museum as simply "a place with a lot of marine creatures gathered together," but it is actually a natural-history space showing how Busan has observed and classified the sea. Unlike an aquarium, where you see living creatures, the key point of a natural history museum's specimens is that they preserve the form and structure of a single organism long-term so it can be compared with others. Seeing a wide variety of marine specimens together makes it clear that the waters off Busan, so familiar to us, are connected to the entire marine ecosystem of the planet.

In the exhibition halls, it's better to think about "why did this evolve into this shape?" rather than focusing on a creature's size or striking appearance. Even among the same fish, mouth, fin, and body shape differ depending on depth, diet, and mode of movement, and shellfish and crustaceans also differ in structure depending on habitat — sea floor, reef, or sand. Comparing specimens side by side is more enjoyable when you read the results of adaptation to environment rather than just memorizing names. If visiting with children, it's a good method to pick the strangest-looking creature and guess the reason for its shape.

It's also interesting that this museum sits near Geumgang Park and the foot of Geumjeongsan Mountain. Having a space dealing with marine natural history right next to a place where you can experience mountain and terrestrial ecology resembles the geographic character of Busan itself. Busan is a city where mountains come down close to the sea, so forest, stream, estuary, and coastal ecosystems change quickly over short distances. So rather than viewing marine life in isolation, you can recall the connection that water and nutrients flowing from land, ocean currents, and climate all affect marine ecosystems.

Because specimens don't move, they may feel static at first. But look closely, and the environment, food relationships, and mode of movement of a single organism are recorded in its body. A local guide would describe this not as "a place to see stuffed animals" but as "a place to read the records the sea has left behind." After leaving the museum, when you encounter real creatures at Busan's beaches or markets, even a single familiar fish stops looking like mere food and starts looking like the result of a long ecological history — that's the real pleasure of this place.
tipsEn:
Route: Follow the classification order of the permanent exhibition, then go back to look more closely at specimens that caught your interest.
Photo spot: Large marine specimens with distinctive shapes and colors make good subjects.
Caution: Avoid flash photography and touching exhibits to protect the specimens.

simpleEn: The Huinnyeoul Culture Village Coastal Tunnel in Yeongdo reconnects a coastal path once cut off beneath a cliff. Inside the tunnel, your view dims but the sound of the waves and your footsteps grow sharper, and when you reach the exit, the sea opens up all at once. Walk both the alleys of the village above and the coastline below. Beyond the striking view at the exit, so often photographed, you can sense the elevation and terrain that Yeongdo's residents have lived with, caught between steep mountains and the sea.
detailEn:
Yeongdo's Huinnyeoul Coastal Tunnel is less a historic relic and more a relatively recent space that connects a broken coastal path beneath a cliff, creating a new kind of scenery in the process. So the core of this place lies not in the tunnel's length or structure, but in the scene of "the sea suddenly opening after passing through darkness." Coming down from the high alleys of Huinnyeoul Culture Village to the coast, you're close to the everyday scenery of a hillside village; but the moment you enter the tunnel, your view closes off and the sound of waves and footsteps grows louder. That brief darkness makes the sea at the exit look far more striking.

The scene often seen in photos is created by exactly this contrast. Looking from inside the tunnel toward the exit, a person remains a silhouette while the horizon outside looks like a bright, framed rectangle. Though it's an artificial passage, it effectively frames the natural scenery like a picture. A local guide would tell you not to just photograph the exit and turn back, but to compare the different directions of sea and cliff visible from the tunnel entrance and the opposite side. Even the same sea feels completely different when viewed from inside the dark tunnel versus facing it directly outside.

It would be a shame to view this tunnel separately from Huinnyeoul Culture Village. The western coast of Yeongdo has a unique terrain where residential areas sit beneath the steep slope of Bongnaesan Mountain, with cliffs and sea continuing below that. The narrow alleys of Huinnyeoul Village above are a living space where people reside, while the Jeolyeong Coastal Walking Trail below runs closest to the waves and rocks. The route of climbing up and down the stairs itself shows how Yeongdo's residents have used the steep space between mountain and sea as a living area.

So it's more interesting to see the Huinnyeoul Coastal Tunnel not just as "a tunnel for taking the perfect photo" but as a connecting point for experiencing Yeongdo's vertical space. From above, you see homes and the harbor; from below, you feel the height of the waves and rocks; and the tunnel briefly cuts off and then reconnects those two views. Once you know this, the sea at the exit isn't simply a pretty backdrop — it looks like the final scene where the terrain of Yeongdo island meets the life of its hillside village.
tipsEn:
Route: From the Huinnyeoul coastal path, descend into the tunnel, walk through it, and continue to the sea view on the opposite side.
Photo spot: From inside the tunnel, frame the sea beyond the exit as a silhouette shot.
Caution: On days with high waves or strong winds, check the condition of coastal access first.

simpleEn: The Yu Chi-hwan Postbox Observatory connects the poet's literature with the view of Busan Port through the emotion of waiting. A letter placed in this slow postbox is delivered a year later, sending a moment from your trip into the future. Look at the harbor and the stepped houses of Choryang beyond the red postbox. As you think about who to write to and what to say, a fast-moving trip transforms into a time that holds longing and memory.
detailEn:
If you only take in the view at the Yu Chi-hwan Postbox Observatory, you've only seen half of it. This place was built on the Choryang hillside road to honor the literary spirit of poet Yu Chi-hwan (pen name Cheongma), and since opening in 2016, it has also become known for its "slow postbox," which delivers letters a year later. Yu Chi-hwan was from Tongyeong but had deep ties to Busan — he served as principal of Gyeongnam Girls' High School and passed away in Dong-gu. So this postbox isn't simply a red photo spot; it's closer to a device that ties the poet's life and the scenery of the hillside road together through the emotion of "waiting."

What catches your eye first here is the vivid red postbox and Busan Port spreading out behind it. But that very combination is interesting. The postbox symbolizes a personal message sent to someone, while Busan Port is a vast space of movement where countless people come and go. A very private act of waiting overlaps in one frame with a great urban movement. Writing a letter now and receiving it a year later also creates an experience of deliberately slowing down time in the middle of a fast travel itinerary.

Inside the observatory, there are exhibits related to Yu Chi-hwan, works by young Busan artists, and a space to listen to music, making it feel more like a small cultural space than simply an observation deck. It's worth noting that although the place borrows the poet's name, it also connects to Busan's creators today. Looking down from the rooftop or windows, Busan Station, the North Port, and the stepped houses of the Choryang hillside road all come into view at once — a scene that shows how Busan grew along slopes rather than flat land.

A local guide would tell you not to just photograph the red postbox and head back down, but to pause and look toward Busan Port while thinking, "who would I want to leave a message for, to be read a year from now?" Once you know this, the place feels less like a hillside observation deck and more like somewhere designed to let you actually experience, through real time and scenery, the longing and waiting that Yu Chi-hwan's poems so often explored.
tipsEn:
Route: View the harbor from the observatory, then continue walking along the nearby Ibagu-gil steps and alleys.
Photo spot: Frame the shot so Busan Port appears beyond the red postbox.
Caution: Since this borders a residential area, keep noise down and watch for passing vehicles.

simpleEn: The Gamcheon Culture Village gift shop holds symbols of the village — its hillside homes, alleys, and its Little Prince figure — in small objects. The living space of refugees and Taegeukdo settlers has, through public art and urban regeneration, been turned into travel memories. Once you pick out something you like, think about where in the actual alleys that image came from. Even a single souvenir carries the process by which daily life and art met in Gamcheon.
detailEn:
The Gamcheon Culture Village gift shop looks like a small retail space, but it compresses the process by which Gamcheon was "reinterpreted from a residential area into a culture village." Gamcheon was a living village formed in the 1950s as members of the Taegeukdo faith community and Korean War refugees settled in large numbers on the hillside. Later, as urban regeneration and public art projects continued, the alleys, houses, and local stories became tourism content, and along the way, souvenirs carrying the village's colors and symbols were also created.

Stepping into the shop, images like the Little Prince, stepped houses, pastel-toned alleys, and cats appear again and again. These images aren't used simply because they're cute characters. They're a kind of "village icon," compressing the scenes tourists remember from Gamcheon into small objects. Look at a single postcard or magnet, and it's designed to bring back the shape and color of the actual alleys. In particular, products by local artists or themed around the village show how public art expanded beyond murals into a small economic activity.

Gamcheon Culture Village's urban regeneration has always had two faces. As tourists increased, the village became known and its commercial district revived, but at the same time, this is still a neighborhood where residents live today. That's why the official gift shop matters so much. Rather than intruding on residents' living spaces to take photos or treating private space like a tourist product, it offers a proper channel to encounter and purchase the village's public content and creative work. Choosing a single souvenir can also be a way to make the relationship between the village and tourists a little healthier.

A local guide would tell you not to just look at the products, but to think about where in the actual village this image came from. If you first see the Little Prince sculpture, the layered rooftops, and the narrow stepped alleys, and then enter the shop, each item stops looking like a mere souvenir and starts looking like an interpretation of Gamcheon's scenery. Seen that way, the gift shop isn't the last stop for shopping at the end of a trip — it feels like a small exhibition room where you choose how to remember the village.
tipsEn:
Route: After finishing your tour of the village, browse the gift shop near the official information center for anything you need.
Photo spot: Capture postcards and small items in Gamcheon's colors together with the backdrop.
Caution: Distinguish between residents' living spaces and private shops when visiting.

simpleEn: The charm of Jeonpo Tool Street lies in how old hardware shops and new cafes meet in the same alley. Small shops have moved into the empty storefronts of what was once an industrial district selling machine parts and hardware, creating today's scenery. Take a look at the worn signs, steel shutters, and work equipment next to the cafes too. What now feels like a vintage atmosphere actually tells the story of a time when Busan's labor and new consumer culture coexisted.
detailEn:
The most interesting scene when walking Jeonpo Tool Street is how old hardware shops and new cafes and concept stores sit side by side in the same alley. Jeonpo wasn't a "hip cafe street" from the start. This area was once an industrial commercial district clustered with shops and workshops handling hardware, machine parts, and tools; as manufacturing shifted and the city changed, empty storefronts increased, and relatively small new shops began moving into that space. The current atmosphere of Jeonpo isn't a case of the old industrial alley disappearing entirely — it's what emerged as new culture overlapped into those gaps.

This is why you'll find a sleek glass-fronted cafe right next to an old sign, a steel shutter, and a display stand piled with parts. Many of the new shops didn't tear down the old buildings but reused the existing warehouse or storefront structures, so high ceilings, exposed walls, and industrial materials sometimes remain as if part of the interior design. Knowing that what now looks like "vintage charm" is actually a trace of the previous business changes how you see the space.

If you view this only as an extension of Jeonpo Cafe Street, the old hardware shops can feel like mere background. But a local guide would say the hardware shops were actually the original protagonists of this alley. The very sight of workers in coveralls and tourists, old parts shops and design boutiques sharing the same passage, is Jeonpo's identity. It shows that urban regeneration doesn't have to mean replacing everything with something new — it can also happen through businesses from different eras coexisting.

As you walk, you'll find many stretches where the alley is narrow and vehicles or work equipment sit close by. This, too, is evidence that this wasn't originally a tourist street but an actual commercial and work space. Once you know this, Jeonpo Tool Street shifts from "a place to find pretty cafes" into a street where you can watch, in real time, downtown Busan's industrial structure changing into a service and cultural industry. Don't just look at the new signs — try spotting the old shop names and building traces behind them too.
tipsEn:
Route: From the main road, turn into the hardware shop alley and look at the old signs and new shops in turn.
Photo spot: Frame worn hardware signs and new shops together in one shot.
Caution: Always ask permission before photographing people at work or shop interiors.

simpleEn: Ttangmoesan is a low forest trail where you slowly walk close to the water and woods of Hoedong Reservoir. Between the texture of the red-clay path and the cypress trees, the scenery of a reservoir that has long managed Busan's water continues. The water that looks like a lake is actually a space built for the city, and the surrounding paths have become today's resting place. Rather than rushing to the summit, alternate your gaze between the waterside and the forest to feel the change in this quiet scenery.
detailEn:
Ttangmoesan is less a mountain aimed at reaching the summit and more a low forest trail where you feel the water and woods of Hoedong Reservoir most closely. Busan residents understand this area within the larger scenery of "around Hoedong Reservoir." Because the reservoir has long been a space for managing the city's water, it has a quieter atmosphere than typical tourist spots, and as walking trails and red-clay forest paths were developed around it, it became a place where citizens could enjoy nature up close.

What stays with you most on Ttangmoesan is the texture created by the red-clay path and the forest of cypress and cedar trees. You'll often see people walking barefoot, which isn't simply a trend but reflects how a culture of "healing walks close to the city" has taken root in Busan. The feel of soil underfoot, the humid air rising from the reservoir, and the shade of the trees combine to create a sense different from the city, even over a short distance. Since the trail isn't high, slowing your pace matters more here than hiking gear.

Looking at Hoedong Reservoir, it appears to be a lake, but it's actually an artificial water space tied to the city's water management. So rather than approaching the water directly, the way to experience this place is to walk the designated path and watch the water's surface overlap with the mountain ridgeline. Connecting it with the nearby Oryundae and the Hoedong Reservoir loop trail, you'll also understand that Ttangmoesan isn't an isolated mountain but one of several walking sections surrounding the reservoir's scenery.

A local guide would tell you not to look for a flashy landmark here, but to think about "why does Busan still have this kind of quiet water scenery?" Busan has a strong image tied to the sea, but there's also a large living zone centered on reservoirs, mountains, and valleys within the city. Once you know this, Ttangmoesan isn't just a red-clay path — it becomes a place showing how Busan residents reuse an old water-management space as today's rest and wellness culture.
tipsEn:
Route: From the Ttangmoesan entrance, follow the red-clay path to the reservoir viewpoint section and back.
Photo spot: A curved path where Hoedong Reservoir is visible through the trees works well.
Caution: If using the barefoot section, check in advance for a place to wash your feet and the condition of the ground.

simpleEn: Lotte World Adventure Busan opened in 2022 in the Oshiria tourism complex, becoming a new destination for travel in eastern Busan. A space of castles, villages, parades, and rides adds the pleasure of lingering to a trip centered on ocean views. Think of the surrounding hotels, outlet mall, and coastal tourist facilities. In this fairytale-like setting, you can see the present state of Busan tourism expanding from Haeundae toward Songjeong and Gijang.
detailEn:
Lotte World Adventure Busan isn't an old historic site, but it's a symbolic facility showing how eastern Busan has transformed into a new tourism zone. It opened in 2022 in the Oshiria tourism complex in Gijang-gun, playing a role in shifting the center of gravity of Busan tourism — once centered on Haeundae — toward Songjeong and Gijang. Viewed together with the surrounding outlet mall, hotels, and coastal tourist facilities, you can see the trend of eastern Busan's development aiming to add stay-oriented entertainment to a trip centered on ocean views.

Entering the park, the layout of castles, villages, and a parade route reminiscent of a fairytale kingdom catches your eye first. If you focus only on efficiently riding attractions, this design is easy to miss — each zone is built as a theme park meant to be moved through following a single story. In particular, intense, experience-driven attractions like large roller coasters and water coasters are placed on one side, while performances, characters, and family-friendly spaces are arranged in other zones so that experiences for different age groups overlap.

Connecting this place to the city of Busan gives it a somewhat different meaning. Busan has long centered its tourism on exploring the city itself — beaches, markets, temples, hillside roads — but Oshiria is gathering large-scale, deliberately planned tourist facilities. Nature- and lifestyle-culture-based tourism now coexists with artificial theme-park tourism within a single city. So Lotte World Busan is less a place to find "a classic Busan story" and more a present-tense place showing the direction in which Busan's tourism industry is expanding.

A local guide would tell you to look at a map of the surrounding area before looking at ride names. To the west, Songjeong and Haeundae connect; to the east, Gijang's coastal tourist areas connect. Rather than spending the whole day only at the theme park, placing it within this route makes clear why Oshiria was built in this location. Once you know this, this place isn't just an amusement park — it's also somewhere to feel firsthand the process by which Busan's eastern coast is being reorganized into a large-scale integrated tourism zone.
tipsEn:
Route: After entering, ride the popular attractions first, then move to the central zone in time for the show schedule.
Photo spot: Capture the plaza in front of the castle and the moment the parade passes through.
Caution: Be sure to check height/age restrictions and rain-closure information.

simpleEn: Haedong Yonggungsa is a distinctive temple with its halls set right into a rocky coastline. Unlike mountain temples, walking down its stairs brings the sea and the sound of waves close to the sacred space. An old founding legend, several reconstructions, and modern renovations have together shaped its present appearance. Look at the whole temple from across the way — in the arrangement of halls, rocks, and waves together, you can feel this coastal temple's distinct scenery.
detailEn:
Compared with other temples in Busan, Haedong Yonggungsa's greatest story is its location itself. Traditional Korean temples are usually set deep in the mountains, but this one has its halls set almost directly against the rocky coast. According to tradition, its founding is linked to the monk Naong Hyegeun in the late Goryeo period, and it has continued to today's form through wars and reconstructions over the centuries. Since much of its current name and appearance were shaped relatively recently, it's more accurate to see it not as a temple with buildings preserved unchanged for a thousand years, but as a place where an old religious tradition and a modern coastal-temple image have been created together.

This is also why the stairs leading down from the entrance into the temple grounds matter. Mountain temples are usually approached by climbing up to reach the halls, but at Yonggungsa, the view opens as you descend toward the sea. Between the steps, the roofs and sea gradually come into view, and once you reach the bottom, the main hall, coastal rocks, and waves all appear at once. Because of this route, visitors naturally get the sense of "descending from the mountain into a prayer space by the sea."

Inside the temple grounds, don't just treat the sea as a backdrop. The sound of the waves, the wind, and the coastal rocks are essential elements shaping the temple's atmosphere. Thinking of Buddhist symbols connected to the sea, such as dragon king worship or Avalokiteshvara (Guanyin) worship, helps explain why the image of a coastal temple stays so strongly with people. The many Buddha statues, zodiac figures, and devices symbolizing wishes and prayers are also tied to the popular image of "a temple you visit to make a single wish."

A local guide would tell you to look at the whole temple from across the way, rather than just the most famous photo angle. That's because you can see how the halls aren't set on flat ground but are arranged in tiers following the cliff's changing height. Once you know this, the sea at Haedong Yonggungsa isn't a pretty backdrop — it's an essential part completing the temple's spatial composition and religious imagery. At the same time, since this is a place with many visitors, it's important to remember that its original function as a space for worship and prayer continues today.
tipsEn:
Route: Pass the zodiac statues at the entrance, descend the stairs, and view the temple grounds and coastal views in that order.
Photo spot: From across the temple grounds, frame the temple and sea together in one shot.
Caution: Observe the etiquette of a religious space and do not climb down past the railing onto the coastal rocks.

simpleEn: Gamcheon's Little Prince is a symbol that became widely known as art was added to this hillside village. In a living village settled by refugees and Taegeukdo community residents, the arrival of public art changed the way people saw the alleys. After viewing the character, look at the layered houses behind it. Seeing the artwork and the actual residential scenery together shows how the Little Prince's popularity brought the village's terrain and daily life into a new light.
detailEn:
The Little Prince of Gamcheon Culture Village now looks like the village's representative image, but the area's original history is far removed from character tourism. Gamcheon formed in the 1950s as members of the Taegeukdo faith community and Korean War refugees settled collectively on the hillside, and for a long time afterward it remained one of Busan's representative hillside villages. From the late 2000s, art and urban regeneration projects brought artworks into the alleys, and the Little Prince and fox sculptures became the most widely known symbols amid that change.

The Little Prince didn't gain popularity simply for being a famous character. The image of a small figure sitting at the edge of the hillside, gazing at the village and the sea, fit well with Gamcheon's scenery. The scene of someone sitting alone, looking far into the distance, resembles a traveler observing the countless houses and alleys of this village. So people taking photos naturally turn their gaze in the same direction as the Little Prince, and the stepped residential area behind the sculpture stays in memory just as much as the figure itself.

In the exhibition hall or related spaces, it's more interesting to think about "why did this image become Gamcheon's representative symbol?" rather than focusing on the character itself. Public art isn't decoration meant to cover up an old neighborhood — it can be a device that makes people see existing scenery in a new way. The Little Prince, too, isn't an artifact explaining Gamcheon's original everyday history, but it played a role in turning tourists' gaze toward the alleys and the whole village, creating new local memories in the process.

A local guide would tell you to definitely look at the houses behind it after taking a photo. The residential structure, layered so that no roof blocks the view from the house behind it, and the narrow alleys too tight for vehicles, are Gamcheon's real history. Once you know this, the Little Prince feels less like the protagonist of the village and more like a "guide of gaze" connecting today's travelers to an old refugee village.
tipsEn:
Route: Walk the village alleys, then stop by the exhibition hall to take in the exhibits and photo spot in order.
Photo spot: Capture the Little Prince sculpture together with Gamcheon's colors.
Caution: Follow the waiting line at the photo spot and don't lean on the exhibits.

simpleEn: Gwangalli Beach Theme Street is an urban promenade for walking and resting while looking out at the sea. As Gwangan Bridge and the surrounding commercial district took shape, the summer beach turned into a year-round destination for lingering. Walk toward the waterfront district near Millak or the residential area near Namcheon. The same bridge looks different depending on the angle and background, and between the sculptures and the walking path, tourists' travels and local residents' daily lives meet naturally.
detailEn:
Gwangalli Beach Theme Street was created to turn Gwangalli's sea into "scenery for walking." Gwangalli had long been used as a beach, but as Gwangan Bridge went up and the surrounding commercial and residential districts grew, the beach's character shifted from simply a place to swim in summer into a year-round urban promenade. The sculptures, rest facilities, and wide pedestrian space along the beach are the result of this change.

The biggest backdrop is, of course, Gwangan Bridge. By day, the massive structure appears to float above the horizon, and at night, when its lights come on, the beach's whole atmosphere changes completely. What's interesting is that this is a place with more people "looking at" the bridge than "crossing" it. At Gwangalli, Gwangan Bridge functions as more than transportation infrastructure — it's a stage prop for the city. Most of the beach's sculptures and benches are placed so the view opens toward the bridge, so the angle of the bridge keeps changing as you walk.

Following the theme street toward Millak, you'll find waterfront commercial areas, raw fish restaurants, and new complex cultural spaces; heading the opposite way toward Namcheon, the residential and coastal-walking atmosphere grows stronger. It's interesting how, within the same Gwangalli, the balance of tourism, residential life, and nightlife culture shifts depending on which direction you walk. For local residents, Gwangalli feels less like "one spot" and more like this entire long beach, used as a space for daily life.

A local guide would tell you not to search for just one famous photo spot, but to change the angle from which you look at the bridge. From the center, the whole bridge appears almost head-on; toward either end, the coastline, buildings, and sculptures overlap, giving Busan's cityscape a more three-dimensional feel. Once you know this, the theme street isn't just a promenade full of sculptures — it feels like a grandstand for the city's beach, from which you can experience how a huge piece of infrastructure like Gwangan Bridge has reshaped both the daily life of Busan's citizens and its tourism culture.
tipsEn:
Route: From the center of the beach, choose either the Millak direction or the Namcheon direction and walk slowly.
Photo spot: Frame the shot so Gwangan Bridge appears between the sculptures.
Caution: On days with high waves, avoid the water's edge and the edge of the breakwater.

simpleEn: At the Nakdong River Estuary Eco Center, you can witness Eulsukdo's journey from degraded land back into a resting place for migratory birds. Space that had been turned into farmland, landfill, and other uses is now being restored, wetland by wetland and feeding ground by feeding ground, through ongoing effort. Rather than just looking for birds beyond the observation window, look at the sandbars, reeds, and shallow water too. Understanding how these different water environments sustain life lets you feel that today's ecological park was shaped by a long restoration.
detailEn:
To understand the Nakdong River Estuary Eco Center, you first need to know how Eulsukdo has changed. Eulsukdo is said to have gotten its name from the meaning "many birds, clear water," and lying along the migration route between East Asia and Australia, it has long been an internationally important stopover for migratory birds. In 1966, the lower Nakdong River migratory bird sanctuary was designated a natural monument, but afterward the ecological environment was severely damaged as the area was used for farmland, sewage treatment facilities, dredged-soil deposits, and landfill. Today's ecological park isn't originally perfectly preserved nature — it's the result of a long process of restoring damaged land.

Restoration projects have been underway on Eulsukdo since the mid-1990s, recreating different water environments — freshwater, brackish, and saltwater wetlands — to restore spaces where migratory birds can rest and feed. The eco center and its trails are also designed with use zones, buffer zones, and core conservation zones, allowing people to observe nature without disturbing the most important habitats. The reason the paths don't freely lead everywhere is precisely this distancing for conservation.

When looking at migratory birds through the observation window, rather than just searching for species, look at the shape of the sandbars, reeds, and shallow water too. Sand and sediment carried by the Nakdong River accumulate, and the estuary environment where river water meets seawater creates diverse food sources that draw migratory birds. In other words, protecting the birds alone isn't enough to sustain a migratory bird sanctuary — the flow of water and the whole wetland must stay alive. Understanding this principle turns even a wide, seemingly empty reed bed into a highly complex ecological system.

A local guide would describe Eulsukdo's most important story as "an island where nature came back." A place severely damaged during Busan's industrialization and urban development took decades to turn back into an ecological space. As you leave the eco center and look at the distant city and roads together, it becomes even clearer that migratory birds and a major metropolis coexist at very close range. This is a place to see Busan's nature, and at the same time, a site showing what kind of relationship a city should have with nature.
tipsEn:
Route: View the indoor exhibition first, then move to the trails and bird observation points.
Photo spot: Capture the wetlands beyond the observation window and birds taking flight from a distance.
Caution: Keep your voice down and do not feed wildlife, so as not to startle the animals.

simpleEn: Oryukdo Lighthouse is a navigational marker guiding ships safely into Busan Port. The rocky islets, said to look like either five or six depending on the viewing angle and the tide, served as an important boundary between the open sea and the harbor. Look at the islands and the waterway between them from land. Behind the small, isolated-looking lighthouse, you can clearly see how countless ships have relied on it as a guide across the sea to reach Busan.
detailEn:
The first thing worth knowing when viewing Oryukdo Lighthouse is that "Oryukdo" doesn't refer to a single island. Several rocky islets off Busan's coast are said to appear as either five or six, depending on the viewing angle and the tide, which is how the name Oryukdo ("Five-Six Islands") came about. For ships entering Busan Port, these islands were an important marker separating the open sea from the harbor, so the lighthouse here was never merely scenic — it was directly tied to the safety of vessels.

The island where the lighthouse stands looks small and isolated from land, but from the sea's perspective, it holds a position guarding the entrance to Busan Port. Ships coming in from the open sea read their course by the island and the lighthouse's light before they see any building on land. Modern GPS and electronic navigation equipment have advanced, but the lighthouse's symbolic significance remains strong. By day, the white tower's shape contrasts against the rocky island; by night, it's distinguished from other lighthouses by its distinct pattern of light flashes.

When viewing Oryukdo from a land observatory, don't just count the islands — look at the waterway too. Where the Korea Strait meets Busan Port, wind and currents are strong, and the cliffs and rocks show rough traces of erosion by waves. Because of these natural conditions, Oryukdo has long been recognized as a boundary of Busan's sea. The reason these islands remain visible from both Oryukdo Sunrise Park and the Igidae coastal trail on land is that they serve as a geographic reference point for Busan's southeastern coast.

A local guide wouldn't say "you have to actually reach the lighthouse to see it properly." In fact, viewing the rocky islands and the lighthouse together from land makes the spatial meaning of "the entrance to the harbor" even clearer. Once you know this, the small white lighthouse isn't just a pretty subject for photos — it feels like a signal of the sea that countless ships have relied on to enter and leave Busan Port, and the farthest, earliest sign that Busan is a port city.
tipsEn:
Route: First view Oryukdo from a land observation point, and only plan sea access if boat passage is confirmed available.
Photo spot: From a land observatory, frame the multiple islands and lighthouse with a telephoto composition.
Caution: Do not attempt to land on the islands without official permission and confirmed sailing schedules.

simpleEn: Dalmaji-gil is a hillside road that follows the sea, pine trees, and moonlight from Haeundae toward Songjeong. Haewoljeong Pavilion and Moontan Road embody this place's character of gazing at the view and enjoying the mood of the night. While looking for a cafe, pause for a moment and watch the sea open up between the trees. As the low sun and moonlight shift the scenery, you can find a calm side of Haeundae, quite different from the energy of the beach.
detailEn:
As its name suggests — "the road for moon-viewing" — Dalmaji-gil's very sentiment has shaped the character of this space. The hillside road climbing from Haeundae toward Songjeong has long been known as a scenic spot, with the sea visible below and pine forests continuing along the way. Today it's familiar as a drive route lined with cafes and restaurants, but at its heart are Haewoljeong Pavilion, Dalmaji Hill, and Moontan Road, where you walk beneath the moonlight. What sets it apart from Haeundae's other coastal roads is that it valued the night and moonlight as an important experience, more than daytime sea views.

Haewoljeong Pavilion, midway along Dalmaji-gil, is known as a good spot to watch the moon rise. Stories are told of people making wishes on the moon or promising their love around the first full moon of the lunar new year, and the name Moontan Road — playing on the idea of "basking in moonlight" — carries this atmosphere forward in a modern way. So this is a place better suited to walking as light shifts through sunset than to simply visiting one lookout point and turning back.

As you walk the road, pine trees and hills open on one side, while the sea toward Haeundae, Cheongsapo, and Songjeong alternates on the other. The road curves because it follows the mountain's terrain, so the frame shifts every few steps even though it's the same sea. Unlike central Haeundae with its many high-rises, Dalmaji-gil lets forest, slope, and sea appear together, so you can feel the boundary where the scenery shifts from "urban beach" to "coastal hill."

A local guide would tell you not to just pass through looking at the daytime view, but to watch how the sea and moon reveal themselves between the trees as the sun gets low. Once you know this, Dalmaji-gil isn't just a hillside road full of cafes — it becomes a place showing how Haeundae's people have long enjoyed the sea's nighttime scenery, now continued today as a space for walking and culture. Looking from Haewoljeong toward Cheongsapo, you can also naturally read how eastern Busan's coast is connected as one long axis of daily life and tourism.
tipsEn:
Route: From the start of Dalmaji-gil, head toward Haewoljeong Pavilion, choosing spots along the way where the view opens up.
Photo spot: A curved stretch of road where Haeundae's sea opens up between the trees works well.
Caution: Traffic can be heavy during cherry blossom season and on weekends.

simpleEn: Busan Cooperative Fish Market is the center of seafood distribution, auctioning catches and sending them nationwide. Since opening in 1963, it has established itself as a major wholesale market for seafood arriving at Namhang, Busan's south port. In the early morning, workers sort fish, set prices, and move goods in constant motion. Think of Busan's seafood dishes and Jagalchi Market — behind that familiar taste lies a huge distribution network connecting boats, merchants, and transport.
detailEn:
Busan Cooperative Fish Market has a different character from the markets tourists visit to eat raw fish. This is a "source wholesale market" where seafood caught by boats is auctioned on a large scale and sent nationwide. It opened in 1963 as the Busan General Fish Market and grew into a facility representing seafood distribution at Busan's Namhang (South Port), later renamed Busan Cooperative Fish Market. For a long time, a significant portion of the country's coastal and offshore catch has passed through here, making it the backbone of Busan's fishing industry.

The most important scene here is the early-morning auction. Mackerel and other catches unloaded from boats are laid out on the wide floor sorted by type and size, and wholesalers and other participants set prices at a rapid pace. Unlike an ordinary market where you buy one fish at a time, here large quantities of seafood are traded all at once, so the scale and pace of the market feel like an industrial site. The floor markings, boxes, transport vehicles, and refrigeration and storage facilities are all part of a system for distributing freshly caught fish as quickly as possible.

To understand why Busan is famous for markets like Jagalchi and for its seafood dishes, you need to see the distribution network behind it, like Cooperative Fish Market. Behind the single plate of raw fish or grilled fish a tourist sees at a restaurant lies a massive industry connecting fishing boats, wholesale auctions, intermediary dealers, transport, and processing. This market is where it becomes clearest that Namhang isn't just a scenic port — it's an actual working space where the fishing industry operates.

Recently, a project to modernize the older facilities has been underway, so you can also see how the seafood distribution infrastructure built during the industrialization era of the 1960s–70s is being transformed in new ways. A local guide would tell you to look first at the scale of the port and market, without interfering with the ongoing work inside. Once you know this, Busan Cooperative Fish Market isn't a "tourist-style market" — it's a massive workplace that has quietly powered Busan residents' dinner tables and the nation's seafood distribution.
tipsEn:
Route: From the publicly accessible outer walkway and designated viewing area, observe the market's scale and workflow.
Photo spot: An outdoor spot where the port and market buildings appear together is the safest choice.
Caution: Do not block work paths or photograph the interior and workers without permission.

simpleEn: Unsusa Temple is a temple in the forest of Baegyangsan Mountain that has kept its faith alive through repeated fires and reconstructions. Its old founding legend and the age visible in its main hall speak of how long this site has been preserved. Rather than only touring the halls, look also at the forest, the mountain ridge, and where the buildings sit. Instead of rushing between flashy attractions, take time to feel the time during which people, deep in the mountains of western Busan, rebuilt and preserved this temple.
detailEn:
Unsusa Temple may look like a quiet temple deep in the forest of Baegyangsan Mountain, but its history runs deeper than it appears. According to tradition and records, a temple is believed to have existed here since the Gaya period; it was once called Sinsuam before being renamed Unsusa sometime before the 18th century. Its buildings burned during the Imjin War (the Japanese invasions of Korea) and were later rebuilt, and the current main hall is known to have been renovated in the 17th century. So rather than a flashy tourist temple, this is a place carrying the time of a mountain temple that has disappeared and been rebuilt more than once.

The main hall (Daeungjeon) is the most important thing to look at in the temple grounds. It is recognized as an important example of old wooden architecture in Busan and is designated a national treasure, and inside are cultural assets including a stone seated Buddha triad. When viewing an old hall, don't just look at the colors of the dancheong (traditional decorative painting) — also look at the thickness of the pillars, the line of the eaves, and how the building is set to match the mountain's slope. Considering that it has undergone repairs and reconstructions over hundreds of years, it's more important to see a single building not simply as "something old," but as the result of preservation through the touch of many generations.

Baegyangsan Mountain, where Unsusa sits, is a major ridge dividing western Busan from the city center. Entering the temple, the noise drops sharply and the forest's presence grows, even though the city is close by. The reason old temples were located deep in the mountains had to do not only with practice and faith, but also with living conditions like water, forest, and travel routes. Looking at the halls and forest paths together within the temple grounds today, it's clear that the architecture isn't separate from nature but arranged to follow the mountain's terrain.

A local guide would tell you not to count attractions the way you would at a large, famous temple, but to think about "why has this temple remained in this spot for so long?" Once you know this, Unsusa isn't just a small temple in Baegyangsan Mountain — it looks like a trace of old regional culture, one that carried on western Busan's forest life and religious practice through fires, destruction, and reconstruction.
tipsEn:
Route: Enter the temple grounds through the one-pillar gate, view the main halls, and then slowly walk through the forest scenery.
Photo spot: Frame the temple roofline against the backdrop of the forest.
Caution: Watch for slippery ground after rain, as there are mountain paths and slopes.

simpleEn: Myeongji-dong Neighborhood Park shows western Busan's transformation from wide plains, waterways, and farmland into a new town. Its deliberately laid walking paths, lawns, and exercise facilities connect residents' rest and play within the new residential area. Look at the apartments and wide roads in and around the park. Where the ecological environment of the Nakdong River estuary meets urban development up close, you can encounter a side of Busan's daily life quite different from the sea or the hillside roads.
detailEn:
Myeongji-dong Neighborhood Park isn't a historic site or a major tourist attraction, but it's a good everyday space for reading how western Busan is changing. The Myeongji area was once a region of wide plains, waterways, and farmland at the Nakdong River estuary, and over the past few decades, large-scale residential and commercial/business developments have dramatically changed the urban scenery. The neighborhood park is planned green space within this new town, meant for residents to walk, rest, and let children play.

Unlike small parks in the old downtown, this park's walking paths, lawns, and exercise facilities are set at relatively wide intervals with a deliberately planned layout. This is because the surrounding residential area and the park were built together. In Busan's old downtown, leftover space between hillsides and alleys was often used for parks, but in Myeongji you can see traces of urban planning coming first, followed by the placement of green space. Even within the same city of Busan, the shape of a park differs depending on the era in which the surrounding city was built.

Looking more broadly, Myeongji is a region where the ecological environment of the Nakdong River estuary meets new town development very closely. Eulsukdo, the migratory bird sanctuary, and the new residential areas and roads of Gangseo and Myeongji share the same living zone. So rather than only looking at the park's trees and lawn, looking at the apartment complexes, the wide sky, and the flat terrain in the distance reveals western Busan's characteristics well. Unlike the old downtown and Haeundae area, where mountains rise directly behind, the flat land of the Nakdong estuary here made the city's expansion possible.

A local guide, asked "why would a tourist bother looking at a neighborhood park," would explain that it's a place showing Busan isn't only a city of beaches and hillside roads. There's no flashy landmark, but watching residents pushing strollers, exercising, and walking pets shows the everyday life of Busan currently being built. Once you know this, this place is both somewhere to rest and, at the same time, a quiet showcase of the growth of western Busan's new town and the changing Nakdong River plain.
tipsEn:
Route: Walk once around the park's perimeter, then take a rest under the shade or on a bench.
Photo spot: Capture the wide paths and seasonal plantings along a continuous stretch.
Caution: Keep pathways clear out of consideration for playground and exercise area users.

simpleEn: Spo1 Park is a complex park centered on a cycling velodrome, connected to sports facilities and green space. A large facility built for watching races has expanded into a space for family outings, community sports, and walks alike. Look at the specialized racing track together with the people exercising and relaxing around it. Between trips to the sea and mountains, you can see how a planned public facility in northern Busan has become part of residents' ordinary days.
detailEn:
Spo1 Park may look like a simple sports park, but it shows how Busan repurposes a large sports facility as a space for citizens' daily lives. At its center is a cycling velodrome, surrounded by sports and leisure facilities and wide green space. During a period when Busan was expanding facilities for international sporting events and large-scale competitions, this facility was established in the Dugu-dong area of Geumjeong-gu, and it later broadened in character from a space purely for watching races into a complex park where families, community sports, and walking coexist.

The velodrome is built around a specialized track for bicycle racing. Unlike an ordinary bike path, the banked oval track, grandstands, and athlete facilities form a single integrated system. From outside it looks like just one stadium, but it's actually a facility precisely designed as a whole for speed, safety, and spectating. Compared with the flat, wide paths of the surrounding park, you can more clearly see how "professional sport" and "citizens' leisure" coexist on a single site.

While Busan's other major tourist spots often rely on the sea or mountains, Spo1 Park is different in that it's a planned facility built in a flat, residential zone of northern Busan. The outskirts of Geumjeong-gu had more room than the city center, allowing a large stadium, parking, and green space to all be laid out together, and today this has become a place to enjoy cycling, walking, and family activities. Another feature is that the park's atmosphere changes greatly depending on whether an event or race is taking place.

A local guide would tell you not to focus on "what you must see here," but rather to observe how Busan's citizens use a large public facility in their daily lives. Watching residents walking the wide open space and exercising on non-race days shows how urban sports infrastructure survives as a living space even after a specific event ends. Once you know this, Spo1 Park looks less like a tourist attraction and more like a present-tense space where Busan's sports-city policy meets citizens' leisure.
tipsEn:
Route: Confirm which sports facility you plan to visit first, then continue on to the park's walking trail.
Photo spot: A spot where the wide plaza and the stadium's exterior appear together works well.
Caution: Stay alert where cycling and pedestrian paths intersect.

simpleEn: Gupo Market is a marketplace that grew at the junction of Nakdong River water transport and land transportation routes. Goods and people moving between Gimhae, Yangsan, and Busan through Gupo Ferry became the market's roots. As you walk the alleys filled with vegetables, seafood, and household goods, imagine the direction of the river. While meeting the noodles and various foods here, feel the old flow of trade that once carried goods gathered along the Nakdong River into the city's daily life.
detailEn:
Gupo Market's history is difficult to explain without mentioning the Nakdong River. Since the Joseon dynasty, Gupo was a junction where Nakdong River water transport met land routes, and through Gupo Ferry, goods and people moved between Gimhae, Yangsan, and inner Busan. A marketplace naturally developed, and Gupojang remains a large traditional market today, retaining both the character of a permanent market and a periodic market day. Because the market came first and the city grew up around it, it has completely different roots from a deliberately planned modern commercial facility.

Walking through the market, the range of goods is very diverse — vegetables, fruit, seafood, salted fish, and household items. This is because Gupojang was never a market selling just one specialty product, but a regional hub market that absorbed the everyday needs of nearby farming and fishing villages as well as urban residents. On market days, outside merchants and customers add to the mix, and you can see a blend of permanent stalls and street vendors. In a changed form, this preserves the old ferry-era function of "a day when people gather."

When you think of Gupo, noodles are hard to leave out. During the Korean War, as refugees poured into Busan, Gupo noodles, relatively cheap and quick to eat, became an important meal. Conditions that made dried noodles easy to store and distribute long-term, along with the railway and ferry transport networks, also influenced the market and its food culture. So noodles and gukbap (rice soup) inside the market aren't simply "famous dishes" — they can be understood as everyday food that developed in a marketplace with heavy labor and movement.

A local guide would tell you to picture the direction of the Nakdong River right from the market. Today roads and railways are more visible than the waterway, but the reason this commercial district was able to grow in the first place was the river and the ferry.
