Photo spot: A composition showing the waterways, fields, and wide sky together works well.
Caution: Don't enter the wetlands, and stay out of farming and management zones.

simpleEn: At the Yeongdo Haenyeo Culture Exhibition Hall, you meet the lives of women haenyeo divers who made the sea their livelihood. Freediving without oxygen tanks to gather seafood required knowledge of tides, wind, rocks, and currents. After looking at the simple tools and photographs, look out at the sea nearby. A culture that migrated from Jeju took root along Yeongdo's coastline, and it's worth remembering that this underwater scenery was, for many years, someone's workplace.
detailEn:
To understand the Yeongdo Haenyeo Culture Exhibition Hall, it helps to start with the question, 'Were there haenyeo divers in Busan too?' Jeju comes to mind first when you think of haenyeo, but in fact, Jeju haenyeo traveled to dive for a living along many coastlines of the Korean peninsula, and Yeongdo was one of the important destinations. Busan tourism materials date the start of Yeongdo's haenyeo history to a 1887 record of Jeju haenyeo diving at Yeongdo, then called Mokdo. Haenyeo who later settled there made Yeongdo's sea their livelihood and built a distinctive local diving culture.

When you look at the diving tools, clothing, and photographs in the exhibition hall, notice first just how simple the equipment is. Haenyeo dive into the sea using only their own breath, with no oxygen tank, to gather abalone, conch, seaweed, and more. The long exhale they make on surfacing is called sumbisori—not just a sound of breathing, but the rhythm of labor made up of repeated dives and recovery. Because they had to memorize the currents, water depth, and rock positions in their bodies by returning to the same spots over and over, the sea was, for haenyeo, not a scenic view but a space of highly skilled labor.

What makes Yeongdo's haenyeo culture interesting isn't simply that 'Jeju's culture moved to Busan unchanged'—rather, it fused with the local sea through the process of migration and settlement. Yeongdo's coastline has many rocky areas and spots with strong currents, so working methods and what was gathered adapted to local conditions. Looking at the migration routes and everyday-life materials in the exhibit, you can see how one region's culture put down new roots in a different city, following the movement of people.

A local guide would tell you, after seeing the exhibit, not to just view the surrounding sea as a pretty coastline. That very water was someone's workplace for decades, a space where knowledge of wind and tides passed down between generations. Once you know this, the exhibition hall stops looking like a display of old diving tools, and starts looking like a small archive documenting women's labor that migrated along the sea and the history of Busan's fishing village life.
tipsEn:
Route: View the exhibit first, then look out at the surrounding coastline from a distance to picture the actual working space.
Photo spot: Capture the exhibited tools together with the sea view through the window.
Caution: Get permission before photographing haenyeo actively at work and their equipment.

simpleEn: Ilgwang Beach holds the memory of a fishing village's life carried into a novel, a film, and a song. Oh Yeong-su's novel The Fishing Village and the sensibility of Choi Baek-ho, who grew up in Gijang, let you meet this sea again through culture. Walk the sandy beach, then take a look at Gangsongjeong Park and the nearby monuments. As you take in the quiet beach and harbor, you'll feel how the lives of people in Busan's fishing villages have carried on through works of art and travelers' memories.
detailEn:
It's easy to think of Ilgwang Beach as just a quiet beach in Gijang, but it's a place where the memory of literature, film, and popular song overlaps unusually heavily. The name 'Ilgwang' is said to come from the nearby Ilgwangsan Mountain, and the area has long been counted among Gijang's scenic spots. Old pine trees once lined the coastline, and records and traditions survive of various figures visiting this area's scenery as far back as the Goryeo dynasty. The shallow water and relatively calm waves, which have long made it a beloved family summer spot, are also part of Ilgwang's long-standing character.

The most interesting cultural trace around the beach is Oh Yeong-su's novel The Fishing Village. Ilgwang's fishing-village scenery is known as the setting for both the novel and its film adaptation, and markers and sculptures recalling the story remain around Gangsongjeong Park. In the novel, the sea is a romantic backdrop, but at the same time it's the livelihood space of fishing-village people whose lives depend on the sea for their husbands and families. Knowing the story, the calm beach turns into a scene with a much stronger sense of everyday life.

Singer Choi Baek-ho's song 'On Romance' is also introduced in connection with Ilgwang. Choi Baek-ho was born in Gijang and spent his childhood in Ilgwang, and he's said to have drawn the song's mood from memories of his hometown Busan, his commuting days through Ilgwang Station, and time gone by. That's why you can find related monuments and lyrics scattered around the beach. Literary and historical elements are scattered around too, such as a poetry monument to Yun Seon-do, the Samseongdae mound, and old black pine trees.

A local guide would tell you not to just take photos from the middle of the beach, but to also visit Gangsongjeong Park and the nearby monuments in sequence. Once you know this, Ilgwang stops looking like just a quiet beach in East Busan, and starts looking like a 'sea within culture'—a place where Busan's fishing-village life has been rewritten again and again through the memory of novels, film, and song.
tipsEn:
Route: From the middle of the beach, walk slowly toward the stream and breakwater, taking in the scenery.
Photo spot: A shot where the sandy beach and the low fishing-village skyline stretch out together works well.
Caution: Check the safety line and wave conditions, and avoid approaching the end of the breakwater.

simpleEn: Democracy Park is a space that continues to honor Busan citizens' democratization movements, from the April 19 Revolution to the Busan-Masan Democratic Uprising and the June Democratic Uprising. The exhibits and memorial facilities capture the reasons students, workers, and citizens took to the streets, and the look of their times. Rather than just noting the years, take a moment before the names and records. Looking down at the ordinary streets of the old downtown below, you can freshly sense that they were once the sites of protest and change.
detailEn:
Democracy Park is a citizens' park built to remember Busan's democratization movement history in one place. The span of time it covers doesn't end with a single event. It presents the memory of multiple democratization movements Busan citizens took part in, one after another—from the April 19 Revolution in 1960, to the Busan-Masan Democratic Uprising in 1979, to the June Democratic Uprising in 1987. That's why the memorial and exhibition spaces here go beyond honoring specific individuals, playing a role in conveying the history of civic participation and democracy itself.

The park grounds also include memorial spaces related to the April 19 Revolution. Busan's students and citizens took part in that uprising, and the memorial tower and facilities built afterward reflect civil society's efforts to keep that spirit alive. Over time, the memory of the Busan-Masan Democratic Uprising and the June Democratic Uprising became connected here as well, making Democracy Park a place linking multiple generations of Busan's democratization movement.

Rather than memorizing years and event names while viewing the exhibits, it's better to consider, alongside them, why people took to the streets, within the social conditions of each era. Citizens' concerns about authoritarian rule, rigged elections, and political repression surfaced in different forms at different times, and the range of participants—students, workers, ordinary citizens—broadened as well. You can also see how, given Busan's character as a port and industrial city, university districts, downtown, and workplaces all became stages for the democratization movement.

A local guide would tell you, in front of the memorial sculptures, to read the names and records before taking a photo. Democracy Park isn't a space that makes political judgments on your behalf—it's a place that invites you to reflect on the historical process through which today's institutions and civil rights were formed. Looking down over the old downtown from the park's high ground, it becomes a bit more real that these ordinary city streets were once the sites of citizens' rallies, resistance, and change.
tipsEn:
Route: View the exhibits at the Democracy Movement Memorial Hall, then walk around the outdoor sculptures and viewpoint.
Photo spot: A spot showing the memorial sculptures together with Busan's old downtown works well.
Caution: Stay quiet in the memorial space and follow the photography guidance for exhibited materials.

simpleEn: In Choryang Ibagu-gil, 'ibagu' is a Gyeongsang-do dialect word for 'story.' The stairs, wells, and houses on the hillside behind Busan Station preserve the memory of refugees and laborers building a life for themselves. Walk, even briefly, the path once traveled between port jobs and hillside homes. The moment you look out at the sea from the observatory, you'll feel that the slope you just climbed was, before it became a tourist route, part of residents' everyday lives.
detailEn:
'Ibagu' in Choryang Ibagu-gil is Gyeongsang-do dialect for 'story.' True to its name, this isn't a route built around one famous building—it's a path that lets you read, alley by alley, the stories of refuge, labor, and daily life that remain along the sanbokdoro behind Busan Station. Refugees who flooded into Busan during the Korean War had to build homes up the hillsides in an old downtown short on flat land, and to work at the port and station, they had to climb steep stairs every single day. Today's tourist route was built directly over that everyday commute.

Climbing from the Busan Station side, you pass old walls, alleys, the 168 Steps, and viewing areas one after another. Looking down from the top, it becomes clear why people came to live on this steep slope. Jobs and markets were down near the port and station, but the higher up the mountain you went, the more empty land there was to build on. So houses climbed the slope in layers, and the alleys were shaped as stepped paths built for people's footsteps rather than cars.

The exhibits and installations along Ibagu-gil hold not only famous figures but also the everyday history of Choryang's residents. Carrying water from a shared well in a time when water was scarce, walking to school and market down the mountain, exchanging news with neighbors in narrow alleys—these everyday moments become the city's history. That's why the stairs, the well, and the old houses matter more here than the kind of grand monument you'd typically find at a tourist site.

A local guide would tell you, rather than just photographing the observatory and taking a taxi down, to walk the stairs yourself, even for a short stretch. Climb just a few minutes and you'll feel the slope in your own body, watching Busan Port grow smaller below. Once you know this, Choryang Ibagu-gil stops looking like 'an old-fashioned alley,' and starts looking like a living-history museum you understand by walking through it—showing how refugee-city Busan built its foothold for life on a mountain slope.
tipsEn:
Route: From the Busan Station side, climb in order past the Wall Art Gallery, the 168 Steps, and the viewing area.
Photo spot: A scene where Busan Port and the old houses overlap through the stairs works well.
Caution: These are alleys where residents actually live, so don't photograph windows or the insides of homes.

simpleEn: Yeongdo Lighthouse first lit up in 1906 and has guided ships to Busan Port ever since. Its light flashes in a fixed pattern, giving distant ships the information to identify their position and this specific lighthouse. Stand at the edge of the Taejongdae cliffs and look at the white lighthouse and the open sea beyond. Countless ships have entered Busan from that direction. Today's observation deck and exhibition space still carry forward the real function of a navigation facility that has helped keep the port safe.
detailEn:
Yeongdo Lighthouse first lit up in December 1906 atop the cliffs of Taejongdae, making it one of Busan's leading modern lighthouses. According to the Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries, it has guided ships navigating Busan Port and its surrounding waters for over a century, and as its facilities aged, it was rebuilt into its current form in 2004. Today it functions as a marine cultural space with observation decks, exhibits, and rest areas, but its origin was, first and foremost, a navigation marker for the safe operation of ships.

A lighthouse's light isn't simply 'a bright light shining at night.' Yeongdo Lighthouse uses a fixed flashing pattern so that ships far out at sea can distinguish it from other lighthouses. The Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries describes its light as reaching about 40 kilometers, flashing three times over an 18-second cycle. Before GPS became widespread, this kind of light pattern and position was crucial information, telling ships exactly where they were.

It's no coincidence that Taejongdae's rugged cliffs and the lighthouse appear together. This is terrain jutting out at the edge of the open sea approaching Busan Port, making it a location easy to spot even from far away. The area was also used as a military fortification site under Japanese colonial rule, with public access restricted at times, and was later opened as a scenic spot and geopark—so the same location's role kept shifting between military use, navigation, and tourism.

A local guide would tell you to look, from the edge of the cliff, at the open sea beyond Busan Port, rather than at the white lighthouse itself. Countless ships came into Busan from that direction, and the lighthouse's light was their signal that the harbor was near. Once you know this, Yeongdo Lighthouse stops looking like a pretty photo spot at Taejongdae, and starts looking like real navigational infrastructure, showing how the port city of Busan has stayed connected to the open sea for over a hundred years.
tipsEn:
Route: Follow the Taejongdae loop trail, taking in the lighthouse viewpoint and the coastal cliffs together.
Photo spot: Frame the white lighthouse, the blue sea, and the cliffs together in one shot.
Caution: Don't go beyond railings or into restricted areas, and watch for strong wind.

simpleEn: At Gadeokdo Lighthouse, compare the old lighthouse with the new one standing side by side, and read the changes in marine technology. Built in 1909, the old facility still has the living quarters and office where its keepers once stayed. The building's layout reflects a life spent guarding the light on an isolated coast. Compare the two structures within whatever area is open to the public, and you'll see, in their contrasting forms facing the same sea, the passage of time for Busan Port and its navigation markers.
detailEn:
Among Busan's lighthouses, Gadeokdo Lighthouse is especially interesting because you can compare its old and new lighthouses in one place. The old lighthouse, first lit in December 1909, is a modern navigation facility that served as an important guide for ships traveling between Busan Port and the Korea Strait. At the time, the southern tip of Gadeokdo was the passage linking the open sea to Busan Port, making the lighthouse's location strategically important. It's also an architectural heritage site reflecting Busan during the early 20th century, when its port and shipping industry were expanding.

Looking at the old lighthouse building, you'll notice a structure combining office and living quarters, quite different from today's tall, simple lighthouse towers. Lighthouses back then weren't automated—a person had to stay on site to maintain the light—so living space for the keeper was essential. Having an office, bedroom, and kitchen all together shows that the lighthouse wasn't just 'a single light,' but a combined living-and-working facility that someone had to keep running 24 hours a day on an isolated coast.

As the facility aged and a stronger navigation marker became necessary, a new lighthouse was built alongside it in the early 2000s, and the old lighthouse was preserved as a cultural heritage site. Seeing the two structures side by side lets you directly compare how lighthouse technology, architecture, and the way keepers worked changed over a century. The old building's low, detailed exterior and the modern tower's functional form, both standing and facing the same sea, form a kind of exhibition of time all on their own.

A local guide would tell you, instead of just gazing out at the distant sea, to first notice the difference between the two lighthouses. Once you know this, Gadeokdo Lighthouse stops looking like a facility at a scenic island's tip, and starts looking like a cultural heritage site of maritime transportation, letting you read the growth of Busan Port, the history of modern navigation markers, and the life of a lighthouse keeper all in one place. Note, however, that nearby port and military-related restricted zones exist, so it's important to follow the areas and guidance that are actually open to the public.
tipsEn:
Route: Confirm official opening or reservation status first, then visit only the guided areas and routes.
Photo spot: A spot showing the old lighthouse building together with the sea horizon works well.
Caution: Don't photograph or approach unauthorized areas and facilities.

simpleEn: Songdo Yonggung Cloud Bridge connects Amnam Park to a rocky island, bringing you close to wind, waves, and height. Songdo once had another cloud bridge, long ago, where people crossed over the sea to enjoy the view. Turn around midway across the bridge and look back the way you came. On one side, the cable car and city beach; on the other, forest and cliffs, all in view together. Rediscover a once-lost tradition of walking over the sea, carried forward in Songdo's present-day facilities.
detailEn:
Songdo Yonggung Cloud Bridge might look like a newly built sea bridge, but Songdo has held the memory of a tourist facility for 'crossing over the sea to enjoy the view' for far longer than this bridge has existed. Old Songdo once had a cloud bridge connecting Songnim Park and Geobukseom (Turtle) Island, which, together with the aerial cable car, formed an iconic scene of the Songdo amusement area. That old cloud bridge disappeared due to natural disasters and aging, but after a long span of time, today's Songdo Yonggung Cloud Bridge revived that memory in a modern form.

The current bridge connects Amnam Park with a rocky island, letting you walk high above the sea. Part of the floor is mesh, so you can see the waves and rocks directly below your feet, and since the bridge isn't a fully fixed concrete structure, you can feel a slight sway as people walk and the wind blows. Because of this sensation, you don't just 'view' the scenery—you experience the height, the waves, and the wind with your whole body.

Turn back toward Songdo from the middle of the bridge, and the cable car, sky park, and beach all come into view at once. In the opposite direction, Amnam Park's forest and rugged coastal cliffs loom larger. This contrast—a city beach packed with artificial tourist facilities on one side, a natural coastline of preserved geology and forest on the other—is remarkably clear on this short bridge. It shows how Songdo's tourism has expanded from an old-fashioned amusement park into today's complex marine tourist destination.

A local guide would tell you to turn around once midway, rather than just rushing to reach the end of the bridge. Once you know this, Songdo Yonggung Cloud Bridge stops looking like a simple thrill ride, and starts looking like a place that reconnects, in a modern form, Songdo's once-lost memory of 'walking over the sea,' tying the city beach and Amnam Park's natural coastline together into a single view.
tipsEn:
Route: Check ticketing and operating status at Amnam Park, then walk the bridge round trip and take in the viewing area.
Photo spot: Capture the coastal cliffs and sea stretching out from the middle of the bridge.
Caution: Follow operational guidance, and don't run or reach objects out past the railing on the bridge.

simpleEn: Amir Park is a coastal space that connects the exhibits of the National Maritime Museum of Korea to the real sea of Busan Port just outside. After viewing ship models and the history of navigation inside, step out and watch actual vessels moving on the water—the museum's stories continue into real life. Walk the lawns and flat promenade, glancing back and forth between the harbor and the direction of Taejongdae. In the Dongsam-dong coastline, where education, port, and tourism facilities cluster together, take a moment to feel what it means for citizens to have a place to look out at the sea and rest.
detailEn:
Amir Park stretches out along the shore in front of the National Maritime Museum of Korea, so at first glance it looks like just a lawn to rest on after visiting the museum. But zoom out a little and it becomes a good place to read how the Dongsam-dong coastline of Yeongdo has changed over time. The area brings together the National Maritime Museum, the Busan International Cruise Terminal, and Korea Maritime and Ocean University, and Busan's Galmaetgil Trail Section 3-3 also ends here at Amir Park. In other words, tourism, education, and port functions all overlap along the same shoreline.

Looking out to sea from the park, what catches the eye isn't massive working facilities like container piers, but passenger ferries, cruise ships, and vessels moving along shipping routes. If you've just come from the museum next door, having seen the history of navigation and shipbuilding, this view feels like an extension of the exhibits. Being able to compare ship models behind glass with real ships out on the water is this space's best feature. The flat, sea-facing promenade also has a completely different mood from Yeongdo's other cliffside coastal paths, like Taejongdae and Jeolyeong Coastal Walk.

The park is also known, depending on the season, for its hydrangea path, but if you only look at the flowers and move on, you'll miss the site's urban significance. Amir Park isn't so much a preserved natural coastline as it is a public waterfront space that gives the sea back to citizens near the Dongsam Innovation District, where maritime-related public facilities are concentrated. In many port cities, the shoreline is blocked off by industrial facilities, making it hard for residents to access the water directly—but here, the lawns and promenade let people look out at the waters of Busan Port as part of everyday life.

A local guide would tell you not to just take a photo with the museum building as your backdrop, but to walk along the shoreline, looking back and forth toward Taejongdae and toward the harbor. Once you know this, Amir Park stops looking like an empty lawn in front of a museum and starts to look like a connecting space where Yeongdo's old port functions and today's maritime culture and tourism functions meet on the same shore.
tipsEn:
Route: After visiting the museum, follow the coastal promenade around the lawn plaza and viewing sections.
Photo spot: A composition where the museum and the sea appear together beyond the open lawn works well.
Caution: Stay alert near the water's edge and in bicycle path sections.

simpleEn: The Busan Museum of Art opened in 1998 and established itself as a public institution linking regional art with international contemporary art. Its work documenting Busan's artists and introducing new forms of expression is tied to the city's cultural transformation. As you view the works, picture the surrounding landscape of BEXCO and Centum City too. Busan's shift from a port-and-industry city to an international cultural city is embedded in the museum's role.
detailEn:
The Busan Museum of Art, opened in 1998, was Busan's first municipal art museum. Today, with large cultural facilities like Centum City, BEXCO, and the Busan Cinema Center clustered nearby, its location seems natural—but back in the early 1990s, when the museum's construction was decided, this area looked very different. Busan wanted to build a public art museum befitting a major city with an international port, and construction on the museum began around the same time as work began on Gwangan Bridge and the city was starting to talk about becoming an 'international film and video culture city.' The museum, in other words, is a product of a period when the city's internationalization and the expansion of its cultural infrastructure advanced together.

From its earliest days, the museum weighed two roles at once: collecting and researching Busan's regional artists and art history, and connecting the flow of international contemporary art to Busan. Its acquisition of Nam June Paik's new-media works and its exhibitions exploring the relationship between video and art were tied to the city's mood at the time, which, alongside the Busan International Film Festival, aspired to become a 'city of film and video culture.' At the same time, the museum kept up a steady stream of exhibitions and archival work organizing the city's first generation of artists and its regional art history.

After a major renovation that began in 2024, the museum reopened in 2026, marking another turning point for the institution itself. Redesigning the galleries, storage facilities, and visitor spaces wasn't just about refreshing the artwork on display—it was also a process of updating how a public museum built in 1998 operates to match today's viewing culture. Looking at the building, the renovation's significance comes through more clearly if you notice how the new entrance, open lobby, and exhibition spaces connect to the surrounding city.

A local guide would tell you not to just follow the titles on the wall labels, but to ask yourself why this museum was built around the same time Centum City itself was taking shape. Once you know this, the Busan Museum of Art stops being just a building for viewing exhibitions and starts to look like an institution that has used art to document, since the 1990s, the city's shift in image from an industrial port city to an international cultural city.
tipsEn:
Route: Check the current exhibition list first, then tour the galleries floor by floor along with the outdoor artworks.
Photo spot: A point where the building's lines and an outdoor sculpture appear together works well.
Caution: Follow each artwork's photography rules and no-flash signage.

simpleEn: Seonamsa is a mountain temple where the valley, rock formations, and halls of Baegyangsan come together. Its founding legend tied to Wonhyo, the stories behind its name, and its many reconstructions all carry the long history of faith kept alive on this site. Rather than just seeing the main hall and moving on, take a look at Geungnakgyo Bridge, the stream, and the rock formations behind it. Instead of trying to date the buildings, look at the relationship between the forest, the water, and the halls—it brings the scenery of this old mountain temple, still standing near the city center, into sharper focus.
detailEn:
Seonamsa is a quiet temple on the slopes of Baegyangsan, but its founding story reaches back to the Silla period. According to Korea Tourism Organization records, it was founded in 675 CE by the monk Wonhyo, and was originally called 'Gyeongangsa.' Two different stories survive about how it later came to be called Seonamsa. One tradition holds that Hwarang warriors trained in martial arts on the cliff rocks behind the temple, giving rise to the name 'Seonam' ('immortal rock'); another account holds that the name changed during a reconstruction under King Seongjong of Joseon. The fact that a single name carries overlapping legend and record is part of what makes an old temple like this interesting.

On the temple grounds, it's worth looking beyond the main hall (Daeungjeon) to take in the valley, the stone bridge, and the rock formations behind it as well. Around the Daeungjeon are arranged several halls—Geungnakjeon, Gwaneumjeon, Myeongbujeon, and others—and the stone bridge crossing the valley is called Geungnakgyo. Behind the Yongwangdan (Dragon King shrine), a small waterfall called Seonam Falls flows, and above it stands a sheer rock formation called Sinseonam ('Immortal Rock'). The temple's name and its surrounding terrain aren't separate things—the rocks and water of the mountain were drawn into the sacred space to form a single continuous story.

Seonamsa has reached its present form through repeated reconstruction over the centuries. Rather than the original buildings surviving intact through the Japanese invasions of the 1590s and the years since, people have kept the faith alive here by rebuilding and repairing again and again. So when viewing the temple, it makes more sense to look at how the old site, the valley, and the halls have been maintained generation after generation, rather than trying to find 'the building that's hundreds of years old.' The camellia trees on the stone terraces and the forest pressing in close to the halls also help create the atmosphere of a mountain temple on Baegyangsan.

A local guide would tell you not to compare Seonamsa to famous large temples, but to notice the relationship between the sound of the water, the rocks, and the halls. Once you know this, the temple stops looking like just a quiet spot near the city and starts to look like a mountain temple that, from its founding legend tied to Wonhyo through the Hwarang story to its many reconstructions, has long sustained the local faith together with the terrain of Baegyangsan.
tipsEn:
Route: From the entrance, climb up into the temple grounds and tour the main halls followed by the surrounding forest paths.
Photo spot: A composition showing the halls and stone steps connected through the forest works well.
Caution: Check on-site signage for whether photography inside the halls is allowed and which areas are open to visitors.

simpleEn: The name of the Cheongsapo Daritdol Skywalk is said to come from five rocks lying offshore like stepping stones ('daritdol'). After watching the waves beneath your feet on the deck's glass floor extending out over the sea, look up and try to spot the rocks the name comes from. The harbor, the lighthouses, and the old railway above all connect into the same story. A coast where residents once read the tides and terrain to make a living has today become a place where travelers read the scenery and the story of the village.
detailEn:
The name of the Cheongsapo Daritdol Skywalk doesn't come from the shape of the observation deck itself, but from the 'daritdol' (stepping stones) offshore. Five rock islets called Andol, Neopdeokdol, Geomutdol, Sangjwa, and Seogudol line up in the sea off Cheongsapo, and from a distance they look like stepping stones laid across the water—hence the name daritdol. With strong currents and good rocky terrain, this area has also long been known as a productive spot for seafood. The skywalk is, in effect, a structure that extends that place name from the land out toward the sea.

Once you step onto the skywalk, the first things you notice are the U-shaped deck extending far out over the sea and its glass floor. Seeing the waves beneath your feet can be nerve-wracking, but a local guide would tell you not to just look down—look outward for the rock islets too. Once you actually spot the five rocks the name comes from, 'Daritdol Skywalk' suddenly starts to read as a description of the terrain rather than just a name. Taking in the coastline, the rocks, and the direction of the waves together also gives you an intuitive sense of why this area was such a good spot for fishing.

Seen alongside Cheongsapo's legend of the pine tree of the waiting wife, its harbor, and its twin lighthouses, the skywalk isn't a standalone attraction. Above it run the Haeundae Blueline Park and the old railway line; below it lie the traces of an old fishing village and its maritime livelihood. A coast where residents once made their living by reading the tides and the rocks has today, through the train, the skywalk, and the walking paths, become a place where travelers read the scenery instead.

Once you know this, the Daritdol Skywalk becomes more than a place to feel a thrill on a glass floor—it looks like a device that lets today's tourist route look anew at the rocks and waterways that the people of Cheongsapo named and used long ago. Before heading out the exit, take one more look for the rocks scattered across the sea, and the skywalk's name will stay with you much longer.
tipsEn:
Route: At the entrance, put on the provided shoe covers and check the safety instructions, then walk slowly out to the far viewing section.
Photo spot: Frame the shot so the skywalk's curve and the blue sea line up in one direction.
Caution: Don't run on the glass floor or reach your phone out past the railing.

simpleEn: Behind Gamcheon Culture Village's bright, colorful houses lies the residential landscape of people who built their lives on a mountain slope. Homes belonging to war refugees and members of the Taegeukdo religious community, stacked layer upon layer along the alleys, have been joined by art and urban regeneration to create today's village. After taking your photo with the Little Prince statue, take a look at how the rooftops and narrow lanes are laid out too. In a place where residents still live their daily lives, read the moment in Busan's history where the life of refugees and community met public art.
detailEn:
Gamcheon Culture Village is famous for its colorful houses and its Little Prince statue, but what deserves attention before the color is the way the houses are set into the mountain slope. Gamcheon began as a hillside village formed by refugees who settled here during the Korean War, and it took on today's form of dense, layered housing in earnest with the founding of a Taegeukdo religious settlement in the 1950s. Official village materials trace the old name 'Gamnae' back to 'geom,' an archaic word for a deity, combined with 'nae,' meaning stream. Even the name carries memories of the village that go back far further than today's tourist attraction.

Looking down at the houses from a high viewpoint, you can see a distinctive structure of rooftops stepping down the slope like a staircase. According to official descriptions, the houses were arranged to preserve sunlight and views for the homes behind them, and the alleys wind through the village like a maze, following the mountain's contour lines. A set of living rules devised so that many people could share a limited, sloped patch of land has become Gamcheon's signature landscape today. What matters is that this form was shaped first by the needs of survival and community, not designed from the start to look picturesque for tourists.

From the late 2000s, community art projects involving local artists and residents brought artwork into empty spaces and alleyways, and Gamcheon became an internationally known tourist destination. But the murals and sculptures don't stand in for the village's history. If anything, they act as a medium drawing visitors into the alleys to see the old housing pattern and residents' daily life with fresh eyes. That's why the stepped houses visible behind the Little Prince statue matter more than the statue itself.

At the most famous photo spot, a local guide would tell you to turn your camera slightly to take in the structure of the alleys and rooftops. Once you know this, Gamcheon Culture Village looks less like its nickname, 'Korea's Machu Picchu,' and more like a living village from Busan's modern history—a settlement built by war refugees that residents and artists, through urban regeneration, reinterpreted into a tourist destination. And above all, the basic rule for visiting is remembering that people still live here.
tipsEn:
Route: Check the recommended route at the information center, then follow it through the main alleys, the Little Prince statue, and the viewpoint sections.
Photo spot: A point where the stepped houses appear layered behind the Little Prince statue works well.
Caution: Avoid photographing front doors and windows, and don't block residents' passage.

simpleEn: The real subject of the Amisan Observatory is the Nakdong River estuary, whose shape keeps changing where the river meets the sea. Sandbars, tidal flats, shallow water, and reed beds create the conditions migratory birds need to feed and rest. Even the building's design, evoking birds and sandbars, is tied to the ecology visible outside its windows. After watching the colors of the sunset, take a look at the lines of the islands and waterways too. In a landscape that shifts with the seasons and the currents, feel how the estuary is still a living, moving stretch of land.
detailEn:
The true star of the Amisan Observatory isn't the observatory building itself, but the Nakdong River estuary outside its windows, whose shape is constantly changing. The building serves as the general information center for the Busan National Geopark, offering a single vantage point to take in the sandbars and tidal flats formed where the river meets the sea, along with migratory birds and sunsets. Sand and silt carried downstream by the Nakdong River slow down and settle where the river meets the sea, and tides and waves keep reshaping them—so the islands and waterways of the estuary aren't a fixed scene but a landform that keeps moving.

The building's exterior carries this estuary story too. Part of the observatory's shape is designed to evoke a bird perched by the water and a sandbar, so that from a distance its character as an ecological observation facility comes through. If you view the indoor exhibits on the estuary's geology and ecology first and then look outside, instead of just thinking 'there's an island out there,' you start picking out which part is a sandbar and where river water and seawater are mixing. The way the exhibits and the actual view sit right up against each other is this place's best feature.

The reason so many migratory birds gather at the Nakdong estuary has less to do with the sandbars themselves than with the combination of shallow water, tidal flats, and reed beds all together. Where river water and seawater mix, plankton, shellfish, and small fish are abundant, and the reeds give birds a place to hide and rest. So while spotting a single bird through binoculars is fun, it's more important to connect why that bird chose to stop here specifically to the shape of the whole estuary.

A local guide wouldn't just tell you the sunset colors are pretty. They'd point out that the outline of the sandbars beneath the sunset can shift from year to year and season to season. Once you know this, the Amisan Observatory stops looking like just a tall building for watching sunsets and starts to look like a classroom of nature, right beside the metropolis of Busan, where you can observe the river and sea still building new land and sustaining the lives of migratory birds.
tipsEn:
Route: Learn about the estuary's ecology through the indoor exhibits first, then take in the outside view from the viewing spaces on each floor.
Photo spot: A composition at dusk where the sandbars and river appear in layers works well.
Caution: Avoid flash and loud noise directed at the birds, and be considerate when using telescope viewing equipment.

simpleEn: Club D Oasis combines Haeundae's high-rise views with water leisure and Korean-style bathing and jjimjilbang culture. You can play in the water while looking out at the sea, then move between warm rooms and rest areas to stay a while. Look out the window at the sandy beach and the city. The view you'd normally see at eye level from the beach becomes something different from up here—a sense of height and rest. Come see how Haeundae has expanded from a place for looking at the sea into a place for a long, restful stay.
detailEn:
Club D Oasis isn't a place to view historical heritage the way one of Busan's old hot spring resorts is, but it's a good example of how Haeundae tourism has shifted from 'a trip to look at the sea' to 'a stay-in-the-city kind of trip where you rest.' Located high up in the LCT Haeundae towers, it's built so visitors can look down at the sea while using its water park, spa, and jjimjilbang facilities. Rather than going into the water at the beach directly, this is a modern style of marine tourism that lets people consume sea views, water play, and rest all at once, indoors.

What's interesting about this space is the way traditional Korean bathing and jjimjilbang culture is blended with resort-style facilities in one place. Korea's jjimjilbang culture developed as a lifestyle where, after bathing, people eat and rest for hours in a shared common area—and at Club D Oasis, this pattern is combined with high-rise views, water leisure, and wellness offerings. For a foreign traveler, it might seem odd that a pool and a jjimjilbang are used at the same facility, but it makes more sense once you remember that in Korea, washing spaces and resting spaces have long developed together as part of the same culture.

The view of Haeundae outside the window is also an important part of the experience. The same sea looks completely different when viewed at eye level from the sand versus looking down from a high floor. Taking in the curve of Haeundae Beach, Mipo and Dongbaekseom Island, and the density of the high-rises lets you physically feel how strongly a natural beach and a super-tall-tower tourist city overlap in this area.

A local guide would talk less about how many facilities there are and more about how the way Busan locals and travelers enjoy the sea has changed. Once you know this, Club D Oasis stops looking like just an indoor water park, and starts to look like a scene from 21st-century Busan tourism, where Haeundae's super-tall-tower development, Korean bathing and rest culture, and modern wellness tourism all come together inside a single building.
tipsEn:
Route: After completing check-in, use the spa and water zones, then move on to the view rest areas.
Photo spot: A window-side shot where the Haeundae sea and the indoor water surface appear together works well.
Caution: Be sure to follow each facility's safety rules and any restrictions on phone photography.

simpleEn: On the Haeundae River Cruise, Centum City, parks, bridges, and the waterfront city all come together into a single view along the Suyeong River. Seen from the low vantage point of the water's surface, the scale of bridges you'd normally just drive across, and the layout of the buildings, feel new again. Pay attention too to the night reflections, the width of the water, and the shifting wind and waves. Busan's waterways, once known mainly as routes for industry and fishing, are expanding into spaces that connect cultural facilities, residents' leisure, and travel.
detailEn:
Boarding the Haeundae River Cruise shows you a completely different Busan than the one you see looking at the sea from Gwangalli or Haeundae on land. It departs from the banks of the Suyeong River, near APEC Naru Park and Centum City. The Suyeong River is an urban stream that gathers water from Geumjeongsan and the Dongnae area and flows into Suyeong Bay; in the past it was a waterway closely tied to the daily life and fishing of the surrounding villages. Today, with high-rises, bridges, parks, and cultural facilities surrounding it, it has changed character into one of Busan's signature urban waterfront spaces.

As the boat moves along the river, buildings in Centum City, the Busan Cinema Center, APEC Naru Park, and Marine City, which look separate from each other when seen from the road, come together into what feels like one continuous waterfront city. Passing under bridges at the low height of the water's surface, in particular, makes the bridges you'd normally just drive across feel far larger in scale. The moment your reference point for viewing the city shifts from land to the water, the river stops looking like an obstacle to be crossed and starts to look like a central axis connecting several districts.

After the sun sets, the lights reflected on the water's surface create the effect of the scenery doubling in size. Marine City and Gwangan Bridge are famous for their night views, but a local guide would tell you not to just watch the lights—also notice how the width of the water, the waves, and the wind change as you move from the river out toward the sea. That shift, from the calm water of the stream to the open sea of Suyeong Bay, is the story told by the route itself.

Once you know this, the Haeundae River Cruise isn't just a boat ride for watching night views. It lets you experience firsthand, on the water, how Busan's waterways—once known mainly as industrial harbors and fishing ports—are changing today into spaces of daily life and tourism connecting citizen parks, cultural facilities, and marine leisure. The biggest pleasure of this cruise is discovering that when the height and direction from which you view the same city change, Busan's structure reads completely differently too.
tipsEn:
Route: Arrive at the boarding dock early to receive boarding instructions, then enjoy the view from your assigned seat and the deck.
Photo spot: A moment on the water where Gwangan Bridge and Marine City appear together works well.
Caution: Follow life jacket rules and crew instructions, and don't lean on the railing while the boat is moving.

simpleEn: On Geumjeongsan, Godangbong Peak, the Geumsaem spring, Beomeosa Temple, and the mountain fortress all connect along a single ridgeline. Water pooling in a hollow of rock became a spring carrying legend and faith, while the high ridge was used as the site for fortress walls built to prepare against invasion. Rather than treating the summit as the only goal, try connecting the rock formations, fortress gates, and the temple's location. Here you can encounter a vast historical landscape where Busan's place names, Buddhist culture, and the defense system that protected the city have built up together with the natural terrain.
detailEn:
To people in Busan, Geumjeongsan is more than just a hiking spot—it's closer to the city's guardian mountain, where the fortress, temple, and legends that have protected the north side of the city all come together. A long ridge extends from the highest peak, Godangbong, and Beomeosa Temple, Geumjeongsanseong Fortress, and Sanseong Village all sit within the same mountain. Both the name Geumjeongsan and the founding legend of Beomeosa Temple feature the story of 'Geumsaem,' a spring on a rock south of Godangbong. According to legend, a golden fish rode down on multicolored clouds to play in the spring, and this is said to be where the name Geumjeong, meaning 'golden well,' comes from.

See Geumsaem in person and you'll find water pooled in a hollow at the top of a massive rock. It's a case where a natural landform—a hollow worn into bedrock by weathering—was interpreted as a sacred spring, combining terrain and faith. The huge granite rocks and tor-like formations found throughout Geumjeongsan are another feature of the mountain. From a distance it looks like a single mountain, but up close there's a lot of rock split apart and rounded by weathering, which is why it's also an important geological site within the Busan National Geopark.

Geumjeongsanseong Fortress, running along the ridge, is another face of the mountain. It's a large-scale mountain fortress built using the mountain's own terrain to prepare against invasion, and walking along its gates and walls lets you feel firsthand why a high ridge was such an advantage for defense. Beomeosa Temple is an old temple with a founding tradition tied to the Silla-era monk Uisang, and Sanseong Village carries on the culture of residents who have lived inside the fortress walls. Nature, military history, faith, and daily life all overlap on this one mountain.

A local guide would tell you not to make a summit photo at Godangbong your only goal, but to connect the rock formations, the fortress walls, and the location of Beomeosa Temple as if reading a single map. Once you know this, Geumjeongsan stops looking like just 'one of Busan's tallest mountains' and starts to look like a vast historical landscape where the city's place names, legends, defense system, and Buddhist culture have built up together for centuries.
tipsEn:
Route: Depending on your fitness level, pick one section—Beomeosa Temple, Sanseong Village, or Godangbong—and hike that.
Photo spot: A ridge section where the fortress walls and Busan's city skyline unfold together works well.
Caution: Avoid hiking in bad weather or after sunset, and stick to the designated trails.

simpleEn: Gwangan Bridge is a sea bridge that, since opening in 2003, has changed both traffic patterns and the beach scenery around Suyeong Bay. Its towers, cables, and long double-deck span connect the city's living areas by day and become the backdrop for Gwangalli by night. Look at it not just head-on, but from different angles too—from Millak, Yongho-dong, and up on the mountain. Once you take in the cities and coastlines on both sides of the bridge, you'll sense that this familiar landmark is a piece of infrastructure that has connected Busan's transportation, housing, and tourism.
detailEn:
Gwangan Bridge feels like a natural symbol of Busan today, but before it opened in 2003, the view of the sea in front of Gwangalli looked completely different. The bridge was built as a large-scale sea road connecting Suyeong-gu with the Haeundae and Centum areas, meant to disperse downtown traffic. After it opened, travel times and living patterns along the surrounding roads changed, and at the same time, the night view of Gwangalli Beach was entirely remade. It's a prime example of a single piece of transportation infrastructure reshaping even a city's tourism image.

Seen from the beach, the bridge looks like a single line, but it's actually a massive structure combining a double-deck design, a long over-water section, and a suspension-bridge span. Crossing it by car, you speed across the water quickly, but viewed from a distance at Gwangalli, the bridge's towers and cables form a horizontal line that shapes the city's skyline. When the lights come on at night, a purely functional roadway turns into a massive urban sculpture. This structure is also why the bridge can be used almost like a stage during the Busan Fireworks Festival.

What's interesting is that Gwangan Bridge leaves a stronger impression on people who look at it than on people who cross it. Viewed from different spots—Gwangalli Beach, Millak, Yongho-dong, Hwangnyeongsan—the bridge's angle and backdrop change, visually tying together several of Busan's different districts. City of Busan records noting that visitor numbers and the surrounding commercial district changed significantly after the bridge opened in 2003 also show that the bridge has played a role that goes beyond transportation.

A local guide would tell you not to stop at 'pretty bridge at night,' but to look at the cities on both sides of it together. Once you know this, Gwangan Bridge stops looking like just a landmark set in the sea off Busan, and starts to look like 21st-century urban infrastructure that reconnected the flows of transportation, housing, and tourism around Suyeong Bay, and changed the very identity of Gwangalli itself.
tipsEn:
Route: Find a spot at Gwangalli Beach or Millak Waterside Park where the whole bridge is visible.
Photo spot: A dusk shot where the water's reflection and the bridge's lighting appear together works well.
Caution: Don't approach the roadway or breakwater, and follow crowd-control instructions during events.

simpleEn: Yongho Byeolbit Park is a place where a working port — the former Yongho Pier — was transformed into a public resting space for citizens. Its wide concrete grounds and open sea view still carry traces of the pier, distinct from the older, tree-filled parks nearby. From here, look at Gwangan Bridge, the harbor, and the direction of Igidae from an angle different from the view at Gwangan Beach. In a workspace once closed to the public, people now walk and enjoy the night view. Feel the shift of a port city returning the sea to everyday life.
detailEn:
Yongho Byeolbit Park was not originally planned as a park. This site was once the working port area known as Yongho Pier, and pier operations stopped after a 2019 accident in which a Russian cargo ship collided with Gwangan Bridge. Afterward, Busan's Nam-gu district signed an agreement with the Busan Port Authority to manage the pier space until redevelopment and temporarily opened it to the public, and in July 2021 it opened under the name "Yongho Byeolbit Park." A pier that ordinary citizens had been unable to freely access for about 30 years was returned as a place of rest.

Entering the park, you take in the wide concrete space, the sea, and Gwangan Bridge all at once. The reason this isn't filled with old trees and forest like a typical city park also traces back to its past as a pier. The flat harbor space once used for ships docking and cargo handling has been kept largely unchanged and repurposed for strolling, events, and night views — leaving visible traces of how an "empty harbor space" was converted into a citizens' park.

The angle from which you see Gwangan Bridge here is also completely different from Gwangan Beach. While Gwangan Beach offers a near-frontal, dazzling night view of the bridge, Yongho-dong shows the bridge's side profile together with the harbor and the coastline toward Igidae. In effect, you're viewing the city's landmark not from the tourist side but from the harbor side. The name "starlight" fits well at night, since the open pier offers a wide view of the sea and the bridge's lights.

A local guide would likely mention, before the pretty night view, that this was a pier ordinary citizens could barely enter until recently. Once you know that, Yongho Byeolbit Park looks less like a newly built coastal park and more like an experiment in transition for Busan's waterfront city — a space where an industrial port's function had stopped, returned to citizens until redevelopment begins.
tipsEn:
Route: Arrive at the park around sunset and take a short walk along the coastal path and viewpoints.
Photo spot: Scenes where the lights of Gwangan Bridge and their reflection on the water appear together are great.
Caution: Watch your step near the water's edge and be mindful of bicycle and kickboard traffic.

simpleEn: Busan Museum displays the city's history while also gathering public memory through citizens' donations. As the museum prepared to open in 1978, personal collections that individuals had kept became part of the region's cultural heritage. Follow the exhibits from prehistoric times through ancient Dongnae to the port-opening era and modern history. As each artifact connects a different span of time, see how personal belongings and local stories both became part of the shared history of Busan on display.
detailEn:
Busan Museum opened in 1978 as Busan's leading comprehensive museum, but the story of citizens is hidden in the very process of its founding. When construction began in 1975, the building was going up, but the museum had not yet secured enough artifacts to fill it. At the time, the city of Busan asked local collectors of antique art to donate pieces, and a key turning point came when the late Hyun Su-myeong, chairman of Dongyang Rubber, expressed his wish to donate his personal collection of antique art to the new museum.

City records also preserve the story of the civil servant in charge, who spent a long time visiting companies and persuading people to secure donations. In accordance with Chairman Hyun's will, his son, Hyun Seung-hoon, handed the collection over to the city of Busan as it was, and donations from other local figures followed. As a result, the museum's early collection was built not simply through purchases by the administration, but largely from cultural properties that citizens and local businesses offered in the belief that "Busan, too, needs a proper museum."

In the galleries, you can trace Busan's changes from prehistoric times through the ancient period, the Joseon dynasty, and into modern and contemporary history. People lived in this region long before the port of Busan opened, and ancient sites such as the Bokcheon-dong Tumuli, Dongnae's administrative and military culture, and the changes of a port city after its opening all connect to one another. Breaking the impression that "Busan is a city that suddenly appeared in modern times" is an important role the museum plays.

A local guide would likely start not by pointing to a single signature artifact, but by explaining how the museum itself came to be. Once you know that, Busan Museum looks like more than a building displaying Busan's history — it appears as the result of citizens in the 1970s turning their own personal collections into public memory and building a regional cultural institution together. Thinking about "who left this behind, and why" behind each artifact makes the exhibits feel far more like a human story.
tipsEn:
Route: View the permanent exhibition in chronological order, then continue to the outdoor stone monuments and the cultural experience space.
Photo spot: Try capturing a signature artifact together with the exhibition hall's arrangement by era.
Caution: Avoid using flash and touching the exhibits to protect the artifacts.

simpleEn: Gijang Market is a marketplace where seafood and farm produce meet according to the season. Alongside the joy of picking a snow crab and eating it on the spot, everyday stalls selling seaweed, fish, and vegetables line up. Rather than just looking at the big tanks, notice what's in season and abundant that day. Spring seaweed and other seasonal catches change the market's whole character. Feel the flow that connects the sea off Gijang and the surrounding farmland to the tables of the city.
detailEn:
Gijang Market is famous for snow crab, but the market's real character is closer to a "seasonal market" where sea and farmland meet. Because Gijang-eup lies close to both the sea and mountains as well as farmland, not just seafood but vegetables, fruit, and daily goods have long been traded here. So looking at the market stalls, you'll find live fish and seafood on one side and farm produce on the other. This isn't a tourist market built around a single specialty item, but a regional hub market that has gathered daily necessities for Gijang residents.

The stars of the stalls also change with the season. In spring, Gijang seaweed and various sea vegetables appear in abundance, while in autumn, seasonal catches like hairtail stand out. Gijang seaweed's fame isn't just a branding matter — it comes from the long-developed seaweed farming in the cold, well-circulated waters of eastern Busan. Comparing dried seaweed with fresh seaweed also shows how the same marine product is processed differently for distribution.

The snow crab restaurants lining both sides of the alley are a relatively recent element that has strongly shaped the market's image. The style of picking a crab from the tank, checking its weight, and having it cooked on the spot has turned Gijang Market into a "destination" for visitors. But step just a little past the crab alley, and you'll find shops selling side dishes, vegetables, and dried goods — the original character of a local everyday market still remains.

A local guide wouldn't just point to the biggest crab tank — they'd tell you to notice what appears on the stalls each season. Once you know that, Gijang Market looks less like a place to just go eat crab, and more like a "calendar of local ingredients," where food produced in the sea off Gijang and the surrounding farmland is delivered to city dwellers in seasonal order.
tipsEn:
Route: Browse the seafood section and compare prices, then check the restaurant's cooking and table-setting terms.
Photo spot: The lively scene of crab tanks lined up with the market signage is a great shot.
Caution: Confirm the total price, any extra charges, and the origin of the seafood before ordering.

simpleEn: The Busan Fishing Village Folk Museum shows the lives of people living along the path from the Nakdong River to the sea. The shapes of boats, nets, and fish traps carry the wisdom of daily life, adapted to water depth, currents, and the creatures being caught. Salt production and distribution at the river's estuary are also a story connecting food and the local economy. After viewing the exhibits, look out at the Nakdong River. Beyond the park and the bridge, you can picture boats coming and going, fish being caught, and salt being made, all overlapping with today's view.
detailEn:
The name Busan Fishing Village Folk Museum might make you think only of a coastal fishing village, but its core theme is really "life extending from the river to the sea." That's why the building sits in Hwamyeong-dong, overlooking the Nakdong River. To the people of Busan, the Nakdong River was never just a big river — it was the foundation of life that made farming, fishing, boat travel, and markets possible. The museum shows this through fishing tools and everyday items used by people who lived along the river, its estuary, and the sea.

When looking at tools like boats, nets, and fish traps in the exhibition, it helps to think not just about their shape but about "what kind of water was this used in?" Fishing in a flowing river and fishing in the sea require different tools, since water depth, current, and species differ. The stories of the sailboats that once traveled the seven-hundred-li length of the Nakdong River and the Gupo Market dock also show that the river was once as important a transportation route as a road. What bridges and cars handle today, waterways and boats once handled.

Recent exhibitions also highlight the salt culture of the Nakdong River estuary. Salt fields once developed around the estuary, and the distribution of jayeom — salt made by boiling down seawater using traditional methods — influenced the local economy and food culture. This shows that "Busan's fishing villages" were not places that only caught fish, but communities whose way of life drew on a range of resources, including salt, seaweed, and both river and sea.

A local guide would tell you to be sure to look out at the Nakdong River after viewing the exhibits. Today you see a riverside park, apartments, and a bridge, but on that same waterway there was once a time when boats came and went, fish were caught, and salt was made. Once you know that, the Busan Fishing Village Folk Museum looks like more than a collection of old tools — it becomes a place that overlays today's cityscape with the living skills and wisdom of the people of the Nakdong River who shaped western Busan.
tipsEn:
Route: View the fishing tools in the permanent exhibition, then continue on to the space related to the Nakdong River ecosystem.
Photo spot: A scene showing boat and fishing gear models displayed together works well.
Caution: Avoid touching the exhibits and using flash photography.

simpleEn: At Oryukdo Sunrise Park, you'll meet the rocky islands said to look like five or six depending on the viewing angle and the tide. Their rock formations hold traces of ancient volcanic activity and the waves that carved away the land over time. From the grassy hill, look down at the cliffs and outer islands below. The terrain connecting to the Skywalk and the Igidae coast reads as a single continuous process. Within the sunrise scenery unfolds the story of how Busan's geology and place names came to be.
detailEn:
Standing at Oryukdo Sunrise Park, the first thing you do is count the islands. Oryukdo actually consists of six rocky islands clustered together, but depending on the viewing direction and tide conditions, some islands appear to overlap or merge, making them look like five or six — which is said to be the origin of the name (oryuk meaning "five or six"). Just knowing this simple story behind the name turns the act of looking at the islands into a small observation. Even coming back to the same spot, the impression can change depending on the sea's condition.

Geologically, an even longer span of time is hidden here. The Busan Geopark explains that Oryukdo's rock formations were created by volcanic activity at the end of the Cretaceous period, about 80 million years ago, and that the islands remained connected to the mainland as a small peninsula until about 120,000 years ago, before long-term wave erosion separated them. Today's steep cliffs, wave-cut platforms, and sea caves are evidence that "the islands were not originally separate — the sea kept carving them out over time."

The grassy hill of Sunrise Park serves as the most comfortable viewing spot to look down on Oryukdo from above. Looking together at the Oryukdo Skywalk below and the Igidae coastal trail also shows that the mainland cliffs and the rocky islands are connected through the same geology and erosion process. That's why it's far more interesting to see Oryukdo not just as six separate islands in a photo, but as one continuous coastal landform extending from Igidae.

A local guide wouldn't just point out the direction of the sunrise — they'd explain why the islands you see now number six, and how long the sea has been carving away at this land. Once you know that, Oryukdo Sunrise Park looks like more than a hillside park for viewing the sea — it becomes a natural observatory for understanding, at a glance, Busan's volcanic activity, coastal erosion, and how the place name Oryukdo came to be.
tipsEn:
Route: Follow the park's walking trail through the viewpoints and on toward the Skywalk direction.
Photo spot: A wide composition with Oryukdo visible beyond the curve of the hill works well.
Caution: Do not approach cliff edges or restricted areas.

simpleEn: Busan Tower is an observation facility built in 1973 atop Yongdusan Park to mark the center of Busan, a port city. Its upper structure echoes the shape of the ornamental canopy (bogae) of Dabotap Pagoda, together with the image of a lighthouse. From the observation deck, look out in different directions toward Nampo-dong, Jagalchi, Yeongdo, and the hillside neighborhoods of Sanbokdoro. Markets, the harbor, and hillside houses overlap closely. In the density of the old downtown — so different from the high-rise new towns — read the growth and passage of time in Busan.
detailEn:
Busan Tower has served as one of Busan's iconic observation facilities ever since it was built atop Yongdusan Park in 1973. Today the ultra-high observation decks of Haeundae stand taller, but what makes Busan Tower special is that it sits right in the middle of the old downtown, connecting the harbor, the markets, and the hillside roads in a single view. At the time it was built, the 120-meter tower symbolized Busan's modernization and its image as a port city, and it also served as a landmark announcing the city's center to anyone arriving by sea.

The tower's design also carries the symbolism of its era. City of Busan materials describe the upper part of the observation deck as modeled on the ornamental canopy (bogae) of Dabotap Pagoda at Bulguksa Temple in Gyeongju, with an overall structure reminiscent of a lighthouse. In effect, the design layers "the lighthouse of a port city" and "the form of traditional Korean architecture" onto a single structure, expressing Busan as both a modern city and a distinctly Korean one. Knowing this symbolism, rather than just seeing the tower itself, reveals how a 1970s city wanted to present itself.

From the observation deck, Nampo-dong, Jagalchi, Yeongdo, the North Port, and the hillside roads unfold in every direction. Where Haeundae's observation deck shows the skyline of a high-rise new town, Busan Tower shows the density of an old port city. Markets, low-rise shops, harbor facilities, and hillside housing sit remarkably close together — a defining feature of the old downtown. Taking in this view naturally helps you understand why Busan's old center formed in this particular area.

A local guide wouldn't just come down after seeing the night view — they'd suggest taking a good look toward the harbor once during the day too. Once you know that, Busan Tower looks like more than an old observation deck — it becomes both a symbol of 1970s Busan trying to present itself as a port city connected to the world, and today, an observation tower for comparing the changes and passage of time in the old downtown.
tipsEn:
Route: Walk through the park first, then go up the tower and take in the views and exhibits in each direction in turn.
Photo spot: A scene where the Port of Busan and the hillside roads overlap beyond the observation window is great.
Caution: Don't lean on the glass, and check operating hours and admission conditions.

simpleEn: The story of Mt. Hwangnyeong Observatory begins not with the night view, but with beacon signals. During the Joseon dynasty, the summit sent urgent news to nearby mountains using smoke by day and fire by night. Being visible from all directions was exactly what a signal network required. After taking in Gwangan Bridge, also look at the beacon mound and the city in other directions. From the spot where we now look down at city lights, people once used fire to relay news and crises across Busan.
detailEn:
Looking out at the night view from Mt. Hwangnyeong Observatory, Gwangan Bridge and the lights of Haeundae catch your eye first, but this mountain's real story begins with "signals" rather than "views." The beacon mound at the summit of Mt. Hwangnyeong was one of the centers of Busan's Joseon-era beacon network. Records already mention the Mt. Hwangnyeong beacon mound in 1425, the seventh year of King Sejong's reign, and it connected with the Ganbio Mountain beacon mound in Haeundae to the east, the Gubong beacon mound to the west, and the Gyemyeong Mountain beacon mound to the north, relaying urgent news onward to the next region.

Beacons were a national communication network that used smoke by day and fire by night. The number of smoke plumes or fires raised varied depending on normal conditions or the degree of an approaching enemy threat, and when bad weather made signals invisible, news was relayed to the next beacon station by other means. The high spot where we now view the night lights was once a "communication base" for exchanging news with distant regions. Being visible from all directions from the summit is an advantage for tourists today, but back then it was a condition for transmitting military intelligence.

Turning to face different directions from the observatory makes this geographic advantage even more apparent. Not just Gwangalli and Haeundae, but areas toward Seomyeon, Nam-gu, and Yeonje-gu come into view all at once. A defining feature of Mt. Hwangnyeong is that, rising in the middle of the city, it offers a field of view connecting Busan in many directions. Reading the lights below as lines of roads and residential areas also reveals how the city has expanded outward in every direction, centered on the mountain.

A local guide wouldn't just call it "Busan's best night-view spot" — they'd first rest a hand on the beacon mound and invite you to imagine which mountain the old signals traveled to. Once you know that, Mt. Hwangnyeong Observatory looks like more than a spot for looking down at the night lights — it becomes one of Busan's ancient observation points, a place that relayed crises and news by fire hundreds of years ago and today lets you read the entire city at a glance.
tipsEn:
Route: From the parking or drop-off point, go up to the observatory and follow the directional signboards around the city.
Photo spot: Near the beacon mound, capture a wide shot of Gwangan Bridge and the downtown lights.
Caution: Avoid parking along the roadside edge and don't go beyond the railings.

simpleEn: The hill of Yongdusan Park layers the time of a colonial-era shrine, refugee housing, and a postwar citizens' park on top of one another. Its name and function changed with the times, and Busan Tower and the flower clock were added to shape today's appearance. In the plaza, look at the surrounding monuments and the direction of the harbor. Beneath what looks like a clean resting space lie traces of war, fire, and urban change. It is the history of a hill used differently by generation after generation.
detailEn:
Yongdusan Park is familiar as the tourist park where Busan Tower stands, but this hill is a place where Busan's modern and contemporary history has been overwritten many times. During Japanese colonial rule, a shrine built by Japanese residents stood here, and after liberation it was redeveloped as a park. During the Korean War, refugees who flooded into Busan built shanty houses around the area, and in the mid-1950s a major fire that burned down the refugee settlement also remains a painful memory. Beneath today's clean plaza, the layers of the colonial period, war, and a refugee city overlap.

The park's name has also changed with the times. After liberation, it was for a time called Unam Park, after President Rhee Syng-man's pen name, before regaining the name Yongdusan Park in the 1960s. The place name Yongdusan is said to come from the mountain's shape, said to resemble a dragon raising its head toward the sea. Combined with its position overlooking the Port of Busan, this naturally created an image like "a dragon guarding the harbor."

When Busan Tower and the flower clock were installed in 1973, the park began taking on the landmark image it has today. A Citizens' Bell and various commemorative monuments were later added, making it a space for national events, the New Year's bell-ringing ceremony, and everyday citizen rest all at once. Walking through the park today, almost no trace of the colonial period remains visible, but that very process of being erased and rebuilt is itself the history of Yongdusan. It shows how even a city park's name and function change according to the values of each era.

A local guide wouldn't just point out Busan Tower and head back down — they'd suggest standing in the middle of the plaza and thinking about how many times this space has been used for different purposes. Once you know that, Yongdusan Park looks like more than a resting park in the old downtown — it becomes a stage of Busan's modern and contemporary history, layering a colonial-era shrine, a refugee settlement, and a postwar citizens' park together with Busan Tower on a single hill.
tipsEn:
Route: Take the Gwangbok-ro escalator up, view the plaza and monuments, then continue on to Busan Tower.
Photo spot: A central composition showing Busan Tower together with the plaza monuments is great.
Caution: During events, follow the barriers and designated viewing route.

simpleEn: The brick building of the Provisional Capital Memorial Hall was built in 1926 as the provincial governor's residence, then used as the presidential residence during the Korean War. War turned an ordinary house into a space where national policy and diplomacy were discussed. Walk through the office, dining room, and living spaces, and picture the refugee village nearby as well. National decisions and the harsh daily lives of citizens unfolded in the same city. The time when Busan took on the role of the nation's capital is held within this house.
detailEn:
The central building of the Provisional Capital Memorial Hall was not originally built as a presidential residence. It was a two-story brick house built in 1926 as the provincial governor's residence, after South Gyeongsang Province's provincial office moved from Jinju to Busan in 1925, and it was used as the presidential residence from 1950 to 1953 after the Korean War broke out and Busan became South Korea's provisional capital. An ordinary official residence suddenly became an important political space for the nation because of the war.

Looking at the office, reception room, dining room, and bedroom inside, the impression is closer to a residential house than a lavish palace. But major wartime policy and diplomatic affairs were discussed in these rooms, while at the same time the daily life of the president's family and staff continued. That national decision-making and personal daily life overlapped within the same house is the building's most distinctive feature. When looking at a desk or piece of furniture, it's worth thinking less about "who used it" and more about "how urgently state institutions had to repurpose Busan's existing spaces during the war."

A separate exhibition hall covers the outbreak of the Korean War, the lives of refugees, and the politics, economy, and culture of the provisional capital period together. During the war, Busan was effectively the nation's center — home to the central government, the National Assembly, diplomatic offices, and gathered journalists and cultural figures — but it was also a city where refugees from across the country suffered severe housing and food shortages. The contrast of national policy being decided on one side while people endured each day in hillside shanty houses on the other is the reality of Busan as a wartime refugee capital.

A local guide wouldn't just present the residence as "the house where the president lived" — they'd suggest viewing it alongside the refugee history of nearby Ami-dong and Bumin-dong. Once you know that, the Provisional Capital Memorial Hall is more than a restored living space of one politician — it becomes a place showing the time when war suddenly forced a provincial city to take on the function of a national capital, and citizens and refugees had to bear that weight together.
tipsEn:
Route: Follow the rooms and exhibition route through the residence building, then take a slow walk through the outdoor garden.
Photo spot: A spot showing the old residence's exterior together with the garden works well.
Caution: Avoid indoor flash photography and touching the exhibits.

simpleEn: The name of Chungmu-dong Dawn Market carries the rhythm of trade that once began each day in step with the boats arriving at Namhang, the South Port. Fish and vegetables from Gimhae gather in the same early morning hours and spread out to restaurants and the tables of the city. Watch the merchants sorting the morning's goods and the movement of handcarts. In the alleys where seafood and farm produce meet, feel how the distribution network linking the harbor and nearby farmland prepares the day for the people of Busan.
detailEn:
The name Chungmu-dong Dawn Market comes from the actual hours when the market once opened. When boats that had fished all night came into Busan's South Port at dawn, seafood was brought ashore immediately, and as merchants and customers gathered at that hour, a market naturally formed.
