Today it has operated as a permanent market since 1965, but the name "Dawn Market" still preserves the rhythm of trade that once moved according to the harbor's schedule.

The market looks most like itself if you go very early in the morning. Boxes of seafood and vegetables arrive, and merchants sort and display their goods to start the day. It may feel like an impossibly early hour to visitors, but for restaurants and retailers, it's the crucial time to secure the freshest goods. Unlike a typical shopping mall, which sets its hours around customer convenience, this market has long begun its day according to the transport schedules of boats and farm produce.

Inside the market, a section known as "Gimhae Alley" is also well known. It got its name because vegetables and side dishes shipped directly from Gimhae gather there, showing that Chungmu-dong Dawn Market wasn't a place trading only in seafood, but a distribution market also connected to Busan's nearby farming region. Fish that came in from the sea and vegetables that came from inland meet in the very same early morning hours. Step just a little beyond the market and it connects onward to Jagalchi, Gukje, and Bupyeong markets, forming a vast market district across the old downtown.

A local guide wouldn't point you to the quieter market around lunchtime — they'd have you watch the handcarts and moving goods early in the morning instead. Once you know that, Chungmu-dong Dawn Market looks like more than an old traditional market — it becomes the scene of "dawn logistics," where fishing from Busan's South Port and produce from the Gimhae plain meet on an hourly basis and spread out to the tables of the city.
tipsEn:
Route: Follow the public passageways around sunrise to observe the market's flow, then continue on toward Jagalchi.
Photo spot: A market scene of boxes and handcarts moving under morning light is great.
Caution: Don't block working paths, and ask permission before photographing merchants or their goods.

simpleEn: The 168 Steps was the everyday route refugees and working-class residents took from their hillside homes down to jobs at Busan Station and the harbor. At the communal well below, residents had to draw water and carry it all the way up to their homes. Rather than counting the steps, pause halfway and look back down. The difference in height between the rooftops and the harbor becomes clear. The slope a traveler feels today was, for the people of Busan, the daily climb required for water and a livelihood.
detailEn:
The 168 Steps are exactly that — 168 steep steps — but the heart of this staircase lies in the question of why people had to climb such a steep path every single day. After the Korean War, refugee and working-class housing rapidly expanded along the Choryang hillside road, while jobs, markets, Busan Station, and the harbor all lay below on the flatland. This kind of vertical staircase was the shortest route connecting the homes above to the workplaces below. Today it's a tourist experience, but for residents at the time, it was their daily commute.

There were said to be three communal wells at the bottom of the steps, and traces of one still remain today. In an era without adequate running water, residents had to line up with water jugs and earthenware jars to fetch water. So the well wasn't just a place to draw water — it became the center of daily information, where neighbors met and exchanged news every day. Stories are said to have spread from the well about what was happening in which household, or who had found work.

Standing halfway up the steps, the Port of Busan opens up below and rooftops appear in layers. This height difference is the very condition of life on the hillside road. Imagining carrying a bucket of water, a briquette of coal, or groceries up 168 steps reveals the weight of daily life hidden behind the phrase "a neighborhood with a great view." Even the mobility aids installed today exist precisely because of this steep terrain.

A local guide wouldn't have you count the steps — they'd have you pause halfway and look back down once. Once you know that, the 168 Steps are more than a photo spot in a hillside neighborhood — they become a place to physically experience, step by step, the elevation of daily life in refugee-era Busan, where people climbed between the mountain and the harbor every day in search of water and work.
tipsEn:
Route: Look up from the bottom of the steps, then climb at your own pace and continue on to Ibagu-gil.
Photo spot: Midway up the steps, capture the layered path and the Port of Busan together.
Caution: The steps are slippery in rain or snow, and since it's a residents' walkway, don't block the path.

simpleEn: The Busan Cinema Center is the place that expanded the everyday life of movie-city Busan by giving the Busan International Film Festival a dedicated home. On one side, the long, sweeping Big Roof creates a plaza and outdoor theater unobstructed by columns. Look up at the roof, then watch the crowds gathering below. Screenings, performances, and exhibitions continue here even outside festival season. What began as a once-a-year event has settled into the everyday life and industry of the city.
detailEn:
The Busan Cinema Center is remembered first as a piece of architecture because of its massive roof and dazzling LED display, but the biggest reason this building exists is the Busan International Film Festival. The festival, launched in 1996, grew rapidly, but for a long time it had to hold its events by moving between Nampo-dong and various theaters, and calls grew within the film industry for a dedicated screening venue and a symbolic space of its own. As a result, the Busan Cinema Center was built in Centum City as both the festival's dedicated venue and a permanent film and performance facility, opening in 2011.

The most striking architectural feature is the Big Roof. Over 160 meters long, it's built as a cantilevered structure that appears to float, supported by a single column, shielding the plaza and outdoor theater below from rain and sun while keeping the view unobstructed by columns. At night, LEDs beneath the roof create images and colors, turning the building itself into a kind of screen. A "building for watching movies" becomes, in effect, an imaging device in its own right.

Even outside the festival period, independent and art-house film screenings, performances, and exhibitions continue here. This matters, because it's the infrastructure that keeps the Busan International Film Festival from ending as a mere ten-day event, letting citizens engage with film year-round. If BIFF Square in Nampo-dong symbolizes the festival's origins and street culture, the Busan Cinema Center can be seen as the next stage in Busan's effort to establish a permanent hub for the film industry and visual culture.

A local guide wouldn't just have you look up beneath the Big Roof — they'd have you watch how people gather in the open plaza. Once you know that, the Busan Cinema Center looks like more than a distinctive piece of architecture — it becomes "the home of movie-city Busan," built so that the Busan International Film Festival could grow beyond a temporary event into part of the city's everyday culture and industry.
tipsEn:
Route: View the outdoor plaza and the architecture, then use the indoor spaces according to the screening or exhibition schedule.
Photo spot: Around sunset, capture a wide shot of the roof lighting together with the outdoor plaza.
Caution: Follow no-photography rules during performances or screenings and respect event barriers.

simpleEn: The name Kkangkkang-i Art Village comes from the sound of hammers chipping rust and barnacles off ship hulls. At the ship-repair yards of Daepyeong-dong on Yeongdo Island, this grueling work was long done by women workers, and it remains part of the village's memory. After viewing the murals and artworks, also take a distant look at the actual ships and workshops. Art has been layered onto an industry that still continues today. It is a living village that passes down shipbuilding-repair skills and the history of labor to the next generation.
detailEn:
The name Kkangkkang-i Art Village comes from the actual sound heard when ships were repaired. Daepyeong-dong on Yeongdo Island was long a district dense with ship-repair businesses, and the "kkang-kkang" sound rang through the alleys all day as hammers struck rusted hull surfaces and attached barnacles to chip them off. At its peak, the sound is said to have carried all the way up to the hillside road. Residents naturally came to call the area Kkangkkang-i Village.

It's easy to assume this work was done by male technicians, but the story of Daepyeong-dong's "kkangkkang-i ajumma" (kkangkkang-i aunties) figures prominently in tourism materials. Women workers, suspended by ropes against the hulls, long carried out the grueling labor of striking away rust and debris. Some are said to have suffered hearing loss and tinnitus from the repeated hammering. Behind the cheerful-sounding village name today lies a history of women's labor, shouldering dangerous work to support their families.

A modern shipyard was established in Daepyeong-dong in the 1910s, and after land reclamation, ship-parts businesses and repair yards multiplied, growing the area into the center of Busan's ship-repair industry. Working shipyards and factories still operate there today, so this art village is not a "stage set recreating industrial heritage." Urban regeneration projects have added public art, a village museum, and tours, but the sound of machinery and working ships remain very much part of the present.

A local guide wouldn't start with the murals — they'd first point out a ship's hull and workshop from a distance and explain what kind of labor produced the "kkang-kkang" sound. Once you know that, Kkangkkang-i Art Village looks like more than an old shipyard dressed up with art — it becomes a living industrial village, interpreting nearly a century of ship-repair skill, women's labor, and today's ongoing industry through art to pass on to the next generation.
tipsEn:
Route: Check the route at the village information center, then follow the alley artworks on to the harbor viewpoint.
Photo spot: A harbor scene where cranes and repair ships appear beyond the murals is great.
Caution: Do not enter the work sites or photograph workers without permission.

simpleEn: Gukje Market began as a marketplace right after Korea's liberation, trading goods left behind by the Japanese and belongings brought back by returning Koreans. During the Korean War, refugees and foreign supplies poured in, growing it into a major commercial district where people built their livelihoods. Walk the alleys grouped by trade — fabric, kitchenware, and general goods. Even in its maze-like passages, an old order of trade remains. The changing names — Dotteogi Market, Jayu Market, and Gukje Market — carry Busan's modern history within them.
detailEn:
Gukje Market is often known simply as a market that sprang up suddenly during the Korean War, but its origins actually go back to right after liberation. In 1945, as the Japanese withdrew, people gathered on what was then an empty lot — today's market site — to buy and sell goods the Japanese had left behind and items that Koreans returning from abroad brought with them, and a marketplace naturally formed. Because of the bustling atmosphere of goods being bought and sold wholesale all at once, it was initially called "Dotteogi Market," and in 1948, after buildings were erected, it took the name Jayu Market ("Freedom Market").

When the Korean War broke out, refugees poured into Busan, and the market's scale and role grew enormously. All kinds of goods flowed in — U.S. military supplies, relief goods, foreign luxury items, and even smuggled goods — and for refugees and returnees with no local ties, running a stall was one of the most realistic ways to start earning a living. The market's image of "everything except what doesn't exist" also formed during this period. The market was not simply a shopping space — it was the economic starting point where refugees rebuilt their lives in Busan.

Walking the alleys, you'll find sections divided by goods — secondhand items, kitchenware, lighting, fabric, food, and more. It looks complicated, but this is a commercial structure long shaped so that the same trade clusters together, making it easy for customers to compare and for wholesale and retail transactions to happen. Looking down from the skywalk connecting the second floors of the buildings, you can see that the maze-like alleys are in fact one enormous market made up of many connected buildings and sections.

A local guide wouldn't just point you toward filming locations or food stalls — they'd have you remember how the market's name changed over time. The three names — Dotteogi Market, Jayu Market, and Gukje Market — hold, in order, Busan's modern history of liberation and return, war and refuge, and the distribution of foreign goods. Once you know that, Gukje Market looks like more than a market full of goods — it becomes the center of the old downtown's postwar economy, where people rebuilt their lives after the war by exchanging what they had for what they could get.
tipsEn:
Route: Check the market's section map, choose an alley for the goods you want, then connect on to the food alley.
Photo spot: A long alley with old signage and displayed goods lined up is great.
Caution: Ask permission before photographing merchants, and watch your belongings in crowded passages.

simpleEn: At Mt. Cheonma Sky Observatory, the lights of the South Port, Yeongdo, and the old downtown extend in layers up to the hillside houses. Below at the harbor lay workplaces, and above, homes gathered for a growing population, shaping Busan's living landscape. Before raising your camera, first connect the height of the harbor and the hillside houses with your own eyes. In the lights curving between mountain and sea, read how the times of refuge and urban growth expanded the old downtown.
detailEn:
Mt. Cheonma Sky Observatory is one of the hillside-road viewpoints offering the widest view of Busan's old downtown at night. But what matters here is not the lights themselves so much as "at what height, and how, those lights are spread out." Below Mt. Cheonma lie the South Port and the commercial districts of Jagalchi and Nampo-dong, while on the hillside sits housing built up in layers during the eras of refuge and industrialization. The observatory shows, in a single view, exactly that difference in elevation between the harbor and the hillside village.

Looking toward the South Port, fishing boats, harbor facilities, and the buildings of Yeongdo and the old downtown spread out, and raising your gaze slightly reveals small hillside houses and alley lights layered above. Unlike a flat metropolis with a grid of roads, Busan's night view is distinctive for its lights curving along the gaps between mountain and sea. By day, the steps, rooftops, and harbor structures are clearly visible, and at night, that complex terrain simplifies into lines of light, making the city's form, if anything, even clearer.

The Mt. Cheonma area is also a region where hillside housing expanded as the population surged after the Korean War. To work at the harbor or the markets, people had to go down, while relatively affordable housing rose upward. The "layered lights" that look so beautiful from the observatory today were, for residents at the time, the slope and the daily distance they had to climb up and down. The beauty of the night view and the hardship of daily life come from the very same terrain.

A local guide wouldn't switch the camera to night mode right away — they'd first have you visually connect the height of the harbor with that of the hillside houses. Once you know that, Mt. Cheonma Sky Observatory looks like more than a photo spot for enjoying Busan's night — it becomes an observation deck for urban geography, letting you read, through its lights, how the old downtown, centered on the South Port, expanded up into the hillsides.
tipsEn:
Route: Follow the lit deck to the viewpoint, then return safely along the same path.
Photo spot: A composition beyond the deck railing showing the harbor and layered house lights is great.
Caution: Don't disturb residents' daily life and watch for dark steps and vehicles.

simpleEn: Seomyeon 1-beonga is a downtown district where Busan locals meet up, shop, and spend their evenings. By day it fills with people heading to work and shops; by evening, the same alleys fill with people looking for restaurants and entertainment. Nearby, you'll also find Bujeon Market and Jeonpo's hardware shops and cafe street. Between finding a good meal, watch how people move — transit, old markets, and new alley commerce all come together here at the heart of Busan.
detailEn:
For Busan locals, Seomyeon 1-beonga is less a tourist spot than the city's meeting place, nightlife, and shopping hub rolled into one. The name Seomyeon comes from an old administrative name for the western part of former Dongnae-bu, and today it refers to the commercial center of Busanjin-gu as a whole. Centered on Seomyeon Station, where Busan Metro Lines 1 and 2 cross, department stores, underground shopping arcades, traditional markets, restaurants, and entertainment and cultural facilities are packed together — making it one of the busiest crossroads of daily life in Busan.

Walk through Seomyeon 1-beonga and even a single building can look completely different by day and by night. During the day, people head for shopping, clinics, and offices; from evening on, the alleys fill with people looking for restaurants, bars, and performance or entertainment venues. The signs stacked one above another exist because so many businesses are packed vertically into this narrow downtown space. Long-running local shops sit right next to the latest franchise stores and pop-ups — a sign that Seomyeon isn't a district frozen in one era, but a downtown that keeps surviving by constantly changing what it sells.

Walk a little further and you reach Bujeon Market and the Jeonpo hardware-shop and cafe streets. On one side is an old-fashioned market economy; on the other, a new consumer culture built out of repurposed hardware shops — and Seomyeon's large commercial district connects the two. Layers of urban change sit within just a few blocks: as Busan's commercial center shifted away from the old downtown around Nampo-dong, Seomyeon grew into a new center, and from there culture expanded outward into surrounding alleys like Jeonpo.

A local guide would tell you to watch where people flow from and to, rather than chase one famous restaurant. Once you know that, Seomyeon 1-beonga looks less like a neon-lit entertainment strip and more like a crossroads of downtown Busan, where the metro, markets, large commercial complexes, and alley shops together shape how locals meet, shop, and spend their nights.
tipsEn:
Route: Walk the main street from Seomyeon Station, then turn into a food alley or shopping street that interests you.
Photo spot: A street scene with neon signs and passersby overlapping is a good choice.
Caution: Watch for vehicles entering the alleys and keep an eye on your belongings.

simpleEn: The Dadaepo Dream of Dusk Fountain is a ground fountain where water and light move together to music. By day it's just a flat plaza, but once the show starts, it turns into a stage you can watch from every side. Catch the sunset over Dadaepo's sea before the show begins — as the natural light fades, the artificial lights switch on and the beach's day continues into night. Feel how this wide, sunset-famous stretch of West Busan's coast has grown into a place people stay after dark, too.
detailEn:
The Dadaepo Dream of Dusk Fountain is known for its dazzling outdoor shows of music and light, but its scale alone is a story. After opening in 2009, it was certified by Guinness World Records in 2010 as the largest ground fountain in the world at the time, with a floor area of about 2,519 square meters, a circular diameter of 60 meters, and a maximum water height of 55 meters. It was an attempt to turn the open space in front of the beach into a performance venue and create a new nighttime attraction for West Busan.

The fountain is designed so that more than a thousand water jets and lights move together in time with the music. By day it looks like a flat plaza, but once the show begins, the floor itself becomes a stage and visitors watch the water and light from every direction. Unlike an ordinary pond-style fountain, people can walk across the space when the water is off, and it also functions as a play fountain. What makes it distinctive is how, in the same spot, it switches between sightseeing you watch and play you step into.

The fountain's arrival in Dadaepo is also tied to changes along West Busan's coast. Dadaepo is famous for the wide sands and sunsets at the Nakdong River estuary, but for a while it had far less tourism infrastructure than Haeundae or Gwangalli. As the beachfront park was redeveloped, the metro line extended, and facilities like the Dream Fountain were added, the area grew from a beach for watching the sunset into a place to stay for shows, walks, and festivals. The natural sunset and the artificial lights following one another in the same evening hour fits well with why "sunset" is in the name.

A local guide wouldn't tell you to just wait for the show to start — they'd tell you to watch the color of the sea before the sun goes down. Follow that through to the moment the artificial lights switch on as daylight fades, and the Dream of Dusk Fountain looks like more than a massive fountain facility — it becomes a stage that shows how Dadaepo has been reshaping West Busan's nightlife.
tipsEn:
Route: Check the show schedule and get a spot early, then continue on to the beach sunset afterward.
Photo spot: Capture the evening sky showing behind the fountain lights.
Caution: Keep the swimming area and viewing area separate, and watch for slippery surfaces.

simpleEn: Bujeon Ginseng Market is where expert knowledge of ginseng and medicinal herbs gathers inside a much larger everyday market. Fresh ginseng (susam), dried ginseng (geonsam), and steamed-and-dried red ginseng (hongsam) look and get used differently depending on how they're processed. Listen for how vendors sort products by size and form. In a market clustered near the railway and downtown transit, come see the working culture of a specialty trade — receiving goods from growing regions, sorting them, and passing that knowledge on to customers.
detailEn:
Bujeon Ginseng Market is a strikingly specialized market even within the vast Bujeon Market Town. Near Bujeon Station and the metro, produce, seafood, side-dish, and household-goods markets are packed close together — and among them, the ginseng market occupies the second floor, where shops specializing in fresh, dried, and red ginseng along with various medicinal herbs are gathered. What sets it apart from an ordinary traditional market is that an entire section is devoted to the knowledge and distribution of one specific category of goods.

Look at the ginseng on display and it can all seem to look alike, but vendors sort it by growing region, age, size and shape, and processing method. How it's processed also changes how it's stored and used — susam is fresh ginseng, geonsam is dried, and hongsam goes through a steaming-and-drying process. Vendors who've handled these goods for years aren't just sellers; they carry the specialized knowledge to judge quality and explain products to fit a customer's needs. So rather than just comparing price tags, ask what criteria they use to sort the goods — it makes the market far more interesting.

It also matters that Bujeon Market developed close to the railway and downtown transit. A traditional market needs to receive goods from growing regions quickly and then distribute them across the city, so access to a station and roads was a major advantage. That distribution network is exactly what let a specialty item like ginseng, grown outside Busan, cluster into a dedicated market here. Seeing farm produce, seafood, and medicinal herbs traded in the same market shows that Busan is both a city of consumers and a major distribution hub for the southern region.

A local guide wouldn't oversell the health benefits — they'd tell you to experience the vendors' language for sorting goods, and the smell of the market itself. Once you know that, Bujeon Ginseng Market looks like more than a place to buy health foods — it becomes a small site of commercial culture, showing how specialized goods and distribution knowledge have accumulated inside a city's traditional market.
tipsEn:
Route: Walk the market aisles first, then compare origin, grade, and price before choosing what you need.
Photo spot: Capture a shop with ginseng and herbs neatly displayed.
Caution: Check origin, weight, and return conditions before buying, and avoid photographing without permission.

simpleEn: Seodong Miro Market gets its name from the narrow, winding alleys that branch off in every direction. Murals and visitor signage have been added for tourists, but residents still come to buy side dishes and vegetables and catch up with familiar vendors. Try the Seodong-style egg mandu, made by pan-frying glass noodles and vegetables in egg batter. Skip the fastest route and take one extra turn through the alleys — old-school snacks and neighborhood life unfold inside this maze-like space.
detailEn:
The "miro" (maze) in Seodong Miro Market's name might sound like a marketing line, but it actually comes from the market's real layout — narrow, winding alleys branching off in several directions. When the local markets of Seodong, Geumjeong-gu, were redeveloped into a culture-and-tourism market, the name leaned into the idea of a market fun to get lost in. Rather than one big straight arcade, side-dish shops, snack stalls, and household-goods stores line small alley after alley, so first-time visitors can walk a full loop and still be unsure whether they've circled back to the same spot.

One food that made this market well known is egg mandu. The name might suggest a meat dumpling with egg inside, but Seodong-style egg mandu is actually a simple, inexpensive snack made by pan-frying glass noodles and vegetables together with beaten egg. For years it was an easygoing snack for students and market-goers, and it later became known beyond Busan through the memories of local celebrities and TV appearances. It wasn't fancy ingredients but the alley market's need for something quick to make and eat that shaped this food.

After becoming a culture-and-tourism market, murals, visitor signage, and food content were added — but the heart of this place is still residents doing their daily shopping. Right next to tourists taking photos, people buy side dishes and vegetables, and vendors greet longtime regulars. Unlike a themed street built for tourism, this is an existing everyday market that turned its own alley layout and food culture into cultural content.

A local guide wouldn't just check a map for the fastest route — they'd tell you to deliberately take a detour down one alley. Once you know that, Seodong Miro Market looks less like a confusing traditional market and more like a local living-culture space, where residents' everyday routes and old snack culture have been reinterpreted through the identity of a "maze."
tipsEn:
Route: Check the entrance signage, pass the main food area, then walk slowly to the market's inner section.
Photo spot: A composition showing the depth of the low signs and winding market alley is a good choice.
Caution: Ask permission before photographing vendors and goods up close.

simpleEn: Haeundae Blueline Park reuses the old Donghae Nambu rail line as a route for travelers. The tracks that once linked Mipo, Cheongsapo, and Songjeong have become the scenery for the Beach Train and Sky Capsule. Follow the coastline with your eyes through the window — the view shifts from a high-rise city to a fishing cove, rocky shore, and surfing beach. The rails laid close to the sea preserve the city's memory of a railway whose original job ended, carried forward instead of erased.
detailEn:
Haeundae Blueline Park looks like a newly built tourist train, but the line's roots go back to the old Donghae Nambu Line railway. The roughly 4.8km coastal stretch from Mipo through Cheongsapo to Songjeong was once a real railway that trains actually ran on. After the tracks were relocated to a new route, rather than tearing down the old railway facilities, the city repurposed them into the Beach Train, Sky Capsule, and a walking path, creating today's Blueline Park. It is a leading example of transportation infrastructure being turned into a tourism resource.

Knowing it was once an old railway explains why the tracks sit unusually close to the coastline. In the past, train passengers looked straight out the window at the sea of Mipo, Cheongsapo, and Songjeong as they traveled. Today's Beach Train revives that same view as a tourist experience, while the Sky Capsule runs on rails set 7–10 meters higher than the original track, moving much more slowly so riders can take in the scenery. The same stretch has shifted from "a railway for reaching your destination quickly" to "tourism that enjoys the journey itself."

As you move from Mipo toward Cheongsapo, the high-rise cityscape of Haeundae recedes and the fishing cove and rocky coast draw closer. Continuing on to Songjeong brings a fishing village, beach, and surf culture. The real appeal of this line is how, within just 4.8km, the boundary between modern Haeundae and the old coastal villages keeps shifting. The stations, too, function less as simple stops and more as doorways into each neighborhood's everyday scenery.

A local guide would tell you to look first at the traces of the old railway outside the window, rather than the capsule's color or your photo composition. Once you know this, Blueline Park stops looking like a seaside amusement ride and starts looking like a site of "railway regeneration" — where Busan's rail infrastructure, its original job finished, was reused as a new tourist route without erasing the coast's memory.
tipsEn:
Route: Choose your starting station and direction, then connect the stops you want by train or capsule.
Photo spot: The ocean-side window view is best heading from Mipo toward Cheongsapo.
Caution: Stay off the tracks, and check boarding times and your drop-off station in advance.

simpleEn: The Beomeosa Seongbo Museum preserves traces of worship, education, and practice carried on at the temple. Its Buddhist paintings, texts, wooden plaques, and ritual objects are both objects to admire and items once used in moments of faith. Picture how a Buddhist painting was used at a great dharma assembly, then go look at the temple halls. You'll see which spaces and rituals the objects behind the glass were once connected to. It's a museum where the temple's long memory carries through to today's visit.
detailEn:
The Beomeosa Seongbo Museum isn't a general art museum with works gathered together — it's a specialized museum built to preserve the Buddhist cultural heritage that Beomeosa and its affiliated temples have kept for a long time. Beomeosa, traditionally said to have been founded by the Silla monk Uisang, is one of Busan's leading temples, and its long history has accumulated a wide range of "seongbo" — Buddhist paintings, texts, wooden plaques, portraits, and ritual objects. The word "seongbo" itself means a precious treasure carrying the meaning of faith and practice in Buddhism.

When viewing the Buddhist paintings on display, don't just note how vivid the colors are. A large painting like a gwaebul (hanging scroll) isn't ordinary decoration hung on a wall — it's a religious tool made to be hung outdoors during a major dharma assembly so that large crowds could worship together. A jinyeong, a monk's portrait, both records an individual's face and carries the temple's dharma lineage and memory. Old books and documents are records showing what rituals and education Beomeosa carried on. What sets each object apart from ordinary art is that it had a real context of use inside the temple.

If you visit the museum before walking into the temple grounds, you'll see the halls differently. You can imagine where the paintings and ritual objects you saw in the display cases were actually used, and how the calligraphy on the wooden plaques connects to the halls themselves. Rather than separating cultural heritage from the temple, the museum safely protects objects that need conservation while explaining their religious context.

A local guide wouldn't send you hunting for the oldest or most valuable item, but would ask you to think about "what moment was this object originally used in?" Once you know this, the Beomeosa Seongbo Museum stops looking like an exhibition hall of Buddhist relics and starts looking like the temple's memory bank — connecting centuries of worship, education, and practice at Beomeosa to the present day.
tipsEn:
Route: Visit the museum exhibits first, then continue on to the halls and stone structures within the Beomeosa temple grounds.
Photo spot: Where permitted, capture the detailed patterns on the Buddhist paintings and crafts.
Caution: Respect the religious cultural heritage — avoid flash photography and touching the exhibits.

simpleEn: Chungnyeolsa is a shrine honoring those who died defending Busan during the Japanese invasions of 1592–98. It began as Songgongsa, built to hold the spirit tablet of Song Sang-hyeon, and later grew to commemorate more people and expand in scale, eventually taking on the educational function of Allak Seowon (Confucian academy). Look at how the layout runs from the entrance to the main hall, and take in the lecture hall too — ritual and learning continue side by side in this one space. Discover how the people of Busan have passed down and preserved their memory of war for later generations.
detailEn:
Chungnyeolsa is a shrine honoring those who died defending Busan during the Japanese invasions of 1592–98, but it wasn't built at its current scale from the start. It began in 1605, when Dongnae magistrate Yun Hwon built "Songgongsa" to enshrine the spirit tablet of Song Sang-hyeon, the Dongnae magistrate who died defending Dongnae fortress during the invasions. In 1624, General Jeong Bal, who died fighting at Busanjin fortress, was enshrined alongside him, and the shrine took the name "Chungnyeolsa." Spirit tablets of other figures were added afterward.

In 1652, the shrine was relocated to its current site in Allak-dong. This wasn't simply because space had grown tight — a lecture hall and east/west wings were built to teach later generations about Song Sang-hyeon's scholarship and loyalty, giving the site the function of "Allak Seowon" as well. So this place was both a memorial space and an educational institution. Once you know why a shrine and lecture hall sit together on the grounds, the layout of the buildings makes much more sense.

The Battle of Dongnae Fortress during the 1592 invasion is a crucial event in how the people of Busan remember the war. It's said that when Song Sang-hyeon was asked to surrender, he wrote back a message meaning, "It is easy to fight and die, but hard to lend you the road." Spirit tablets are enshrined not only for Jeong Bal and Yun Heung-sin but also for military officers, commoners, and women. With 93 spirit tablets currently enshrined and memorial rites still held, this is less a site honoring a single hero than a place preserving the entire region's memory of war.

A local guide would tell you not to just photograph the shrine's façade, but to take in the whole axis from the entrance to the main hall together with the lecture hall. Once you know this, Chungnyeolsa stops looking like an old memorial facility and starts looking like an "institutionalized space of regional memory" — showing how the people of Busan have remembered, taught, and ritually preserved their experience of the 1592 invasion.
tipsEn:
Route: Read the information panel at the entrance, then visit the memorial hall, the shrine, and the grounds' garden in that order.
Photo spot: The symmetrical view of the red-spiked gate (hongsalmun) and the shrine atop the steps works well.
Caution: Avoid loud noise and playful photography in this memorial space.

simpleEn: 75 Plaza is an old coastal rest area on Yeongdo, named for the year it was built, 1975. From its octagonal pavilion, you can take in the boats of Namhang harbor, the rocky coast, and the open sea horizon. Walk part of the Jeolyeong Coastal Walkway, then look back over the coastline you've covered from up high. This resting spot along the walk shows that Yeongdo sits right at the boundary between the harbor's sheltered waters and the open sea. Even in its plain numerical name lies the long history of Busan residents enjoying the sea.
detailEn:
The name "75 Plaza" is unusual from the start — it isn't tied to a historical figure's number, but simply comes from the plaza being built in 1975. This small rest area sits partway along the Jeolyeong Coastal Walkway on Yeongdo's west side, and thanks to its octagonal pavilion and ocean views, Yeongdo residents have long used it as a place to catch the breeze and rest. Today it may look like just one point along the coastal path, but it was a leading local viewpoint over the sea even before the walkway as a whole was developed.

Climbing up to the octagonal pavilion reveals a much more open sea than beaches close to land. Ships in Namhang harbor, the rocky coast, and the horizon all come into view at once, making it easy to feel that Yeongdo sits right at the boundary between the inner waters of Busan Port and the open sea. Even within Yeongdo, the northern district of Bongnae-dong carries a strong harbor-and-shipyard atmosphere, while this western spot feels much more like cliffs and open ocean. The character of the sea changes quickly across this small island.

After the Jeolyeong Coastal Walkway was built, 75 Plaza took on more the role of a punctuation mark along the walking route than an independent lookout. Starting from Huinnyeoul Culture Village or the coastal tunnel and continuing along stairs and decks, arriving here lets you look back at the coastline you've just walked, all at once, from a height. It's the point where the waves and rocks you saw up close while walking read, from a distance, as a single landform.

A local guide would start with the simple story behind the name: "It's called 75 Plaza because it was built in 1975." Once you know this, the plain name itself — without any polished tourism branding — reveals the long history of this old citizens' park. 75 Plaza matters less as the latest photo spot and more as a living lookout where Yeongdo residents have rested, gazing at the same sea, for decades.
tipsEn:
Route: Rest at the plaza, then, depending on your stamina, continue along part of the Jeolyeong Coastal Walkway.
Photo spot: Capture the rocky coast and wide horizon beyond the railing.
Caution: Watch your footing on the coastal stairs and wet surfaces.

simpleEn: Peace Park was created ahead of the 2005 APEC summit, redeveloping a site that had been full of scrap metal yards and freight trucks. Its wide lawns and walking paths connect the UN Memorial Cemetery with the historical and memorial facilities nearby. After taking in heavy history, catch your breath in this open space and take a look at its sculptures too. Land once crowded with industrial facilities has become a place linking citizens' everyday life with the memory of peace — a park where ordinary strolling leads into remembrance.
detailEn:
Peace Park wasn't originally a clean lawn park. Ahead of the 2005 APEC Summit, the City of Busan turned this site into a park to create a symbolic space of peace linked with the nearby UN Memorial Cemetery. Before that, it was an industrial area crowded with some 50 businesses — scrap metal processors, auto repair shops, freight truck lots, and transport companies — causing noise, dust, and soil contamination. The change in function is so complete that it's hard to imagine today's greenery once looked like that.

The park's wide lawns and walking paths aren't just rest facilities — they serve as a buffer space connecting the nearby UN Memorial Cemetery, Busan Museum, National Memorial Museum of Forced Mobilization under Japanese Occupation, and UN Peace Memorial Hall into a single cultural zone. Touring history and memorial facilities back to back can feel heavy, and Peace Park's open space lets you catch your breath in between. From an urban planning perspective too, it's the central green space tying previously separate facilities into one story — the "UN Peace Culture Special Zone."

The park includes sculptures commemorating UN forces' activities, and nearby facilities cover the memory of the Korean War from various countries' perspectives. When looking at the sculptures, paying attention to the surrounding paths as much as the design shows that remembrance was designed to extend beyond indoor museums and into everyday park strolls. The living space where residents exercise and children walk naturally overlaps with historical memory.

A local guide would mention that this land originally held scrap metal and freight trucks. Once you know this, Peace Park stops looking like greenery that was beautifully preserved from the start, and instead looks like the result of urban regeneration — turning a site crowded with industrial facilities into a park connecting remembrance with citizens' daily life.
tipsEn:
Route: Walk the park path to see the sculptures, then continue on to the UN Memorial Cemetery or Busan Museum.
Photo spot: Scenes with wide lawns, memorial sculptures, and trees together work well.
Caution: Check for event areas and bicycle traffic, and follow lawn-protection guidance.

simpleEn: The name Hocheon Village carries a story that a tiger once appeared on this hillside. Known as a filming location for the drama "Third Charm" (Ssam, My Way), its real backdrop is the steep alleys and homes where residents have long lived. From the viewing area, look at the nearby rooftops and, further off, Seomyeon's high-rises. The warm lights along the alley are real lights from people's actual homes. Discover a Busan village where the pop-culture spotlight has added a new layer of memory atop a long history of hillside living.
detailEn:
"Hocheon" in Hocheon Village's name is said to come from a story that tigers once frequently appeared on this hillside long ago. Houses and streetlights now fill the space where tigers once roamed, but walking the steep alleys quickly shows how rugged the terrain once was. As Busan's population grew during the Korean War and industrialization era and flat land ran short, homes climbed even these steep hillsides, and Hocheon Village became a typical sanbokdoro (hillside road) residential village.

The village became nationally known through the drama "Third Charm" (Ssam, My Way). Scenes around the "Namil Bar" where the main characters lived were filmed here, and the nighttime view of terraced houses and warm streetlights became hugely popular. Afterward, the Hocheon Culture Platform was built, along with spaces evoking the filming scenes, turning an ordinary residential area into a new tourist destination. But the drama set didn't come first and the village after — the drama borrowed the scenery of residents' actual daily life.

Looking down from the viewing area, rooftops and windows layer downward one after another, with Seomyeon's high-rise downtown visible beyond. The contrast between the close hillside village and the distant modern downtown is the heart of Hocheon Village's night view. That's also exactly why it's worth remembering that each pretty little light is actually someone's real home.

Rather than recreating drama scenes right away, a local guide would first tell the story of how a hillside once roamed by tigers became a human neighborhood. Once you know this, Hocheon Village stops looking like a filming location or night-view spot, and instead looks like a living village where pop culture has added new memory on top of Busan's hillside terrain and residential history.
tipsEn:
Route: Take in the view around the Hocheon Culture Platform, then walk only the short, publicly accessible alley route.
Photo spot: The viewing area, where rooftops and downtown lights layer on top of each other, works well.
Caution: Don't photograph residents' windows or the residents themselves, and don't block alley traffic.

simpleEn: Busan Healing Forest is a place to go beyond simply viewing scenery and actually feel nature through the senses. Activities here use the forest's sunlight, scents, sounds, and temperature to rest both body and mind. Rather than hurrying toward a destination, stay a while and notice the sound of leaves and the feel of the soil. Set slightly inland from the Gijang coast, this forest offers a side of Busan's nature quite different from the sea. As you walk, even the pace of your trip changes.
detailEn:
Busan Healing Forest serves a somewhat different purpose than an ordinary recreational forest you simply walk through. What's called "forest healing" here isn't medical treatment for illness, but activities that use sunlight, forest scenery, and the forest environment — scent, sound, temperature, humidity — to help maintain and restore health of body and mind. So what matters here isn't just the trail itself, but experiencing programs like breathing, meditation, and walking together with a forest healing guide.

The first thing that changes once you enter the forest is your pace. In the city, how fast you reach your destination matters; in a healing program, you're encouraged to slow your steps and consciously notice the sound of leaves, the texture of soil, and the scent of the air. Sensations that usually fade into the background are brought forward one at a time. Programs also vary by group — adults and working professionals, families, older adults — because each person's purpose for using the forest and physical condition differs.

Gijang is famous for coastal tourism, but move a little inland and wide forests and valleys remain. Busan Healing Forest shows that the forest is also a major natural asset of this city, beyond the "Busan = sea" image most travelers have. It's also interesting that a space of a completely different pace exists not far from busy eastern Busan tourist sites like Haedong Yonggungsa Temple or Osiria.

A local guide wouldn't rush you toward the best viewpoint, but would suggest staying in one section for ten minutes just to notice the sounds and scents. Once you know this, Busan Healing Forest is more than just "a nice forest to walk through" — it looks like a modern forest culture space that uses nature not merely as scenery to consume, but as a tool for restoring your own body and senses.
tipsEn:
Route: Check trail conditions at the information center, then use forest paths and rest areas suited to your stamina.
Photo spot: A quiet forest path with sunlight filtering through the trees works well.
Caution: Stay on designated trails and watch for insects and slippery ground.

simpleEn: The main hall of the Busan Modern History Museum was once a financial institution and now conveys the city's history. The underground vault that once stored actual bank assets now leads into an art space. Before viewing the exhibits, look closely at the exterior walls and the vault's structure. Records of the port, railways, commerce, and daily life connect to the building's own history. A place once devoted to Busan's development and finance has become a resource for reading how the city changed after its port opened.
detailEn:
The main hall of the Busan Modern History Museum is itself an exhibit testifying to Busan's financial history. A Bank of Korea branch office of the Korean Empire era once stood on this site, and it's believed the Bank of Chosen's Busan branch building was constructed here around 1912. After liberation, it served as the Bank of Korea's Busan branch and later regional headquarters, until the Bank of Korea relocated to Munhyeon-dong in 2013. A building that handled money and finance for nearly a century became, in 2024, a museum covering Busan's modern and contemporary history.

Inside the building, the underground vault is especially interesting. Now used as the "Vault Art Museum," it originally stored the bank's actual assets and cash. The thick walls and heavy door show how a financial institution expressed trust and security through architecture. Because the museum wasn't built in a new structure but reused the old building while keeping some of its original function, you don't have to view the building and the exhibits separately.

The permanent exhibition shows how Busan became a modern city after its port opened, through materials on the harbor, railways, streetcars, commerce, and daily life. After Busan's port opened in 1876, its position as the closest harbor to Japan meant it was strongly shaped by colonial urban development, industry, and finance, and it grew rapidly again after liberation and the Korean War. It's symbolic that a building once occupied by a bank, right in the middle of that modernization process, now explains that very era.

A local guide would tell you to look at the exterior walls and the vault before entering the exhibition halls. Once you know this, the Busan Modern History Museum stops looking like an old building nicely remodeled into a cultural space, and instead looks like a "history museum where the building itself is the artifact" — a place that once took part in Busan's finance and urban development, now explaining its own era.
tipsEn:
Route: View the permanent exhibition in chronological order, then connect the building's old traces with the surrounding old downtown area.
Photo spot: A spot showing both the old building's exterior and the old downtown streets works well.
Caution: Follow photography rules to help protect the records and exhibits.

simpleEn: Igidae holds records, legend, and the long history of volcanic rock tied to its name. Cliffs and coastline carved by waves became a walking path open to citizens after military restrictions were lifted. After taking in Gwangan Bridge and Marine City, look down at the rock and stone layers beneath your feet too. Modern high-rises on the opposite shore face natural coastline here. Listen for the line between legend and fact as you take in the terrain — the many layers of time along Busan's coast come into view.
detailEn:
There isn't a single settled answer behind Igidae's name — several stories overlap. The 1850 gazetteer Dongnae-yeongji records that "there are two gisaeng's graves here, so it is called Igidae." A later, widely told legend holds that during the 1592 Japanese invasion, a gisaeng who attended a victory feast held by Japanese forces who had taken Suyeong Fortress embraced an enemy general and leapt into the sea with him. The City of Busan presents these various accounts together. So a local guide would talk not about pinning the legend down as historical fact, but about what memory people have attached to this cliff over time.

Rock is Igidae's other main character. Volcanic rock and tuffaceous sedimentary rock, formed by volcanic activity around 80 million years ago at the end of the Cretaceous period, are widely exposed along the coast, and waves and weathering have carved cliffs, wave-cut platforms, and potholes. If you see round hollows in a flat rock surface, they aren't something someone dug — they may be a trace of nature, formed by rainwater, small pebbles, and weathering repeating over a long span of time.

This area was long restricted as a military operations zone, closed to civilians, and opened to the public only after 1993. That's why, even though Gwangalli and Marine City sit right across the water, its coastal forest and cliffs remain relatively continuous. Walking from Dongsaengmal to Oryukdo, the change is striking — the ultra-high-rise cityscape gradually recedes while the rugged rocky coast draws closer.

A local guide would tell you not to just photograph Gwangan Bridge, but to take in the rock beneath your feet, the legend behind the name, and the distant city all at once. Once you know this, Igidae stops looking like a coastal walking path, and instead looks like a compressed coastal history of Busan — where 80 million years of geology, Joseon-era records and local legend, and military restriction and today's urban skyline all overlap along a single trail.
tipsEn:
Route: Depending on your stamina, choose and walk one section among Dongsaengmal, Eoulmadang, and Oryukdo.
Photo spot: A section where Gwangan Bridge appears beyond the coastal cliffs works well.
Caution: Avoid approaching the rocky coast in rain or strong wind, and stay on the designated path.

simpleEn: Songdo Sky Park is a viewing area where you look back at the coastline you started from after getting off the cable car. The forest and cliffs of Amnam Park, long closed to the public, are now linked into a coastal tourism route. Before hunting for a photo spot, take in the cable car line and the beach on the opposite shore. Urban beach and natural coastline connect along a single line over the sea. See how Songdo Beach has expanded into a destination offering walking, forest, and rocky islets alongside its beach.
detailEn:
Songdo Sky Park is the space you arrive at when the Songdo Marine Cable Car brings you to the Amnam Park side — better understood not as an independent park, but as "a second viewing platform where you look back at Songdo's coast after getting off the cable car." After crossing about 1.62km of sea from Songdo Bay Station, you look down from a height at the beach, downtown, and the forest of Amnam Park you started from — the scenery you passed through while riding is gathered together in one spot.

Amnam Park, where Sky Park sits, was originally a military protection zone long closed to public access. It later opened to the public and became a park built around its forest and coastal cliffs, and once the cable car connected it, it turned into an easily accessible coastal tourism hub. In other words, the starting point, Songdo Beach, is an old urban beach, while the destination, Amnam Park, is a coastal forest that has kept more of its natural character.

Looking back at the cable car line from the viewing point, you can see that a single straight line over the sea connects two very different coastlines. Below lie Yonggung Cloud Bridge, rocky islets, and coastal cliffs; across the water are the beach, high-rises, and the Cloud Walk. Reading this contrast is far more interesting than the cable car ride itself. The park's various sculptures and photo spots extend how long you linger, but the most distinctly Busan scene remains the one where city and forest face each other across the sea.

A local guide wouldn't head straight for the photo spot on arrival, but would first turn back to look at where you started. Once you know this, Songdo Sky Park stops looking like a mere appendage at the cable car's endpoint, and instead looks like the viewing space that best shows how Songdo has expanded from an old beach into a complex coastal destination combining sea transport, walking, forest, and cliffs.
tipsEn:
Route: After getting off the cable car, tour the viewing area and park facilities, then continue on to Yonggung Cloud Bridge.
Photo spot: A viewpoint showing both the cable car and Songdo's sea works well.
Caution: Stay away from beyond the railing and keep to the queue lines at photo spots.

simpleEn: Jagalchi Market layers together the livelihoods of war refugees, the labor of women merchants, and Busan's seafood trade. Outside, plastic basins and street stalls; inside the modern building, live-fish tanks and restaurants — different eras of the market meet here. Watch the flow of choosing, haggling over, and immediately eating fish. As the saying goes — "Come look, come see, come buy" — merchants and customers meet up close. Walk on to the harbor beyond the market, and Busan's sea and dinner table connect.
detailEn:
Even Jagalchi Market's name carries the texture of Busan's seaside life. Official Busan tourism materials explain that the name "Jagalchi" comes from the many fist-sized pebbles (jagal) once found along this shoreline. Street stalls selling seafood had already formed here since the Japanese colonial era, but the market grew dramatically in scale because of the Korean War. As refugees poured into Busan from across the country, shanties rose along the shore, and stalls selling fish to make a living quickly multiplied, developing into today's large seafood market.

That history is still visible in the market's layout, inside and out. Outside, rubber basins and street stalls line up; inside the modern building, live-fish tanks and floors of restaurants are neatly arranged. Both deal in the same seafood, but one side shows traces of a refugee city and street-stall culture, the other the present-day, modernized hygiene and distribution of a Busan seafood market. The term "Jagalchi ajumma" is familiar enough to show how central women merchants have been to the market's identity — the labor of women who supported their families through war and poverty played a huge role in the market's energy and image.

The phrase "Oiso, boiso, saiso" ("Come look, come see, come buy") fits the market's hawking culture well, beyond being a mere tourism slogan. The essence of Jagalchi lies in checking the goods with your own eyes, haggling, and eating them right away. Choosing fish on the first floor and eating it upstairs, then stepping outside to see Namhang harbor and fishing boats right there — this structure shows a Busan seafood culture where the distance from sea to table is unusually short.

So at Jagalchi, it's worth taking in the market buildings, street stalls, and harbor together, rather than just looking at the types of fish. Once you know this, Jagalchi Market stops looking like "a tourist market for eating raw fish," and instead looks like a living history of Busan's old downtown — shaped by the layered livelihoods of war refugees, the labor of women merchants, and the city's seafood trade.
tipsEn:
Route: Compare fish types and prices on the first floor, then check the restaurant's serving conditions before heading upstairs.
Photo spot: A scene with the tanks and market signs, with the harbor visible beyond, works well.
Caution: Check for raw-food and allergy concerns, and ask permission before photographing merchants.

simpleEn: At Nampo-dong Dried Seafood Wholesale Market, the sea's harvest becomes food that can be stored and shipped. Anchovies, kelp, dried seaweed, and dried squid are piled in sacks and boxes instead of tanks. Watch how merchants sort goods by size and condition. These same ingredients flow into Busan's noodle and fishcake broths. Amid a different scent and texture than the live-fish market, discover the distribution culture that has preserved seafood and sent it to tables across the country.
detailEn:
The Nampo-dong Dried Seafood Wholesale Market sits somewhat less in the spotlight than Jagalchi's flashy live-fish tanks next door, but it shows how Busan's seafood becomes goods that can be "stored and transported." Dried seafood like anchovies, seaweed, kelp, and squid was, even before refrigeration technology developed, an important trade good for a port city, since it could be preserved long-term and shipped far away. Dried-seafood shops clustered around Namhang harbor and Jagalchi in part because the location was ideal for processing and gathering seafood brought in by boat and shipping it back out nationwide.

Walking the alley brings a completely different sensation from a fish market. Instead of the wet feel of a live-fish market, the strong scent of dried seaweed and fish dominates, and goods are stacked in layers — not in tanks, but in nets, boxes, large sacks, and display shelves. Even the same anchovies are sorted by size, origin, and use — for broth or for stir-frying — and kelp and seaweed are distinguished by thickness, color, and dryness. Merchants who have traded here for years can judge quality and use just by looking at the packaging — that eye is the market's specialized knowledge.

Dried seafood connects directly to Busan's food culture. Anchovies and kelp go into fishcake broth and noodle stock, and various stews and side dishes; seaweed is essential to everyday soups and ceremonial dishes. In other words, the goods sold here aren't tourist souvenirs but basic ingredients that have long supported the flavor of Busan's homes and restaurants behind the scenes. If live fish is "the sea eaten today," dried seafood is a way of drying the sea to use it across seasons and distances.

A local guide would point you not toward famous fish but toward the old sacks, handwritten price tags, and the standards merchants use to sort goods. Once you know this, the Nampo-dong Dried Seafood Wholesale Market stops looking like just an old back-alley market, and instead looks like another face of Busan's seafood distribution — turning the sea's harvest brought into port into storable ingredients sent out to tables across the country.
tipsEn:
Route: Walk the alley once to compare quality and prices, then check packaging methods.
Photo spot: Shelves stacked layer upon layer with dried seafood, alongside old signboards, work well.
Caution: Check origin, weight, and storage method, and ask merchants before photographing.

simpleEn: Suyeong Historic Park sits on the site that was once the center of the Joseon-era Gyeongsang Jwasuyeong naval command. Today's district name, Suyeong-gu, carries on from this naval garrison. Look at the traces of the fortress wall, the 25 Loyalists Shrine commemorating the 1592 invasion, and the old zelkova and black pine trees. Military history, residents' faith, and folk arts remain layered in this one space. In this quiet neighborhood park, you can read where the name "Suyeong" and its local culture began.
detailEn:
Suyeong Historic Park looks like a quiet neighborhood park, but this site was once the center of the Joseon-era Gyeongsang Jwado Suguncheoldosa-yeong — the "Gyeongsang Jwasuyeong," the naval command that guarded the southeastern coast. Today's district name, "Suyeong-gu," comes directly from this garrison's name. Gyeongsang Jwasuyeong was a military base commanding naval forces to guard against Japanese pirates and other invaders; after moving location several times, it settled in today's Suyeong-dong area during King Hyojong's reign and remained until King Gojong's time. At its peak the fortress wall stretched over 2.7km, but most of it disappeared under Japanese colonial rule, and today only fragments remain — a gate, wall traces, and a dismounting stone marker (hamabi).

One story worth remembering especially at this park is the "25 Loyalists Shrine." When the 1592 invasion broke out, Gyeongsang Jwasusa Park Hong abandoned the fortress and fled, and Japanese forces occupied Suyeong Fortress. Busan city records note that 25 soldiers and residents carried on guerrilla resistance for several years afterward, and the Loyalists Shrine was built in 1853 to honor them. So this place preserves, at once, the failure of the government garrison's command and the resistance of unnamed local residents.

The old zelkova and black pine trees here aren't just large trees. Revered for centuries almost like the village's guardian trees, they hold both the garrison's history and residents' faith together. At the nearby Suyeong Folk Art Museum, local traditions like Suyeong Yaryu (mask dance) and Jwasuyeong Eobang Nori (fishing-village performance) continue — showing that the old military city left behind not just fortress walls, but a whole living culture of markets, fishing, and performance.

So when viewing Suyeong Historic Park, it's worth reading it not as "a park with a few scattered relics," but as the place where today's Suyeong-gu name and culture began. Though the fortress wall traces, the 25 Loyalists Shrine, the old trees, and the folk arts may look like records of different eras, they are all fragments of local memory formed around the old Jwasuyeong garrison.
tipsEn:
Route: Follow the information panels to tour the fortress traces, memorial spaces, and old trees in order.
Photo spot: A composition showing the old trees, traditional architecture, and stone walls together works well.
Caution: Don't climb on cultural heritage, and avoid loud noise in the memorial ritual space.

simpleEn: Jeolyeong Coastal Walkway connects the once-inaccessible, steep western coast of Yeongdo to the public. Above lie hillside villages and alleys; below, rocky shore carved by waves and a narrow coastline continue along. Feel the change in elevation as you move between stairs and decks. Look, too, at the rocks and the direction of the waves beyond the railing. Built in the early 2000s, this path holds the terrain of Yeongdo, where mountain and sea have long served as everyday living space.
detailEn:
The Jeolyeong Coastal Walkway is now Yeongdo's signature walking trail, but it wasn't originally open to visitors. Yeongdo's western coast had steep cliffs and rugged terrain, and part of it was managed as a military protection zone; once the walkway opened in 2001, citizens were finally able to walk down close to the sea. The roughly 3km coastal path running from the Namhang-dong management office toward Jungni Port and Gamji Beach alternates, as a result, between "untouched natural cliffs" and "boardwalks newly built by people."

Walking the path lets you physically understand Yeongdo's terrain. Above are Huinnyeoul Culture Village and the hillside road; below, rock directly carved by waves and a narrow shoreline. On a map, the distance from home to the sea looks short, but in reality you have to descend a long staircase, and climbing back up means gaining considerable height. This vertical distance is exactly what shaped both residents' living space and the coastal nature here at once.

Don't just look at the railings and decks — the rock surfaces, the cliff's layers, and the direction the waves strike are worth noticing too. Yeongdo's west side is heavily exposed to the open sea, so the path's character changes greatly with weather and wave conditions. Along the stretch through Huinnyeoul Coastal Tunnel, 75 Plaza, and toward Jungni, coves, cliffs, and residential areas repeat in turn, and within the same island, harbor city and natural coast quickly trade places.

A local guide wouldn't just describe this as "a pretty path along the sea," but would first mention that it was only developed into a citizens' walkway in the early 2000s. Once you know this, the Jeolyeong Coastal Walkway stops looking like a simple perimeter trail, and instead looks like a path reconnecting citizens and travelers to Yeongdo's long-inaccessible, steep coast — the space where you most directly feel the elevation between the hillside village and the sea.
tipsEn:
Route: Starting from Huinnyeoul, walk only the section toward 75 Plaza that suits your stamina.
Photo spot: Capture the blue railing, rocky coast, and a distant boat together.
Caution: Check for wet stairs and falling-rock warnings, and don't go beyond the railing.

simpleEn: UN Sculpture Park holds the memory of peace in sculpture, created to mark an international sculpture symposium for the 50th anniversary of the Korean War. Artists from 21 countries expressed freedom, peace, and unification through different materials and forms. Rather than hunting for the prettiest piece, compare how each work expresses wounds, reconciliation, and connection. Walk here after visiting the graves at the nearby UN Memorial Cemetery, and the works' questions about what to leave behind after war will land more deeply.
detailEn:
UN Sculpture Park turns the abstract word "peace" into "different forms made by sculptors from each country." The park began with an international sculpture symposium held in 2000 to mark the 50th anniversary of the Korean War. Sculptors from 21 countries that took part in the war participated, donating 34 works on the themes of freedom, peace, and harmony. The sculpture park was completed beside the UN Memorial Cemetery in 2001, placing a space for mourning war's sacrifices at the graves side by side with a space for reflecting on peace through art.

When viewing the works, it's more rewarding to compare how differently each country's artist handled the same theme than to ask "which one is prettiest." Materials range from stone to metal, forms from geometric shapes to figures — some works emphasize reconciliation and connection, others wounds and memory. The fact that many countries, each having experienced the same war directly or indirectly, left their own perspective on peace in one shared park is itself what makes the diversity of the works meaningful.

Local public-works laborers took part in building the park on a large scale. Official records note that more than 8,000 public-works workers were involved in the park's construction over the course of a year. It's interesting that an international project commemorating the war's 50th anniversary became an actual physical space through the labor of local citizens at the same time. Unlike the cemetery, the park has lawns, paths, and benches, designed as a space for citizens' everyday rest — fitting the intent of connecting "peace" not only to solemn mourning but to everyday value as well.

A local guide wouldn't make you memorize every artwork's title, but would suggest walking here after viewing the graves at the UN Memorial Cemetery. Once you know this, UN Sculpture Park stops looking like an outdoor art park, and instead looks like an international space of peace where 21 countries reinterpreted their memory of the Korean War through the language of sculpture, asking "what should be left behind after war?"
tipsEn:
Route: Follow the artwork guide from the park entrance for one loop, then continue on to Peace Park and the museum.
Photo spot: Capture the shapes formed together by the sculptures and tree shadows.
Caution: Don't climb on or damage the artworks, and respect the memorial atmosphere.

simpleEn: Centum City Spa Land brings Korea's traditional bathhouse and jjimjilbang (sauna) culture into a modern urban facility. Soaking in hot spring baths and moving between heated rooms and lounges in a jjimjilbang are two different kinds of rest. Think, too, about the fast pace of Centum City, packed with shopping and business facilities. Through the long stretches of lingering, resting, and talking even after bathing, feel how traditional communal bathing culture meets everyday life in Busan.
detailEn:
Centum City Spa Land is a space that brings Korea's traditional bathing culture into a modern form inside a massive complex commercial facility. When people think of hot springs in Busan, an old bathhouse town like Dongnae Hot Spring usually comes to mind first, but Spa Land is a 21st-century urban hot spring inside Shinsegae Centum City, combining shopping, dining, and rest in one building. According to official information, it uses two types of natural hot spring water drawn from about 1,000m underground, and operates several hot spring baths and 13 themed jjimjilbang spaces.

What's interesting is that "hot spring" and "jjimjilbang" aren't the same thing. A hot spring bath is about soaking your body in water, while a jjimjilbang space is closer to the Korean leisure custom of lingering a long time, moving between heated rooms and lounges. In Korea's large jjimjilbang, even after bathing is done, family and friends rest, eat, and talk together in the shared common area. Spa Land reconstructs this lifestyle with various themes, including a Finnish-style sauna, and upscale interiors, making it accessible for foreign visitors to experience easily.

Its location in Centum City also carries meaning. This area is packed with BEXCO, the Busan Cinema Center, department stores, and business facilities, the exact opposite of the quiet atmosphere of a traditional hot spring village. Fitting bathing and rest into a schedule of sightseeing and shopping shows how "rest time" itself has become a product in modern urban travel. The experience of lingering, changing your body's temperature, and resting creates a strong contrast with the fast pace of the city center.

A local guide wouldn't count how many baths there are, but would explain why Koreans linger in a jjimjilbang for hours even after bathing. Once you know this, Spa Land stops looking like a fancy sauna, and instead looks like Busan's urban wellness space — reinterpreting Korea's long-standing communal bathing and rest culture for Centum City's modern lifestyle.
tipsEn:
Route: After entering, check the usage rules, then use the hot spring area and jjimjilbang area separately without overexertion.
Photo spot: Where permitted, capture the tidy layout of the shared lounge area.
Caution: Photography is banned in the baths and changing areas; use the facility according to your health condition.

simpleEn: Hwangnyeongsan (Mt. Hwangnyeong) layers together the mountain's place name, its geology, and the history of Joseon-era beacon-fire communication. At the summit, open on every side, the beacon mound was once an observation point exchanging signal fires with neighboring mountains. In Jeonpo-dong, spheroidal gabbro and rock at the summit hold traces of geology far older than the city. After taking in the night view, look at the ridge line and the beacon mound's position too — you'll realize this scenic viewpoint was long a place for reading Busan's terrain and news.
detailEn:
If you look only at its observatory, Hwangnyeongsan is a night-view spot, but taking in the whole mountain reveals Busan's place-name history, geology, and military communication history all at once. Hwangnyeongsan is a roughly 428m urban mountain spanning Yeonje-gu, Nam-gu, and Busanjin-gu, and one interpretation traces its name back to the ancient "Geochilsanguk" or "rugged mountain" of the old Dongnae area. Behind the current Sino-Korean name "Hwangnyeongsan" lies a much older local place name.

The restored beacon mound (bongsudae) at the summit best shows why this mountain's location mattered. Records say a beacon mound stood here even before 1425, relaying signals received from Gubong Beacon Mound to the west onward to Ganbio-san to the east and Gyemyeong-san to the north, making it a central point in Busan's beacon-fire network. Records also note that in 1592, when the Japanese invasion began, beacon guard Bae Dol-i reported that Japanese forces had entered Busanpo. Where people today watch the city lights, people long ago sent urgent military information by fire signal.

Hwangnyeongsan also hides distinctive geology. Spheroidal gabbro, designated a natural monument, is found in the Jeonpo-dong area — an extremely rare rock in which round patterns repeat inside the stone, a geological feature of the mountain that's hard to tell just by looking at its surface. Large boulders near the summit, rounded by weathering like tors, also show the mountain's long history.

A local guide would ask you, after taking in Busan from the observatory, to consider "why has this mountain been an observation point for centuries?" Once you know this, Hwangnyeongsan stops looking like a mountain you climb just for the night view, and instead looks like an old benchmark of downtown Busan — where traces of an ancient place name, rare rock, Joseon's beacon communication network, and today's urban view all layer together at the same summit.
tipsEn:
Route: Choose a hiking trail or vehicle-accessible point suited to your stamina, and head up to the summit viewing area.
Photo spot: The scene of downtown and Gwangan Bridge's lights spreading out beyond the beacon mound works well.
Caution: Avoid approaching the summit in strong wind or heavy fog, and stay on the designated path.

simpleEn: Sasang Neighborhood Park is a space linking residents' daily life and forest between the flatlands of the Nakdong River and the foot of Baegyangsan mountain. Past the walking paths, exercise facilities, and playgrounds, city buildings and mountain ridges come into a single view. In western Busan, where industry and transportation dominate, a nearby patch of green becomes everyday rest. Walk here between visits to famous sights — discover a different face of Busan, where residents use the mountain as part of daily life.
detailEn:
Sasang Neighborhood Park isn't one of Busan's signature tourist spots so much as a "middle ground between neighborhood mountain and park" close to the everyday life of Sasang-gu residents. Sasang-gu is a living area formed between the flatlands of the Nakdong River and the foot of Baegyangsan mountain, and the park itself sits at the border where the city's residential area gives way to the mountain's greenery. It's a place that shows how western Busan residents use the mountain — a completely different scene from the sea-focused tourism most associate with Busan.

The park's walking paths, exercise facilities, and children's playground aren't simply leftover natural forest — they're the result of shaping mountainside greenery into a living park that residents can use every day. Flat plazas and forest paths alternate, and climbing just a little brings downtown buildings and the Baegyangsan ridge into a single view. In this sense, the park feels less like "trees planted within the city" and more like a mountain foothill originally there, pulled into urban daily life.

Sasang has long grown as a gateway to western Busan with strong industrial and transportation functions. The more roads, railways, and industrial facilities an area has, the more important the role of accessible greenery becomes for residents. So while a neighborhood park like this may seem to lack any special landmark for tourists, for local residents it is the most frequently experienced piece of everyday nature — for exercise, walking, children's play, and seasonal change. Understanding city life means these "places used every day" matter just as much as famous landmarks.

A local guide wouldn't oversell this park as a must-see to a visitor who's traveled far. Instead, they'd show that Busan isn't just beaches and the old downtown — that each neighborhood in the living area between the Nakdong River and Baegyangsan has its own patch of green. Once you know this, Sasang Neighborhood Park stops looking like an ordinary neighborhood park, and instead looks like a space for observing the living boundary where western Busan's city meets its mountain.
tipsEn:
Route: Walk the park's perimeter path briefly, then linger at a viewpoint or rest area.
Photo spot: An everyday scene where trees, the walking path, and downtown buildings overlap works well.
Caution: Respect the paths of exercise-facility users and dog walkers.

simpleEn: The UN Memorial Cemetery began in 1951 as a cemetery built to bury Korean War fallen soldiers. Remains transferred from several regions carry the memory of the war itself into what is now an internationally managed memorial space.
