After viewing the row of flags and gravestones, read the names and ages on the headstones. The war's vast scale becomes the story of a short life. Walking here in silence, encounter the memory and sacrifice that many nations have preserved.
detailEn:
The UN Memorial Cemetery began with a much more specific history than simply "a park commemorating the countries that fought in the Korean War." In January 1951, the year after the Korean War broke out, the UN Command built this cemetery to bury fallen soldiers; it was completed that April, and the remains of UN soldiers temporarily buried in various regions — Gaeseong, Incheon, Daejeon, Daegu, Miryang, Masan, and others — began to be moved to Busan. It is officially recognized as "the world's only UN memorial cemetery," which makes this site especially significant.

In 1955, South Korea's National Assembly resolved to permanently donate this land to the UN in gratitude for the sacrifice of UN forces, and the UN General Assembly decided to manage the cemetery permanently. In 1959, an agreement on the cemetery's establishment and maintenance was signed between South Korea and the UN. So while located in Korea, this is a site with an international management structure unlike a single nation's national cemetery.

When walking the grounds, look first at the row of flags and gravestones. In the symbolic area, the flags of the 22 nations that took part in the Korean War fly alongside South Korea's and the UN's flags, and the graves of fallen soldiers from various countries are arranged in different ways. The "Path of the Unknown Soldier" and the Wall of Remembrance extend the scope of memory to include those whose identities were never confirmed or who aren't buried in the cemetery. Looking closely at a single headstone, a person's age and name come through before the country's name, turning the scale of war into the story of one individual life.

A local guide would say that silence matters more than photographs here. Once you know this, the UN Memorial Cemetery stops looking like a tourist landmark symbolizing international solidarity, and instead carries the far greater weight of being the actual site where fallen soldiers were recovered and buried in 1951 — maintained as an international memorial space to this day.
tipsEn:
Route: Understand the background at the visitor center, then walk quietly through the graves, memorial hall, and memorial space in order.
Photo spot: Capture the neat axis of flags and graves from a distance.
Caution: Avoid eating, loud noise, and playful photography within the burial grounds.

simpleEn: Millak The Market is a complex cultural space in Millak-dong where you enjoy food, shopping, and performances together with an ocean view. From the tiered seating in front of the floor-to-ceiling windows, Gwangan Bridge and Millak Harbor unfold like a stage backdrop. Look, too, at the outdoor raw-fish center and the harbor. A new way of eating and staying has been added inside a neighborhood once centered on the seafood market. Discover a place where an old livelihood and today's lifestyle coexist on the same shoreline.
detailEn:
Millak The Market isn't an old established commercial district like a traditional market — it's a relatively recent complex cultural space showing the new consumer culture of the Millak waterfront and Gwangalli area. Inside a roughly 2,300-pyeong (about 7,600㎡) building, restaurants, cafés, fashion and accessory shops mix with pop-up and performance spaces, and its most famous spot is the "Busking Square," where Gwangan Bridge and Millak Harbor are visible through floor-to-ceiling windows. Sitting on tiered steps, eating or watching a performance while looking out at the sea, captures the character of this space in a nutshell.

What's interesting is the sharp contrast with the old image of neighboring Millak-dong. Millak has long been known for its raw-fish center, seafood market, harbor, and sashimi restaurants — enjoying the sea here traditionally meant "buying raw fish and sitting by the waterfront." Millak The Market uses the same sea as its backdrop, but combines local brands, pop-up stores, busking, and design spaces to turn it into a place for a younger generation to linger and consume. It's fascinating that a seafood-market culture and a lifestyle market coexist within the same neighborhood.

Even the Busking Square's steps aren't simply seating for a crowd. They're designed so that everyone faces the same direction — toward Gwangan Bridge and the sea — even when there's no performance, so the view through the window itself functions like a constant backdrop performance. The layout keeps you feeling Gwangalli's night view and changing weather even while indoors.

A local guide wouldn't stop at calling it "a trendy market," but would point outside to Millak Harbor and the raw-fish center as well. Once you know this, Millak The Market stops looking like a new shopping mall, and instead looks like a present-day scene of Millak-dong — showing how the way Busan people eat, stay, and consume culture at the seaside is expanding from a seafood-market center toward a complex-cultural-space model.
tipsEn:
Route: Browse the shops and event spaces, then enjoy the Gwangalli view from the ocean-facing seats.
Photo spot: A composition with Gwangan Bridge visible through the large window along with the tiered seating works well.
Caution: Check photography rules for each event and the conditions for pet entry.

simpleEn: Ahopsan Forest holds within it about 400 years of one family's private woodland, carefully kept over time. Among the straight-growing bamboo and other trees, you can see the texture of a forest shaped by both nature and generations of care. Rather than just hunting for the film-location marker, feel the gaps where sunlight filters in and the sound of leaves brushing together. Behind the beautiful scenery lies the time of people who tended the trees and kept this forest as their living ground — a story carried into Busan's woods today.
detailEn:
Walking into Ahopsan Forest, the first question that comes to mind is "how did a forest like this survive in Busan?" Visit Busan introduces this forest as private woodland one family has kept for about 400 years. Through Japanese colonial rule, liberation, the Korean War, and industrialization, it was never widely opened or developed, which let the bamboo, Korean red pine, hinoki cypress, and oak forest keep its old form. The name "Ahopsan" is said to come from a native Korean phrase meaning it holds nine valleys.

It's surprisingly recent that this forest became widely known. Its distinctive bamboo groves drew attention after being used as a filming location for the 2014 film Kundo, and in 2016 the family that had long managed the forest opened it to the public, letting visitors enter. That's why the atmosphere differs from a tidy public arboretum. Rather than trees arranged by species for display, the forest keeps the texture of a "living private woodland" — tended by people according to need for a long time, and in part left to nature.

Walking into the bamboo grove, the straight-rising stalks naturally draw your eyes upward. Sunlight filters in through narrow gaps, and when wind blows, the sound of stalks and leaves knocking against each other rings out loudly. Bamboo grows fast, so if left alone the forest's density keeps rising, making proper management necessary. In other words, even this dense, beautiful scenery isn't "nature left completely untouched" — it's the result of generations of care.

A local guide would ask you to think first about the forest's age and how it's been managed, rather than just hunting for the filming-location marker. Once you know this, Ahopsan Forest stops looking like a spot for bamboo photos, and instead looks like a place where one family's centuries of keeping the forest as both asset and living ground remain today as one of Busan's rare private-woodland landscapes.
tipsEn:
Route: Follow the designated loop route from the entrance guide and tour the main bamboo grove section.
Photo spot: The path winding between the straight-rising bamboo stalks works well.
Caution: Don't leave the designated path or pick plants, and watch for slippery ground.

simpleEn: Marine City's skyline of high-rises was built on land expanded by reclaiming part of Suyeong Bay. It's a coastline where the city has pushed outward into the sea, right beside Dongbaekseom Island. After taking in the night lights and their reflection on the water, look too at the coastal seawall and the waves beyond. A city built to live close to the sea also faces the challenge of coping with waves and wind. Behind the glamorous skyline lies Busan's present-day reality of confronting coastal development and nature together.
detailEn:
Marine City's night view is one of Busan's most modern images, but this skyline wasn't built on a coastline that was always there. The Marine City area was developed on reclaimed land in Suyeong Bay. Turning what was once sea into land, then planning ultra-high-rise residential and commercial buildings and roads, created today's straight coastline and high-rise skyline. The sharpest contrast in this area is that artificially expanded land sits right beside the old, natural landform of Dongbaekseom Island.

Looking up at the buildings from the coastal walkway, their height is overwhelming, but from the opposite side, at The Bay 101 or Dongbaekseom, the whole cluster of buildings appears more like a single wall standing on the water. At night, the lights reflect off the water, creating a "doubled city" effect — this is the scene that made Marine City one of Busan's signature night views. But behind the glamorous scenery lies a challenge that comes with building a city so close to the sea.

During typhoons or storm surges, high waves repeatedly overtop the coastal seawall — a problem known as wave overtopping — so the City of Busan is pushing forward projects to reinforce disaster-prevention facilities, including underwater breakwaters, off the coast of Marine City. This shows that even with ultra-high-rise buildings and cutting-edge housing, the waves and wind of the sea right outside can't be fully controlled. This is a place that needs both urban design maximizing closeness to the sea and disaster-prevention technology for safety, at the same time.

A local guide wouldn't stop at the night view and call it "like a city of the future" — they'd point out that the coastline beneath your feet was made by land reclamation, and ask you to look at the waves beyond as well. Once you know this, Marine City stops looking like just a luxury high-rise residential district, and instead looks like an experimental ground for a coastal city — showing, at once, Busan's ambition to expand the city out toward the sea and the ongoing reality of having to keep negotiating with that same sea.
tipsEn:
Route: Slowly take in the skyline from the coastal walkway near Dongbaekseom or Yeonghwa-ui-geori (Movie Street).
Photo spot: A night view with water reflections and high-rises stretching vertically in a row works well.
Caution: Avoid entering roadways or private property, and refrain from coastal walks in strong wind.

simpleEn: Heosimcheong carries forward the long history of Dongnae Hot Spring culture in a large-scale urban rest facility built in 1991. The neighborhood's name, Oncheonjang ("hot spring town"), and the legend of the white crane preserve the region's memory of treasuring this hot spring water. Notice how you move between different baths and rest areas — bathing here isn't just about washing, it unfolds into a leisure culture of resting and lingering. Looking out at the neighborhood too, the old hot spring town connects with modern Busan's culture of rest.
detailEn:
The history of Dongnae Hot Spring runs so deep that the neighborhood where Heosimcheong sits is itself named "Oncheonjang," meaning hot spring town. A legend here tells of a grandmother who couldn't use her legs, who watched an injured crane dip into the hot spring water and fly away, then dipped her own legs in the same water and was healed — the "White Crane Legend." The legend can't be taken as fact, but it shows the local memory that this area's hot spring water was seen as special from a very long time ago.

Heosimcheong opened in 1991, reconstructing this long history of Dongnae Hot Spring culture into a large-scale, urban-style hot spring facility. Official Dongnae-gu materials describe a hot spring bath area of about 4,300㎡, with various types of baths, using naturally sourced hot spring water the facility developed itself. Unlike traditional small bathhouses or inn-style hot springs, applying the concept of an "onsen health land" — where many people bathe, rest, and eat all at once — was a new approach at the time.

Inside, the ceilings are high, the space is wide, and various baths are arranged in different forms. The variety of baths isn't just for fun — in Korean bathing culture, it's common to move between hot baths, lukewarm baths, outdoor baths, and rest areas, lingering a long time. If Dongnae Hot Spring once carried more the character of a hot spring village combining treatment and lodging, Heosimcheong expanded that into a leisure and rest culture within the big city.

A local guide wouldn't emphasize numbers like "the largest in Asia," but would point you toward the Oncheonjang neighborhood outside Heosimcheong as well, since the old hot spring place name, the White Crane Legend, and this modern large-scale bathing facility all overlap in the same living area. Once you know this, Heosimcheong stops looking like just a big jjimjilbang, and instead looks like a place showing how centuries of Dongnae's hot spring culture transformed into a 1990s urban leisure facility.
tipsEn:
Route: Check entry rules, then slowly use the hot bath and rest areas according to your physical condition.
Photo spot: Capture the building's exterior along with the streetscape of Oncheonjang.
Caution: Photography is banned in the baths and changing rooms; avoid using the facility after drinking or when unwell.

simpleEn: The Hoedong Reservoir seen from Oryundae Observatory looks like a natural lake, but it's actually a reservoir built to supply the city with water. The name "Oryundae" carries on from the memory of a scenic valley that existed before the lake was formed. Follow the curving water's edge and the mountainside with your eyes. Remember that beneath the water there were once paths and living spaces too. Discover how an old scenic spot took on a different landscape through the creation of a water-supply reservoir, while keeping its old name.
detailEn:
Hoedong Reservoir, seen from Oryundae Observatory, looks like a natural lake, but the name "Oryundae" existed long before the lake was formed. The 1740 gazetteer Dongnae-bu-ji records that the streams and unusual rock formations of this area were beautiful, and that a person who exemplified "the five relationships" (oryun, Confucian ethical principles) lived nearby, giving the area its name, Oryundae. Another tradition holds that five elders once planted their walking sticks here and enjoyed poetic pursuits — either way, it's clear this was long recognized as a scenic spot.

The view from today's observatory differs considerably from what's described in old records. As Hoedong Reservoir was built, the original valley and stream became a wide reservoir, and some of the surrounding old villages and terrain were submerged or altered. So today's still water surface is both a lake shaped by nature and, at the same time, urban infrastructure built by people to secure Busan's water supply. The name of an old scenic spot has carried on, now sitting atop the scenery of a new artificial lake.

Looking at the curving lines of the water's surface from the observatory, you can somewhat imagine where the mountain valleys once were. The way the water reaches deep between the mountains follows the shape of the original valley, since the reservoir was built along it. Looking together at Ahopsan and Ttangmoesan mountains on the opposite side and Oryun-dong village, you can see that Hoedong Reservoir isn't just "one lake" but a structure where mountain, village, and water supply are intertwined in a single space.

A local guide wouldn't just say the view is pretty, but would mention that "beneath the water you're looking at now, there were once roads and living spaces too." Once you know this, Oryundae Observatory stops looking like a viewpoint for photographing Hoedong Reservoir, and instead looks like a place to see, at a glance, how a scenic spot renowned since the Joseon dynasty took on an entirely different landscape through the development of Busan's water supply.
tipsEn:
Route: Walk slowly up from the entrance to the observatory and take in the view in each direction over the reservoir.
Photo spot: From the observatory, widely capture the reservoir's curving shoreline and the mountain ridges.
Caution: Watch for slippery surfaces near the railing after rain, and follow any restricted-area guidance.

simpleEn: Gwangalli Beach transformed into an urban beach people linger at day and night after Gwangan Bridge opened. A bridge built for transportation now creates scenery with its lights at night, while the beach itself brings together walking, performances, dining, and travel. Compare the same spot in the morning and evening. Walk toward Millak's harbor or Namcheon's residential area, and the crowd and atmosphere change too. A city's daily life and Busan's nighttime tourism meet on this one beach.
detailEn:
Gwangalli Beach is best known today for Gwangan Bridge's night view and drone shows, but this image was largely built up from the 2000s onward. In the past, Gwangalli was a beach centered on summer swimming and the surrounding residential and commercial district; once Gwangan Bridge opened in 2003, a massive urban structure appeared in the middle of the sea. Afterward, the bridge's lighting combined with beachside cafés, restaurants, and various performances, and Gwangalli's character shifted dramatically from "a daytime beach" to "an urban beach people linger at even at night."

Standing on the sand, Gwangan Bridge looks so large it becomes familiar like natural scenery, but it's actually a transportation facility crossing Suyeong Bay to connect several living areas. By day it's a functional road for vehicles; by night it becomes the lit backdrop for the entire beach. During the Busan Fireworks Festival, the bridge itself becomes a stage for fireworks displays, and more recently, regular drone light shows held on the beach have extended the performance space up into the sky. It's a case where infrastructure and tourism content have reinforced each other.

What's interesting about Gwangalli is how travelers and residents mix in their use of the beach. In the morning, it's exercise and walking; during the day, the beach and cafés; in the evening, busking, dining, night views, and performances — the same place's role shifts by time of day. Walking toward Millak, the seafood market and harbor culture continue; toward Namcheon, the everyday feel of a residential area grows stronger — so many different faces of Busan appear even within one beach.

A local guide would suggest comparing the same spot in the morning and at night, rather than settling for one photo facing Gwangan Bridge. Once you know this, Gwangalli Beach stops looking like a simple swimming beach, and instead looks like "a living-room-like beach for the city" — where Busan's nighttime tourism and performance culture overlap most vividly with citizens' daily life, ever since Gwangan Bridge opened.
tipsEn:
Route: Walk along the beach, then enjoy the bridge's lighting from the sand or a café around sunset.
Photo spot: From the center of the beach, capture the whole of Gwangan Bridge together with its reflection on the water.
Caution: Check swimming zones and wave conditions, and follow event control lines.

simpleEn: From the Eco-friendly Skyway Observatory, you look down over Choryang's hillside homes, the North Port, and the old downtown. This terrain preserves the daily life of refugees and laborers who worked below at the port and station, yet built their homes high on the hillside. Walk part of Ibagu-gil, then stand on the deck. The slope of the stairs you climbed connects with the harbor spread out before you. Feel, through height and view, how the paths of hillside residents became a travel route on Busan's sanbokdoro (hillside road).
detailEn:
The Eco-friendly Skyway Observatory sits at the high end of Choryang's Ibagu-gil, looking down over Busan Port and the old downtown. Despite the name "Skyway," it isn't a massive tourist facility so much as a small deck-style observatory built as both a rest spot for hillside residents and a viewing route for travelers. Climbing the stairs and alleys of Ibagu-gil and standing here, Busan Port Bridge, the North Port, Sinseondae Pier, Yeongdo, and even Nampo-dong and Jagalchi come into a single view, making it clear why the sanbokdoro is like "the city's balcony."

What matters most is the path before you reach the observatory. Choryang's sanbokdoro is a living area formed after the Korean War, as refugees and laborers built homes on the hillside. Workplaces and markets were down below, near the port and Busan Station, while homes climbed the steep slope, so stairs and winding alleys became the daily commuting route. Today's observatory is close to the result of urban regeneration — reconnecting that once-hard living terrain into a route travelers can walk and understand.

The observatory's eco-friendly deck and the surrounding healing forest path are devices that insert greenery between the old downtown's concrete and harbor scenery, giving even residents a place to rest. Looking at the massive North Port development and container docks below, then at the hillside homes and forest right next to it, you can see just how closely Busan has grown its port industry and residential living side by side.

A local guide would suggest walking part of Ibagu-gil rather than taking a taxi straight up. Once you know this, the Eco-friendly Skyway Observatory stops looking like a high deck for night-view photos, and instead looks like the final panel of the sanbokdoro's story — explaining, through the height and view of your own walk, how the city that began at Busan Station and the port climbed all the way up the hillside.
tipsEn:
Route: Connect with the stair sections of Ibagu-gil, rest at the observatory, then briefly tour the surrounding alleys.
Photo spot: The scene where the observatory's structure frames Busan Port and rooftops overlapping works well.
Caution: Avoid photographing residents' windows and watch for stairs and vehicle traffic.

simpleEn: Songdo Beach is recorded as Korea's first public beach, developed in 1913. It preserves the moment when the sea began to be used not just for livelihood and transport, but as a place to rest and enjoy. The rest enjoyed during the refugee period and the old amusement-park facilities carry forward into today's cable car and Cloud Walk. From the sand, look out at Turtle Island and the facilities built over the water. See the long thread of Busan tourism, reinventing the same beach anew in each era.
detailEn:
Songdo Beach is more than just "an old Busan beach" — it's recorded as Korea's first public beach. According to Busan City's future-heritage records, it was developed into a beach in 1913 when Songdo Yuwon (Songdo Resort) was built, and the name "Songdo" ("Pine Island") comes from the dense pine trees on Turtle Island and the surrounding hills. It's a place that shows the early stage of using the sea, in the modern era, not just for livelihood and transportation but as a leisure space for swimming and resting.

During the Korean War, its meaning was even more special. Busan City records that for refugees and citizens who poured into Busan, Songdo served as a kind of "liberated zone," a brief escape from the tension of war and the hardship of refugee life. Afterward, in the 1960s–70s, very novel amusement facilities for the time — a cable car, a suspension bridge, and a diving platform — were built, turning it into a nationally known tourist destination. That's why old family photos of Songdo tend to show so many amusement facilities and crowds.

Over time, some of the old facilities disappeared and the beach's popularity shifted, but recently the cable car and Cloud Walk have returned, modernly recreating the old memory of "tourism enjoyed over the water." The new cable car isn't identical to the old facilities, but the continuity remains — Songdo has been a place offering new ways to experience the sea for over 100 years.

A local guide would ask you to remember the number "1913" before even looking at the sand. Once you know this, Songdo Beach stops looking like just a pretty beach with a cable car, and instead looks like a 100-year timeline of Busan tourism — where the start of modern beach culture, wartime refugee rest, 1960s–70s amusement-park culture, and today's marine tourism have kept layering on the same beach.
tipsEn:
Route: Walk the sand, cross the Cloud Walk, then continue on to the cable car or the coastal park.
Photo spot: Capture the cable car passing over the sea from the beach.
Caution: Check swimming zones and wave conditions, and don't run on the wet deck.

simpleEn: Taejongdae Hot Spring Jjimjilbang is a place to bathe and rest after walking Yeongdo's cliffs and forest trails. Beyond the sea wind and slopes outside, the warm baths, sauna rooms, and lounge inside shift the pace of your trip. Notice the difference between rushing out right after washing and choosing to rest and linger. On Yeongdo, where itineraries involve a lot of walking, bathing becomes leisure that lets you set down the day's fatigue. A trip focused on nature meets everyday rest culture along the same route.
detailEn:
Taejongdae Hot Spring Jjimjilbang isn't known as the star attraction of Taejongdae tourism, but it fits quite naturally into the Yeongdo-style travel route of resting your body after a full day of walking cliffs and forest trails. Close to the Taejongdae entrance, you can go straight from touring the Danubi Train, lighthouse, and pebble beach into a hot spring and sauna. It's essentially a space that follows "sightseeing tourism" of coastal scenery with Korean-style bathing and rest.

Public tourism information describes the hot spring water here as saline hot spring water with a relatively high mineral content. The facility offers various hot spring baths, outdoor baths, a jjimjilbang, and lounge areas. Rather than expecting medicinal effects from the hot spring, it's more interesting to experience how Koreans use bathing as leisure. Soaking in hot water, then resting in the sauna area, eating, or lying down for a while, is a different kind of culture from bathing where you wash and leave right away.

The contrast with Taejongdae itself is also interesting. Outside, you feel the sea wind, slopes, waves, and cliffs with your whole body; inside, warm water and indoor rest completely change the pace of your trip. Yeongdo especially has a lot of elevation change between mountain and sea, so itineraries involve a lot of walking, making a bathing facility feel less like a mere convenience and more like a living-culture space that relieves travel fatigue.

A local guide wouldn't oversell this place as a special historic site. Instead, they'd explain why even Busan locals who've visited Taejongdae naturally fit bathing and sauna into the end of a day's itinerary. Once you know this, Taejongdae Hot Spring Jjimjilbang stops looking like "just a sauna next to a tourist site," and instead looks like Yeongdo's living-culture wellness space — connecting nature tourism and Korea's communal bathing and rest culture along a single route.
tipsEn:
Route: After entering, check the usage rules, then use the bath, sauna, and rest areas in order without overexertion.
Photo spot: Capture the outdoor signage together with the surrounding Taejongdae scenery.
Caution: Photography is banned in the baths and changing areas; follow bathing etiquette and safety rules.

simpleEn: Nurimaru APEC House means "the house where the world's leaders gather at the summit." In this space where the 2005 APEC meeting was held, traces of that moment remain — including the desks and chairs actually used at the time. After taking in the sea, look at the round roof and the diagonal columns too. Starting from a traditional pavilion, the building's design captures Dongbaekseom's ridge line and Busan's dynamic energy. It's a place connecting Korean form, modern technology, and coastal scenery into a stage for international diplomacy.
detailEn:
Even the name Nurimaru APEC House is a piece of explanation in itself. "Nuri" means "world" and "maru" means "summit" or "peak" in native Korean, combined with "APEC House" to mean "the house where the world's leaders gather to meet." On November 19, 2005, leaders from the 21 member economies of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum actually held their second summit session and a luncheon here. Today's image as a tourist landmark grew directly out of opening that very site of international diplomacy to the public.

The exterior looks like a modern glass building, but its design started from a traditional Korean pavilion. According to the City of Busan's official explanation, the round roof represents the ridge line of Dongbaekseom Island, and the 12 diagonal columns outside express Busan's dynamic energy. Inside, traditional dancheong colors, patterns, and elements like Hunminjeongeum (the Korean alphabet) are used in modern form. The building embeds, at once, its international function as a world summit venue and its identity as "a meeting held in Korea."

On the third floor, the summit meeting room preserves, close to their original state, the desks, chairs, microphones, nameplates, and carpet used by the leaders at the time. Beyond the room's windows, Gwangan Bridge and Suyeong Bay open up dramatically. It's striking that the diplomatic event wasn't confined indoors — Busan's sea and cityscape themselves became the backdrop for the international meeting. Major results, including the "Busan Declaration," were announced at the 2005 meeting.

A local guide would suggest photographing the building with Gwangan Bridge behind you, then looking again at the shape of the roof and columns. Once you know this, Nurimaru stops looking like just a conference room with a nice view, and instead looks like the place where Busan showcased its image as an international conference city through the 2005 APEC meeting — staging traditional architecture, modern technology, and coastal scenery together as a single diplomatic stage.
tipsEn:
Route: View the exhibits inside the meeting room, then continue on to the outdoor deck and the Dongbaekseom coastal path.
Photo spot: A point where Gwangan Bridge and the sea appear beyond the building's curves works well.
Caution: Follow photography guidelines for exhibits and restricted areas in the meeting room.

simpleEn: The name Gwangbok-ro Fashion Street carries both the joy of liberation and the modern history of Busan's old downtown. Part of the road was built by covering over a stream, and it has become a commercial strip of fashion stores, cafés, and passersby. While shopping, notice the width of the street and the alleys leading off to Gukje Market. Old shops, new brands, and seasonal lighting all shift the street's mood with the times. Walk it and read how a waterway became one of Busan's shopping streets.
detailEn:
The name Gwangbok-ro Fashion Street carries the modern history of Busan's old downtown right in its name. This area near the sea was the center of colonial-era Busan under Japanese rule, and after liberation, Busan residents named the neighborhood "Gwangbok-dong," carrying the joy of liberation and the memory of resistance against Japanese rule. Today's name, Gwangbok-ro, continues from that. This is why tourism sources like Busan On and Visit Busan begin explanations of this street by pointing to the word "gwangbok" (liberation).

Another interesting fact is that part of today's wide road was built by covering over a stream that once flowed here. Fashion stores and cafés now line both sides densely, but tracing the city's terrain back reveals that a waterway became a commercial strip where people and goods now move. In old cities, traces of the original landform are often hidden this way in the shape of roads and alleys.

Gwangbok-ro has long been called Busan's "number one fashion district." Commercial facilities like the old Miwha Department Store gathered together with clothing, shoe, eyewear, and cosmetics shops, and connected with the nearby Gukje Market, BIFF Square, and Nampo-dong commercial district, it grew into one of Busan's busiest shopping streets. Today, large brands, curated boutiques, and old shops mix together, showing how the old downtown's commercial district has changed its business mix to survive across different eras.

In winter, the whole street turns into lights and Christmas trees, which shows off Gwangbok-ro's character of "using the street itself as a stage." A local guide wouldn't just have you look into shopping bags, but would point out the street's name, its width, and the alleys branching off toward Gukje Market. Once you know this, Gwangbok-ro Fashion Street stops looking like a simple shopping street, and instead becomes a street you read while walking — one where the center of a colonial port city took on the name of liberation, and a road built over a stream became the leading commercial strip of Busan's old downtown.
tipsEn:
Route: From the Gwangbok-ro entrance, connect the Yongdusan Park escalator with the direction toward BIFF Square.
Photo spot: A central composition showing the street decorations together with Busan Tower works well.
Caution: Watch for delivery vehicles and event structures even on the pedestrian street.
